Less work has been performed on using neural networks to process floating point numbers and it is sometimes stated that neural networks are somehow inherently inaccu(cid:173) rate and therefore best suited for "fuzzy" qualitative reasoning. Nevertheless, the potential speed of massively parallel operations make neural net "number crunching" an interesting topic to explore. In this paper we discuss some of our work in which we demonstrate that for certain applications neural networks can achieve significantly higher numerical accuracy than more conventional tech(cid:173) niques. paragraphs: The paper examines neural networks as tools for accurate numerical computation. It challenges the view that their main strength must be approximate qualitative reasoning by presenting applications in which their numerical accuracy exceeds that of conventional techniques. Prediction of future values in a chaotic time series is a central example.

To explain this behavior, the authors analyze networks geometrically as function approximators. They show that a large class of mappings between real-valued vector spaces can be accurately approximated by a backpropagation network with two hidden layers. The learned mapping provides a mathematical account of how a network transforms inputs into outputs.

The paper interprets signal-processing applications through interpolation and symbol-processing applications through extrapolation. This connects apparently different uses of neural networks to familiar operations on an approximated function. The stated accuracy results concern particular applications, while the broader contribution is an explanatory framework: network behavior can be understood through the geometry of the functions it represents and its relationship to established function-approximation methods.
summary.tldr: The paper explains accurate neural computation through function approximation, including two-hidden-layer networks and chaotic time-series prediction.

title: How Neural Nets Work

paragraphs: This paper introduces a training method for situations in which an expert chooses among several alternatives. Each training input contains two alternatives, and the target output says which one the expert prefers. The network learns through comparisons, using the expert's relative judgments as its teaching signal.

The authors apply this approach to backgammon, where a player must select a move from the available legal moves. Comparing alternatives makes the learning task closely match the decision being demonstrated: determining which option is better. It also provides a way to learn preferences without requiring the expert to supply an absolute numerical value for each option.

The abstract reports much higher performance with smaller networks and simpler, more understandable coding schemes. It also states that the network can be arranged to always produce consistent rankings. This matters because individual pairwise judgments need to fit together when choosing from a larger set. The contribution therefore concerns both learning expert preferences efficiently and organizing those preferences into coherent orderings.
summary.tldr: Training on expert comparisons improves backgammon move selection while enabling smaller networks, simpler representations, and consistent rankings.

title: Connectionist Learning of Expert Preferences by Comparison Training

Questions such as how many training patterns and training cycles are needed for a problem of a given size and difficulty, how to represent the inllUh and how to choose useful training exemplars, are of considerable theoretical and practical importance. Several intuitive rules of thumb have been obtained from empirical studies, but as yet there are few rig(cid:173) orous results. In this paper we summarize a study Qf generalization in the simplest possible case-perceptron networks learning linearly separa(cid:173) ble functions. The task chosen was the majority function (i.e. return a 1 if a majority of the input units are on), a predicate with a num(cid:173) ber of useful properties. We find that many aspects of.generalization in multilayer networks learning large, difficult tasks are reproduced in this simple domain, in which concrete numerical results and even some analytic understanding can be achieved.

paragraphs: The paper studies how neural networks generalize from examples by choosing a deliberately simple learning problem. It considers perceptrons learning linearly separable functions, focusing on the majority function: the output is one when more than half of the inputs are on. This creates a tractable setting for examining questions that arise in larger learning systems.

The motivating questions include how many examples and training cycles a task needs, how inputs should be represented, and which training examples are useful. The authors note that practical rules of thumb exist but rigorous results are scarce. Their case study seeks concrete numerical evidence and some analytical understanding within a problem simple enough to examine closely.

They find that many aspects of generalization seen in multilayer networks on large, difficult tasks also appear in this simpler domain. That makes the majority-function setting informative beyond its immediate task. The contribution is a manageable case study that reproduces broader learning phenomena and gives those phenomena a setting where more precise analysis is possible.
summary.tldr: Perceptrons learning the majority function reproduce several generalization phenomena associated with larger networks while allowing more concrete analysis.

title: Scaling and Generalization in Neural Networks: A Case Study

paragraphs: This paper describes a method for soft classification: estimating the probability of a binary outcome from an attribute vector. The model learns a real-valued function and passes it through a logistic transformation to obtain a probability. This makes the output a graded estimate of an outcome's likelihood rather than only a category assignment.

The learned function has a structured decomposition using smoothing spline analysis of variance. It combines smooth effects of individual attributes, smooth interactions between pairs of attributes, and potentially higher-order interactions. This organization connects the probability estimate to both separate attribute effects and the ways attributes act together.

Training uses penalized log likelihood, with smoothing parameters selected through iterative unbiased risk estimation or iterative generalized cross-validation. Those parameters control how flexibly the component functions follow the training data, making them central to the bias-variance tradeoff. Confidence intervals are also available for the estimates. The resulting framework combines probabilistic prediction, an explicit interaction structure, and uncertainty estimates, with medical risk-factor analysis serving as a motivating setting.
summary.tldr: Smoothing spline ANOVA estimates binary-outcome probabilities through smooth attribute effects and interactions, with tuned regularization and confidence intervals.

title: Structured Machine Learning for 'Soft' Classification with Smoothing Spline ANOVA and Stacked Tuning, Testing and Evaluation

abstract: In consideration of attention as a means for goal-directed behav(cid:173) ior in non-stationary environments, we argue that the dynamics of attention should satisfy two opposing demands: long-term main(cid:173) tenance and quick transition. These two characteristics are con(cid:173) tradictory within the linear domain. We propose the near saddle(cid:173) node bifurcation behavior of a sigmoidal unit with self-connection as a candidate of dynamical mechanism that satisfies both of these demands. We further show in simulations of the 'bug-eat-food' tasks that the near saddle-node bifurcation behavior of recurrent networks can emerge as a functional property for survival in non(cid:173) stationary environments.

We propose the near saddle(cid:173) node bifurcation behavior of a sigmoidal unit with self-connection as a candidate of dynamical mechanism that satisfies both of these demands. paragraphs: Goal-directed attention needs to persist long enough to support an activity while remaining able to shift quickly when circumstances change. This paper frames those requirements as a dynamical problem. The authors argue that long maintenance and rapid transition impose conflicting demands within linear dynamics, motivating a nonlinear mechanism.

Their proposed mechanism is a sigmoid unit that feeds its output back into itself and operates near a saddle-node bifurcation. A bifurcation marks a qualitative change in a system's dynamics. Operating near this transition provides a candidate way for the same unit to support both sustained attention and quick switching.

The authors also examine recurrent networks in simulated bug-eat-food tasks set in changing environments. They show that behavior near a saddle-node bifurcation can emerge as a functional property supporting survival. This links the proposed mechanism to the demands of acting in an environment: the relevant dynamics arise in networks facing a need to maintain useful behavior while responding to change.
summary.tldr: Dynamics near a saddle-node bifurcation offer a mechanism for attention that both persists and switches rapidly.

title: Dynamics of Attention as Near Saddle-Node Bifurcation Behavior

The task is framed as an optimal control problem in which both comfort and energy costs are considered as part of the con(cid:173) trol objective. Because the consequences of control decisions are delayed in time, the N eurothermostat must anticipate heating de(cid:173) mands with predictive models of occupancy patterns and the ther(cid:173) mal response of the house and furnace. Occupancy pattern predic(cid:173) tion is achieved by a hybrid neural net / look-up table. The first decision in this sequence is taken, and this pro(cid:173) cess repeats. paragraphs: The Neurothermostat controls residential heating by deciding when to switch a furnace on or off. Its objective combines occupant comfort with energy cost. Because heating decisions have delayed effects, the controller must anticipate demand using predictions of occupancy and of how the house and furnace respond thermally.

Occupancy prediction combines a neural network with a lookup table. At each decision time, the controller searches for a sequence of furnace actions that minimizes expected cost over a fixed future horizon. It executes the first action and then repeats the search, continually updating its plan rather than committing to the entire sequence at once.

The authors test the controller in simulations using artificial occupancy patterns with varied regularity and occupancy data from a real residence. It achieves consistently lower costs than three conventional policies. The advantage persists across different comfort-versus-energy weightings and levels of occupancy variability. These findings support predictive control that learns household patterns and uses them to coordinate heating with expected need.
summary.tldr: The Neurothermostat predicts occupancy and thermal behavior to reduce combined comfort and energy costs in heating simulations.

title: The Neurothermostat: Predictive Optimal Control of Residential Heating Systems

abstract: We present a new approximate learning algorithm for Boltzmann Machines, using a systematic expansion of the Gibbs free energy to second order in the weights. The linear response correction to the correlations is given by the Hessian of the Gibbs free energy. The computational complexity of the algorithm is cubic in the number of neurons. We compare the performance of the exact BM learning algorithm with first order (Weiss) mean field theory and second order (TAP) mean field theory. The learning task consists of a fully connected Ising spin glass model on 10 neurons. We conclude that 1) the method works well for paramagnetic problems 2) the TAP correction gives a significant improvement over the Weiss mean field theory, both for paramagnetic and spin glass problems and 3) that the inclusion of diagonal weights improves the Weiss approximation for paramagnetic problems , but not for spin glass problems.

paragraphs: This paper develops an approximate learning algorithm for Boltzmann machines using a second-order expansion of Gibbs free energy in the connection weights. It combines mean-field approximation with a linear-response correction to correlations. That correction comes from the Hessian of the free energy, a description of its curvature. The resulting computational cost grows cubically with the number of neurons.

The evaluation uses a fully connected, ten-neuron Ising spin-glass learning task. The authors compare exact Boltzmann-machine learning with first-order Weiss mean-field theory and second-order TAP mean-field theory. This comparison tests whether retaining the additional second-order terms improves the approximation used during learning.

The reported method works well for paramagnetic problems, and the TAP correction substantially improves on Weiss theory for both paramagnetic and spin-glass problems. Adding diagonal weights also improves the Weiss approximation in paramagnetic cases, but not in spin-glass cases. These findings distinguish two proposed improvements: the second-order correction helps across both regimes tested, while the benefit of diagonal weights depends on the regime.
summary.tldr: Second-order mean-field corrections improve approximate Boltzmann-machine learning, with cubic computational cost in the number of neurons.

title: Boltzmann Machine Learning Using Mean Field Theory and Linear Response Correction

abstract: We apply information maximization / maximum likelihood blind source separation [2, 6) to complex valued signals mixed with com(cid:173) plex valued nonstationary matrices. This case arises in radio com(cid:173) munications with baseband signals. We incorporate known source signal distributions in the adaptation, thus making the algorithms less "blind". This results in drastic reduction of the amount of data needed for successful convergence. Adaptation to rapidly changing signal mixing conditions, such as to fading in mobile communica(cid:173) tions, becomes now feasible as demonstrated by simulations.

paragraphs: The paper addresses separating radio signals when the received measurements contain mixtures that change over time. Both the signals and the matrices describing their mixtures are complex valued, as occurs with baseband radio signals. The changing mixture is especially important: a separation method must adapt before its description of the channel becomes outdated.

The authors apply blind source separation based on information maximization or maximum likelihood. They modify the adaptation process to incorporate known probability distributions of the source signals. This makes the method less blind, because it uses information about what the sources should statistically look like even while working to recover them from their mixtures.

Using that prior knowledge substantially reduces the amount of data needed for convergence, according to the abstract. Simulations demonstrate that the resulting adaptation can handle rapidly changing mixing conditions, including fading in mobile communications. The contribution is therefore not just separating complex signals, but making separation responsive enough to track a moving statistical target.
summary.tldr: Using known source distributions helps blind radio-signal separation adapt with less data to rapidly changing channels.

title: Blind Separation of Radio Signals in Fading Channels

abstract: Recently, a number of authors have proposed treating dialogue systems as Markov decision processes (MDPs). However, the practical application ofMDP algorithms to dialogue systems faces a number of severe technical challenges. We have built a general software tool (RLDS, for Reinforcement Learning for Dialogue Systems) based on the MDP framework, and have applied it to dialogue corpora gathered from two dialogue systems built at AT&T Labs. Our experiments demonstrate that RLDS holds promise as a tool for "browsing" and understanding correlations in complex, temporally dependent dialogue corpora.

However, the practical application ofMDP algorithms to dialogue systems faces a number of severe technical challenges. paragraphs: This paper explores the practical use of reinforcement learning in spoken dialogue systems through a software tool called RLDS. The tool uses a Markov decision process framework, which treats dialogue as a sequence of states and decisions. The authors place the work in the context of substantial technical challenges in applying that framework to real dialogue systems.

They apply RLDS to dialogue corpora collected from two systems built at AT&T Labs. The data contain temporally dependent interactions, so understanding a conversation requires attending to relationships across its sequence. The tool brings the MDP framework to those recorded dialogues as a way to explore their structure.

The experiments indicate promise for browsing complex dialogue corpora and understanding correlations within them. This is the stated practical finding: RLDS can help investigate how aspects of dialogue relate over time. The contribution therefore includes a general software tool and an empirical demonstration of its potential for analysis, with the reported outcome centered on understanding dialogue data.
summary.tldr: RLDS applies an MDP framework to recorded dialogues and shows promise for exploring correlations across conversation sequences.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Spoken Dialogue Systems

abstract: We establish a new hardness result that shows that the difﬁculty of plan- ning in factored Markov decision processes is representational rather than just computational. More precisely, we give a ﬁxed family of fac- tored MDPs with linear rewards whose optimal policies and value func- tions simply cannot be represented succinctly in any standard parametric form. Previous hardness results indicated that computing good policies from the MDP parameters was difﬁcult, but left open the possibility of succinct function approximation for any ﬁxed factored MDP. Our result applies even to policies which yield a polynomially poor approximation to the optimal value, and highlights interesting connectionswith the com- plexity class of Arthur-Merlin games.

More precisely, we give a ﬁxed family of fac- tored MDPs with linear rewards whose optimal policies and value func- tions simply cannot be represented succinctly in any standard parametric form. Previous hardness results indicated that computing good policies from the MDP parameters was difﬁcult, but left open the possibility of succinct function approximation for any ﬁxed factored MDP. Our result applies even to policies which yield a polynomially poor approximation to the optimal value, and highlights interesting connectionswith the com- plexity class of Arthur-Merlin games.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether compact descriptions of a decision problem also permit compact descriptions of its solutions. Its setting is factored Markov decision processes, where the dynamics have a structured representation. The central distinction is between the difficulty of computing a policy and the difficulty of representing that policy once it has been found.

The authors establish a hardness result using a fixed family of factored problems with linear rewards. For this family, optimal policies and value functions cannot be represented succinctly in standard parametric forms. Thus, a compact account of how the system changes and assigns rewards does not guarantee an equally compact account of how to act or what outcomes are worth.

Earlier computational hardness results left open the possibility that compact solutions existed but were difficult to discover. This result addresses that possibility directly. It also extends to policies providing even a polynomially poor approximation to optimal value and identifies connections to Arthur–Merlin complexity. The implication concerns the constructed family: choosing a function approximator can encounter a representational obstacle before optimization even begins.
summary.tldr: A hardness result shows that some compactly described factored decision problems lack compact policy and value representations, even for weak approximations.

title: A Note on the Representational Incompatibility of Function Approximation and Factored Dynamics

abstract: We have constructed a second generation CPG chip capable of generating the necessary timing to control the leg of a walking machine. We demonstrate improvements over a previous chip by moving toward a significantly more versatile device. This includes a larger number of silicon neurons, more sophisticated neurons including voltage dependent charging and relative and absolute refractory periods, and enhanced programmability of neural networks. This chip builds on the basic results achieved on a previous chip and expands its versatility to get closer to a self-contained locomotion controller for walking robots. 1
originalAbstract: We have constructed a second generation CPG chip capable of generating the necessary timing to control the leg of a walking machine. We demonstrate improvements over a previous chip by moving toward a significantly more versatile device. This includes a larger number of silicon neurons, more sophisticated neurons including voltage dependent charging and relative and absolute refractory periods, and enhanced programmability of neural networks. This chip builds on the basic results achieved on a previous chip and expands its versatility to get closer to a self-contained locomotion controller for walking robots. 1

paragraphs: This paper presents a second-generation central pattern generator chip that can produce the timing needed to control a walking machine’s leg. The focus is on implementing the neural timing component in silicon and making it more versatile than the authors’ previous chip. Such timing is a component of organizing leg movement during walking.

The new device contains more silicon neurons and uses more sophisticated neuron models. These include voltage-dependent charging as well as relative and absolute refractory periods, features that affect how a neuron responds over time. The chip also provides enhanced programmability of its neural networks, broadening the configurations available within the device.

The authors describe these changes as improvements over the earlier chip and as progress toward a self-contained locomotion controller. The distinction matters: the demonstrated contribution is a more capable timing-generating device, with greater neural complexity and programmability. A fully self-contained walking controller remains the direction of development described in the abstract, rather than the completed outcome claimed for this chip.
summary.tldr: A second-generation silicon pattern-generator chip adds richer neurons and programmability, advancing timing control for robotic legs toward a self-contained locomotion controller.

title: Entrainment of Silicon Central Pattern Generators for Legged Locomotory Control

abstract: We present a graphical model for beat tracking in recorded music. Using a probabilistic graphical model allows us to incorporate local information and global smoothness constraints in a principled manner. We evaluate our model on a set of varied and difficult examples, and achieve impres- sive results. By using a fast dual-tree algorithm for graphical model in- ference, our system runs in less time than the duration of the music being processed.
originalAbstract: We present a graphical model for beat tracking in recorded music. Using a probabilistic graphical model allows us to incorporate local information and global smoothness constraints in a principled manner. We evaluate our model on a set of varied and difficult examples, and achieve impres- sive results. By using a fast dual-tree algorithm for graphical model in- ference, our system runs in less time than the duration of the music being processed.

paragraphs: The paper presents a probabilistic graphical model for tracking beats in recorded music. The task requires relating evidence at particular moments to a beat pattern extending across the recording. The authors organize these two sources of information within one model, combining local observations with constraints that encourage global smoothness.

This combination matters because a beat estimate is part of a sequence, so its interpretation depends on more than the information at a single instant. The graphical model provides a principled way to express how local evidence and sequence-wide regularity should interact. The approach therefore connects individual timing decisions to the overall structure of the estimated beat sequence.

The authors evaluate the model on varied, difficult musical examples and describe the results as impressive. They also address computational speed by using a fast dual-tree inference algorithm. The resulting system processes a recording in less time than the recording's duration, demonstrating that the probabilistic approach can operate efficiently in the reported setting.
summary.tldr: A graphical model combines local musical evidence with global smoothness to track beats faster than the duration of the processed recording.

title: Beat Tracking the Graphical Model Way

abstract: Two neural networks that are trained on their mutual output synchronize to an identical time dependant weight vector. This novel phenomenon can be used for creation of a secure cryptographic secret-key using a public channel. Several models for this cryptographic system have been suggested, and have been tested for their security under different sophis- ticated attack strategies. The most promising models are networks that involve chaos synchronization. The synchronization process of mutual learning is described analytically using statistical physics methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies a synchronization phenomenon in two neural networks trained using each other's outputs. Through mutual learning, the networks reach an identical weight vector that continues to change over time. Their shared evolving internal state is the central phenomenon on which the proposed application depends.

The authors connect this behavior to creating a cryptographic secret key through a public communication channel. Several models of such a system have been proposed and examined under sophisticated attack strategies. The abstract identifies models involving chaos synchronization as the most promising among those considered, making the security investigation part of the comparison between constructions.

The paper also uses methods from statistical physics to describe mutual-learning synchronization analytically. This supplies a theoretical account alongside the cryptographic application and attack testing. The stated promise is that synchronization can support secret-key creation; the reported examination of attacks should be read as evidence about the studied models, rather than an unrestricted guarantee against every possible attack.
summary.tldr: Mutually learning neural networks synchronize their weights, supporting proposed secret-key systems examined through attack testing and statistical-physics analysis.

title: Synchronization of neural networks by mutual learning and its application to cryptography

abstract: We propose efﬁcient algorithms for learning ranking functions from or- der constraints between sets—i.e. classes—of training samples. Our al- gorithms may be used for maximizing the generalized Wilcoxon Mann Whitney statistic that accounts for the partial ordering of the classes: spe- cial cases include maximizing the area under the ROC curve for binary classiﬁcation and its generalization for ordinal regression. Experiments on public benchmarks indicate that: (a) the proposed algorithm is at least as accurate as the current state-of-the-art; (b) computationally, it is sev- eral orders of magnitude faster and—unlike current methods—it is easily able to handle even large datasets with over 20,000 samples.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a ranking from ordering constraints between groups of training examples. These groups act as classes, and the constraints can specify a partial ordering rather than requiring every class to be ordered against every other. The goal is a ranking function that respects the comparisons supplied by this structure.

The proposed algorithms can maximize a generalized Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney statistic that accounts for the class ordering. This connects the method to familiar ranking objectives: maximizing area under the ROC curve in binary classification is one special case, and an extension for ordinal regression is another. The same formulation therefore covers several related ways to judge ordering quality.

On public benchmarks, the authors report accuracy at least comparable to the then-current state of the art, alongside computation that is several orders of magnitude faster. They also report handling datasets with more than 20,000 examples. These experimental findings support the method's practical appeal for larger ranking problems, while the relative accuracy and speed claims refer to the comparisons performed.
summary.tldr: Efficient ranking algorithms handle partially ordered classes and show competitive accuracy with major speed gains on public benchmarks.

title: Learning Rankings via Convex Hull Separation

abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of finding sets of points that conform to a given underlying model from within a dense, noisy set of observations. This problem is motivated by the task of efficiently linking faint asteroid detections, but is applicable to a range of spatial queries. We survey current tree-based approaches, showing a trade-off exists between single tree and multiple tree algorithms. To this end, we present a new type of multiple tree algorithm that uses a variable number of trees to exploit the advantages of both approaches. We empirically show that this algorithm performs well using both simulated and astronomical data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to find groups of observed points that fit an underlying model when the observations are dense and noisy. Its motivating application is linking faint asteroid detections. The broader computational problem is to identify compatible sets of points efficiently within a collection containing many observations that need not belong together.

The authors survey tree-based search approaches and identify a trade-off between algorithms using a single tree and those using multiple trees. They then introduce a multiple-tree algorithm that uses a variable number of trees. This variable choice is intended to exploit advantages from both existing approaches within one search method.

Experiments on simulated and astronomical data show that the proposed algorithm performs well. The use of both kinds of data connects the algorithmic idea to its motivating application while also testing it on constructed observations. The contribution is an adaptable tree-based search strategy for model-consistent point sets, with potential applicability to a range of spatial queries.
summary.tldr: A spatial-search algorithm varies its number of trees to combine advantages of single-tree and multiple-tree methods.

title: Variable KD-Tree Algorithms for Spatial Pattern Search and Discovery

abstract: Go is an ancient board game that poses unique opportunities and challenges for AI and machine learning. Here we develop a machine learning approach to Go, and related board games, focusing primarily on the problem of learning a good eval- uation function in a scalable way. Scalability is essential at multiple levels, from the library of local tactical patterns, to the integration of patterns across the board, to the size of the board itself. The system we propose is capable of automatically learning the propensity of local patterns from a library of games. Propensity and other local tactical information are fed into a recursive neural network, derived from a Bayesian network architecture. The network integrates local information across the board and produces local outputs that represent local territory owner- ship probabilities. The aggregation of these probabilities provides an effective strategic evaluation function that is an estimate of the expected area at the end (or at other stages) of the game. Local area targets for training can be derived from datasets of human games. A system trained using only 9 × 9 amateur game data performs surprisingly well on a test set derived from 19 × 19 professional game data. Possible directions for further improvements are brieﬂy discussed.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to evaluate Go positions by learning from recorded games. The central challenge is connecting small tactical patterns to an assessment of the whole board. A useful evaluation method must accommodate a growing collection of patterns, interactions between different regions, and changes in board size.

The system learns the propensities of local patterns from a game library. It feeds these values and other tactical information into a recursive neural network whose architecture comes from a Bayesian network. The network combines information across the board and predicts the probability that each local region belongs to either player. Combining those probabilities gives an estimate of expected territory at the end of the game or another stage.

Human games provide the local territory targets needed for training. The authors report that a system trained only on amateur games played on a 9-by-9 board performs surprisingly well on a test set drawn from professional 19-by-19 games. That finding supports the approach's ability to transfer across board sizes and game sources in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: A recursive neural network combines learned local Go patterns into territory estimates that transfer well from small amateur boards to a larger professional-game test set.

title: A Scalable Machine Learning Approach to Go

abstract: Large repositories of source code create new challenges and opportunities for statistical machine learning. Here we first develop an infrastructure for the automated crawling, parsing, and database storage of open source software. The infrastructure allows us to gather Internet-scale source code. For instance, in one experiment, we gather 4,632 java projects from SourceForge and Apache totaling over 38 million lines of code from 9,250 developers. Simple statistical analyses of the data first reveal robust power-law behavior for package, SLOC, and method call distributions. We then develop and apply unsupervised author-topic, probabilistic models to automatically discover the topics embedded in the code and extract topic-word and author-topic distributions. In addition to serving as a convenient summary for program function and developer activities, these and other related distributions provide a statistical and information-theoretic basis for quantifying and analyzing developer similarity and competence, topic scattering, and document tangling, with direct applications to software engineering. Finally, by combining software textual content with structural information captured by our CodeRank approach, we are able to significantly improve software retrieval performance, increasing the AUC metric to 0.86-- roughly 10-30% better than previous approaches based on text alone.

Statistical analyses reveal robust power-law patterns in package, source-line-count, and method-call distributions. The authors then apply unsupervised probabilistic author-topic models to discover topics in code and estimate relationships between topics, words, and developers. These distributions summarize program functionality and developer activities, while providing a statistical basis for analyzing developer similarity and competence, topic scattering, and document tangling.

For software retrieval, the authors combine textual content with structural information captured by CodeRank. They report an AUC of 0.86, approximately 10–30% better than earlier approaches using text alone. The work therefore connects collection infrastructure, exploratory statistical analysis, and learned representations to a concrete retrieval improvement. It shows how repository-scale code analysis can support both descriptions of software activity and an applied software-engineering task.
summary.tldr: Repository-scale statistical models summarize code and developers, while combining text with CodeRank structure improves software retrieval.

title: Mining Internet-Scale Software Repositories

abstract: How much information does a neural population convey about a stimulus? Answers to this question are known to strongly depend on the correlation of response variability in neural populations. These noise correlations, however, are essentially immeasurable as the number of parameters in a noise correlation matrix grows quadratically with population size. Here, we suggest to bypass this problem by imposing a parametric model on a noise correlation matrix. Our basic assumption is that noise correlations arise due to common inputs between neurons. On average, noise correlations will therefore reflect signal correlations, which can be measured in neural populations. We suggest an explicit parametric dependency between signal and noise correlations. We show how this dependency can be used to fill the gaps" in noise correlations matrices using an iterative application of the Wishart distribution over positive definitive matrices. We apply our method to data from the primary somatosensory cortex of monkeys performing a two-alternative-forced choice task. We compare the discrimination thresholds read out from the population of recorded neurons with the discrimination threshold of the monkey and show that our method predicts different results than simpler, average schemes of noise correlations."

paragraphs: Estimating how much information a group of neurons carries depends strongly on correlations in their response variability. Measuring all such noise correlations becomes difficult because the number of pairwise parameters grows quadratically with population size. This paper proposes a parametric model for filling in missing correlation information.

The main assumption is that shared inputs give rise to noise correlations. On average, these correlations should therefore reflect signal correlations, which can be measured in neural populations. The authors specify a parametric relationship between the two and use an iterative procedure involving the Wishart distribution to complete the noise correlation matrix while working with positive definite matrices.

They apply the method to recordings from monkeys' primary somatosensory cortex during a two-alternative forced-choice task. They compare discrimination thresholds read out from the recorded population with the monkey's behavioral threshold. The method predicts different results from simpler schemes based on average noise correlations. This demonstrates that the structure used to complete missing correlations can materially affect conclusions about population information.
summary.tldr: A model relating signal and noise correlations fills missing neural correlation data and yields different population-readout predictions from average-correlation schemes.

title: Linear readout from a neural population with partial correlation data

abstract: We consider the problem of apprenticeship learning where the examples, demonstrated by an expert, cover only a small part of a large state space. Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) provides an efficient tool for generalizing the demonstration, based on the assumption that the expert is maximizing a utility function that is a linear combination of state-action features. Most IRL algorithms use a simple Monte Carlo estimation to approximate the expected feature counts under the expert's policy. In this paper, we show that the quality of the learned policies is highly sensitive to the error in estimating the feature counts. To reduce this error, we introduce a novel approach for bootstrapping the demonstration by assuming that: (i), the expert is (near-)optimal, and (ii), the dynamics of the system is known. Empirical results on gridworlds and car racing problems show that our approach is able to learn good policies from a small number of demonstrations.

paragraphs: Expert demonstrations often cover only a small fraction of the situations an apprentice may encounter. Inverse reinforcement learning can generalize from those demonstrations by assuming that the expert maximizes a utility expressed as a linear combination of state-action features. Learning then depends on estimating the expected accumulated feature counts under the expert’s behavior.

The paper shows that the quality of the resulting policy is highly sensitive to errors in those estimates. Many inverse reinforcement learning methods use straightforward Monte Carlo estimates from demonstrations. The authors propose bootstrapping the demonstrations to reduce estimation error, drawing on two explicit assumptions: the expert is optimal or nearly optimal, and the system’s dynamics are known.

Experiments on gridworld and car racing problems show that the approach can learn good policies from few demonstrations. The result connects a practical data shortage to a specific estimation problem. Under the stated assumptions, using knowledge about expert quality and system behavior can help extract more useful learning information from limited demonstrations.
summary.tldr: Bootstrapping expert demonstrations improves feature-count estimation and learns good policies from few examples when expert quality and system dynamics are known.

title: Bootstrapping Apprenticeship Learning

abstract: With the increase in available data parallel machine learning has become an increasingly pressing problem. In this paper we present the first parallel stochastic gradient descent algorithm including a detailed analysis and experimental evidence. Unlike prior work on parallel optimization algorithms our variant comes with parallel acceleration guarantees and it poses no overly tight latency constraints, which might only be available in the multicore setting. Our analysis introduces a novel proof technique --- contractive mappings to quantify the speed of convergence of parameter distributions to their asymptotic limits. As a side effect this answers the question of how quickly stochastic gradient descent algorithms reach the asymptotically normal regime.

Our analysis introduces a novel proof technique --- contractive mappings to quantify the speed of convergence of parameter distributions to their asymptotic limits. As a side effect this answers the question of how quickly stochastic gradient descent algorithms reach the asymptotically normal regime.

paragraphs: As datasets grow, distributing learning across parallel computation becomes increasingly important. This paper presents a parallel stochastic gradient descent algorithm supported by both a detailed analysis and experiments. Its contribution includes guarantees of parallel acceleration, making the speed benefit part of the theoretical treatment rather than solely an experimental observation.

The proposed variant avoids overly tight latency requirements of the kind that might be practical only in a multicore setting. This addresses a constraint on where parallel optimization can be useful. The abstract does not make the stronger claim that communication timing is irrelevant; it states that the required latency conditions are not excessively restrictive.

The analysis uses contractive mappings to measure how quickly distributions of the algorithm's parameters approach their asymptotic limits. This distributional perspective also answers how quickly stochastic gradient descent reaches its asymptotically normal regime. The paper therefore contributes both a parallel learning method with acceleration guarantees and a proof technique that yields insight into the statistical behavior of stochastic gradient descent.
summary.tldr: A parallel SGD algorithm comes with acceleration guarantees and an analysis of how quickly parameter distributions approach their asymptotic behavior.

title: Parallelized Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: The nested Chinese restaurant process is extended to design a nonparametric topic-model tree for representation of human choices. Each tree branch corresponds to a type of person, and each node (topic) has a corresponding probability vector over items that may be selected. The observed data are assumed to have associated temporal covariates (corresponding to the time at which choices are made), and we wish to impose that with increasing time it is more probable that topics deeper in the tree are utilized. This structure is imposed by developing a new “change point" stick-breaking model that is coupled with a Poisson and product-of-gammas construction. To share topics across the tree nodes, topic distributions are drawn from a Dirichlet process. As a demonstration of this concept, we analyze real data on course selections of undergraduate students at Duke University, with the goal of uncovering and concisely representing structure in the curriculum and in the characteristics of the student body.

paragraphs: The paper develops a hierarchical topic model for choices people make over time. A branch of the model's tree corresponds to a type of person, while each node contains probabilities over selectable items. This gives the model a way to describe both broad patterns of choice and more detailed patterns along a branch.

The construction extends the nested Chinese restaurant process and assumes that observations include the times at which choices were made. It deliberately makes deeper topics more likely to be used as time increases. A new change-point stick-breaking model, coupled with Poisson and product-of-gammas components, imposes that temporal structure. A Dirichlet process allows topic distributions to be shared across nodes.

The authors demonstrate the approach using undergraduate course selections at Duke University. Their aim is to reveal and compactly describe structure in both the curriculum and the student population. The temporal progression toward deeper topics is an explicit modeling preference: it shapes how changing choices are represented, rather than being presented as a universal law of personal behavior.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric topic tree models personal choices over time by making deeper topics increasingly likely and sharing topics across nodes.

title: Hierarchical Topic Modeling for Analysis of Time-Evolving Personal Choices

abstract: In this paper, a novel, computationally fast, and alternative algorithm for com- puting weighted v-statistics in resampling both univariate and multivariate data is proposed. To avoid any real resampling, we have linked this problem with finite group action and converted it into a problem of orbit enumeration. For further computational cost reduction, an efficient method is developed to list all orbits by their symmetry order and calculate all index function orbit sums and data function orbit sums recursively. The computational complexity analysis shows reduction in the computational cost from n! or nn level to low-order polynomial level.
originalAbstract: In this paper, a novel, computationally fast, and alternative algorithm for com- puting weighted v-statistics in resampling both univariate and multivariate data is proposed. To avoid any real resampling, we have linked this problem with finite group action and converted it into a problem of orbit enumeration. For further computational cost reduction, an efficient method is developed to list all orbits by their symmetry order and calculate all index function orbit sums and data function orbit sums recursively. The computational complexity analysis shows reduction in the computational cost from n! or nn level to low-order polynomial level.

paragraphs: The paper presents a faster way to compute weighted V-statistics in resampling problems involving either univariate or multivariate data. Directly working through resampled arrangements can create an enormous computational burden. The authors replace explicit resampling with an algebraic formulation designed to exploit relationships among the arrangements that would otherwise be processed.

The key step connects resampling to a finite group action and reformulates the calculation as orbit enumeration. Orbits organize arrangements according to the symmetries induced by that action. This gives the algorithm a structured way to account for related cases without carrying out the corresponding resampling operations individually.

To reduce the work further, the method lists orbits by symmetry order and recursively computes sums for both index functions and data functions. The complexity analysis reports a reduction from factorial or n-to-the-n cost to a low-order polynomial. The significance is computational: recognizing symmetry changes how the required statistical calculation is organized and makes a much larger reduction possible.
summary.tldr: A symmetry-based reformulation computes weighted V-statistics without explicit resampling, reducing the analyzed cost to low-order polynomial complexity.

title: Fast Resampling Weighted v-Statistics

abstract: This paper introduces a novel classification method for functional magnetic resonance imaging datasets with tens of classes. The method is designed to make predictions using information from as many brain locations as possible, instead of resorting to feature selection, and does this by decomposing the pattern of brain activation into differently informative sub-regions. We provide results over a complex semantic processing dataset that show that the method is competitive with state-of-the-art feature selection and also suggest how the method may be used to perform group or exploratory analyses of complex class structure.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces a novel classification method for functional magnetic resonance imaging datasets with tens of classes. The method is designed to make predictions using information from as many brain locations as possible, instead of resorting to feature selection, and does this by decomposing the pattern of brain activation into differently informative sub-regions. We provide results over a complex semantic processing dataset that show that the method is competitive with state-of-the-art feature selection and also suggest how the method may be used to perform group or exploratory analyses of complex class structure.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a method for classifying functional MRI data when the prediction task contains tens of classes. Its central design choice is to draw on information from as many brain locations as possible. That matters for semantic analysis because the method is intended to use the wider activation pattern, rather than first narrowing the input through feature selection.

The approach decomposes brain activation into subregions that differ in how informative they are. This gives the classifier a way to organize a broad collection of brain measurements while acknowledging that different regions contribute different amounts of predictive information. Keeping a wide spatial scope therefore does not require treating every location as equally useful.

Results on a complex semantic processing dataset show performance competitive with state-of-the-art feature selection. The findings suggest that this decomposition can preserve useful predictive information without relying on the usual selection step. They also suggest possible applications to group analysis and exploration of relationships among many classes; these are proposed uses rather than established general conclusions about brain organization.
summary.tldr: A classifier organizes fMRI activation into differently informative subregions, using broad brain coverage while achieving competitive semantic classification.

title: A systematic approach to extracting semantic information from functional MRI data

abstract: In this paper, we address the problem of learning the structure of Gaussian chain graph models in a high-dimensional space. Chain graph models are generalizations of undirected and directed graphical models that contain a mixed set of directed and undirected edges. While the problem of sparse structure learning has been studied extensively for Gaussian graphical models and more recently for conditional Gaussian graphical models (CGGMs), there has been little previous work on the structure recovery of Gaussian chain graph models. We consider linear regression models and a re-parameterization of the linear regression models using CGGMs as building blocks of chain graph models. We argue that when the goal is to recover model structures, there are many advantages of using CGGMs as chain component models over linear regression models, including convexity of the optimization problem, computational efficiency, recovery of structured sparsity, and ability to leverage the model structure for semi-supervised learning. We demonstrate our approach on simulated and genomic datasets.

We argue that when the goal is to recover model structures, there are many advantages of using CGGMs as chain component models over linear regression models, including convexity of the optimization problem, computational efficiency, recovery of structured sparsity, and ability to leverage the model structure for semi-supervised learning. paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover sparse relationships among many variables using Gaussian chain graphs. These models contain both directed and undirected edges, extending the types of relationships represented by either graph family alone. The authors focus on identifying the graph structure in high-dimensional settings, an area they describe as less developed than related Gaussian structure-learning problems.

They compare linear-regression formulations with a reparameterization built from conditional Gaussian graphical models. These conditional models serve as the components of the larger chain graph. The choice of parameterization matters because the intended output is the structure of relationships among variables, so the representation used during fitting affects how that structure can be recovered.

The authors argue that conditional Gaussian components offer several advantages for this goal: convex optimization, computational efficiency, recovery of structured sparsity, and use of the model structure in semi-supervised learning. They demonstrate their approach with simulated and genomic datasets. The contribution is a formulation that connects structural modeling choices with more favorable learning and optimization properties.
summary.tldr: Conditional Gaussian components provide a convex, computationally efficient formulation for learning sparse Gaussian chain-graph structures.

title: On Sparse Gaussian Chain Graph Models

abstract: In many important machine learning applications, the source distribution used to estimate a probabilistic classifier differs from the target distribution on which the classifier will be used to make predictions. Due to its asymptotic properties, sample-reweighted loss minimization is a commonly employed technique to deal with this difference. However, given finite amounts of labeled source data, this technique suffers from significant estimation errors in settings with large sample selection bias. We develop a framework for robustly learning a probabilistic classifier that adapts to different sample selection biases using a minimax estimation formulation. Our approach requires only accurate estimates of statistics under the source distribution and is otherwise as robust as possible to unknown properties of the conditional label distribution, except when explicit generalization assumptions are incorporated. We demonstrate the behavior and effectiveness of our approach on synthetic and UCI binary classification tasks.

Due to its asymptotic properties, sample-reweighted loss minimization is a commonly employed technique to deal with this difference. However, given finite amounts of labeled source data, this technique suffers from significant estimation errors in settings with large sample selection bias. We develop a framework for robustly learning a probabilistic classifier that adapts to different sample selection biases using a minimax estimation formulation. Our approach requires only accurate estimates of statistics under the source distribution and is otherwise as robust as possible to unknown properties of the conditional label distribution, except when explicit generalization assumptions are incorporated. We demonstrate the behavior and effectiveness of our approach on synthetic and UCI binary classification tasks.

paragraphs: A classifier may be trained on data drawn from a different distribution than the one it encounters in use. Reweighting training losses is a common response, supported by asymptotic arguments. This paper focuses on the finite-data difficulty: under substantial sample-selection bias, reweighting can produce large estimation errors.

The authors propose a minimax framework for learning a probabilistic classifier that adapts to different selection biases. Its information requirement is accurate estimates of statistics under the source distribution. Beyond that information, the formulation seeks as much robustness as possible to unknown aspects of the conditional label distribution, unless additional generalization assumptions are explicitly supplied.

This makes the treatment of uncertainty central to the learning problem. The framework distinguishes information supported by source statistics from assumptions about how labels generalize to the target distribution. Experiments on synthetic data and UCI binary classification tasks demonstrate its behavior and effectiveness. The stated robustness remains tied to accurate source-statistic estimates and to any explicit generalization assumptions incorporated into the formulation.
summary.tldr: A minimax classification framework handles sample-selection bias using accurate source statistics while remaining robust to unspecified label-distribution properties.

title: Robust Classification Under Sample Selection Bias

abstract: An algorithm for learning fast multiclass object detection cascades is introduced. It produces multi-resolution (MRes) cascades, whose early stages are binary target vs. non-target detectors that eliminate false positives, late stages multiclass classifiers that finely discriminate target classes, and middle stages have intermediate numbers of classes, determined in a data-driven manner. This MRes structure is achieved with a new structurally biased boosting algorithm (SBBoost). SBBost extends previous multiclass boosting approaches, whose boosting mechanisms are shown to implement two complementary data-driven biases: 1) the standard bias towards examples difficult to classify, and 2) a bias towards difficult classes. It is shown that structural biases can be implemented by generalizing this class-based bias, so as to encourage the desired MRes structure. This is accomplished through a generalized definition of multiclass margin, which includes a set of bias parameters. SBBoost is a boosting algorithm for maximization of this margin. It can also be interpreted as standard multiclass boosting algorithm augmented with margin thresholds or a cost-sensitive boosting algorithm with costs defined by the bias parameters. A stage adaptive bias policy is then introduced to determine bias parameters in a data driven manner. This is shown to produce MRes cascades that have high detection rate and are computationally efficient. Experiments on multiclass object detection show improved performance over previous solutions.

paragraphs: A multiclass object detector must reject non-targets and distinguish among target categories. This paper organizes those decisions into a cascade with progressively finer class distinctions. Early stages make binary target-versus-non-target decisions, later stages separate target classes in detail, and intermediate stages use numbers of classes learned from data.

The authors create this structure through structurally biased boosting, or SBBoost. Their analysis identifies two complementary tendencies in earlier multiclass boosting methods: emphasizing difficult examples and emphasizing difficult classes. A stage-adaptive policy chooses those parameters from data. The algorithm can also be understood through margin thresholds or as cost-sensitive boosting, giving several views of the same structural control. The resulting cascades combine high detection rates with computational efficiency, and experiments report improvements over earlier solutions. The practical idea is to reserve fine distinctions for later stages while using simpler decisions to eliminate false positives early.
summary.tldr: Structurally biased boosting learns efficient object-detection cascades that progress from binary rejection to fine multiclass discrimination.

title: Multi-Resolution Cascades for Multiclass Object Detection

abstract: We present a data-driven, probabilistic trajectory optimization framework for systems with unknown dynamics, called Probabilistic Differential Dynamic Programming (PDDP). PDDP takes into account uncertainty explicitly for dynamics models using Gaussian processes (GPs). Based on the second-order local approximation of the value function, PDDP performs Dynamic Programming around a nominal trajectory in Gaussian belief spaces. Different from typical gradient-based policy search methods, PDDP does not require a policy parameterization and learns a locally optimal, time-varying control policy. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm using two nontrivial tasks. Compared with the classical DDP and a state-of-the-art GP-based policy search method, PDDP offers a superior combination of data-efficiency, learning speed, and applicability.

paragraphs: Probabilistic Differential Dynamic Programming addresses control when a system's dynamics are unknown and must be learned from data. The framework uses Gaussian processes to model those dynamics and explicitly accounts for uncertainty. This brings uncertainty about the learned system into the trajectory optimization procedure.

The method performs dynamic programming around a nominal trajectory in a Gaussian belief space, where the trajectory is described probabilistically. It uses a second-order local approximation of the value function to guide optimization. Unlike typical gradient-based policy search methods, it does not require a policy parameterization and learns a locally optimal control policy that can vary over time.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency on two nontrivial tasks. Compared with classical differential dynamic programming and a state-of-the-art Gaussian-process-based policy search method, they report a superior combination of data efficiency, learning speed, and applicability. The claim concerns this combination in the demonstrations, while the policy's optimality is explicitly local. The contribution links learned uncertain dynamics with a trajectory-centered method for improving control.
summary.tldr: PDDP optimizes trajectories under Gaussian-process dynamics uncertainty to learn locally optimal, time-varying control policies without a policy parameterization.

title: Probabilistic Differential Dynamic Programming

abstract: The optimization problem behind neural networks is highly non-convex. Training with stochastic gradient descent and variants requires careful parameter tuning and provides no guarantee to achieve the global optimum. In contrast we show under quite weak assumptions on the data that a particular class of feedforward neural networks can be trained globally optimal with a linear convergence rate. Up to our knowledge this is the first practically feasible method which achieves such a guarantee. While the method can in principle be applied to deep networks, we restrict ourselves for simplicity in this paper to one- and two hidden layer networks. Our experiments confirms that these models are already rich enough to achieve good performance on a series of real-world datasets.

In contrast we show under quite weak assumptions on the data that a particular class of feedforward neural networks can be trained globally optimal with a linear convergence rate. Up to our knowledge this is the first practically feasible method which achieves such a guarantee. Our experiments confirms that these models are already rich enough to achieve good performance on a series of real-world datasets.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of guaranteeing globally optimal neural-network training. Neural-network objectives are highly nonconvex, and stochastic gradient methods generally require parameter tuning without guaranteeing a global optimum. The authors focus on a particular class of feedforward networks, identified in the title as generalized polynomial neural networks.

For this class, they present a method with a global-optimality guarantee and a linear convergence rate under assumptions on the data that they characterize as relatively weak. The title identifies nonlinear spectral methods as the approach. The guarantee is tied to the specified network class and data assumptions, making those conditions central to the result's meaning.

Although the method can in principle extend to deep networks, the paper studies networks with one or two hidden layers for simplicity. Experiments on several real-world datasets show that these models already achieve good performance. The work thus brings together a conditional optimization guarantee and evidence that the covered models have useful representational capacity in practice.
summary.tldr: Under stated data assumptions, a particular class of polynomial neural networks admits globally optimal training with linear convergence.

title: Globally Optimal Training of Generalized Polynomial Neural Networks with Nonlinear Spectral Methods

abstract: Behavioral experiments on humans and animals suggest that the brain performs probabilistic inference to interpret its environment. Here we present a new general-purpose, biologically-plausible neural implementation of approximate inference. The neural network represents uncertainty using Probabilistic Population Codes (PPCs), which are distributed neural representations that naturally encode probability distributions, and support marginalization and evidence integration in a biologically-plausible manner. By connecting multiple PPCs together as a probabilistic graphical model, we represent multivariate probability distributions. Approximate inference in graphical models can be accomplished by message-passing algorithms that disseminate local information throughout the graph. An attractive and often accurate example of such an algorithm is Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP), which uses local marginalization and evidence integration operations to perform approximate inference efficiently even for complex models. Unfortunately, a subtle feature of LBP renders it neurally implausible. However, LBP can be elegantly reformulated as a sequence of Tree-based Reparameterizations (TRP) of the graphical model. We re-express the TRP updates as a nonlinear dynamical system with both fast and slow timescales, and show that this produces a neurally plausible solution. By combining all of these ideas, we show that a network of PPCs can represent multivariate probability distributions and implement the TRP updates to perform probabilistic inference. Simulations with Gaussian graphical models demonstrate that the neural network inference quality is comparable to the direct evaluation of LBP and robust to noise, and thus provides a promising mechanism for general probabilistic inference in the population codes of the brain.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a biologically plausible neural implementation of approximate probabilistic inference. It uses probabilistic population codes, where distributed neural activity represents probability distributions. Connecting several such codes through a graphical model lets the network represent uncertainty about multiple variables and combine evidence across their relationships.

Combining that dynamical system with population codes yields the proposed inference network. Simulations on Gaussian graphical models show inference quality comparable to directly evaluating loopy belief propagation, together with robustness to noise. These results support the network as a possible mechanism for probabilistic computation in the brain. The evidence establishes a promising implementation in the simulated setting, rather than demonstrating that biological brains use this particular procedure.
summary.tldr: Reformulating belief propagation as fast-and-slow neural dynamics enables a biologically plausible population-code implementation of approximate inference.

title: Inference by Reparameterization in Neural Population Codes

abstract: We consider a model of game-theoretic learning based on online mirror descent (OMD) with asynchronous and delayed feedback information. Instead of focusing on specific games, we consider a broad class of continuous games defined by the general equilibrium stability notion, which we call λ-variational stability. Our first contribution is that, in this class of games, the actual sequence of play induced by OMD-based learning converges to Nash equilibria provided that the feedback delays faced by the players are synchronous and bounded. Subsequently, to tackle fully decentralized, asynchronous environments with (possibly) unbounded delays between actions and feedback, we propose a variant of OMD which we call delayed mirror descent (DMD), and which relies on the repeated leveraging of past information. With this modification, the algorithm converges to Nash equilibria with no feedback synchronicity assumptions and even when the delays grow superlinearly relative to the horizon of play.

paragraphs: In multi-agent learning, feedback about an action may arrive after later decisions have already been made. Different players may also receive information on different schedules. This paper studies those difficulties for online mirror descent in a broad class of continuous games characterized by a condition called lambda-variational stability.

The first result shows that the actual sequence of actions converges to Nash equilibria when feedback delays are synchronized across players and bounded. This concerns the evolving play itself, giving a convergence guarantee under explicit restrictions on both the game and the timing of information.

The authors then introduce delayed mirror descent, which repeatedly reuses past information to handle decentralized environments. Within the considered game class, this variant converges without synchronized feedback, even when delays can grow superlinearly with the horizon of play. The modification substantially broadens the permitted feedback schedules while retaining the equilibrium convergence result. The stability condition on the games remains part of the setting supporting these claims.
summary.tldr: Delayed mirror descent reuses past information to guarantee equilibrium convergence in the studied stable games despite asynchronous, potentially growing delays.

title: Countering Feedback Delays in Multi-Agent Learning

abstract: We prove near-tight concentration of measure for polynomial functions of the Ising model, under high temperature, improving the radius of concentration guaranteed by known results by polynomial factors in the dimension (i.e.~the number of nodes in the Ising model). We show that our results are optimal up to logarithmic factors in the dimension. We obtain our results by extending and strengthening the exchangeable-pairs approach used to prove concentration of measure in this setting by Chatterjee. We demonstrate the efficacy of such functions as statistics for testing the strength of interactions in social networks in both synthetic and real world data.

We show that our results are optimal up to logarithmic factors in the dimension. We obtain our results by extending and strengthening the exchangeable-pairs approach used to prove concentration of measure in this setting by Chatterjee. paragraphs: Statistics computed from interacting variables can fluctuate in ways that are harder to control than statistics of independent observations. This paper studies polynomial functions of the Ising model and asks how tightly their values concentrate. Such bounds help establish how much variation a statistic can exhibit under the model.

Under a high-temperature assumption, the authors prove concentration bounds that improve the guaranteed concentration radius by factors polynomial in the number of nodes. They also show that their results are optimal up to logarithmic factors in that number. The proof extends and strengthens an exchangeable-pairs approach, a technique for analyzing fluctuations through carefully related random quantities.

The paper connects these mathematical results to statistics for testing interaction strength in social networks. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate their usefulness in that role. The contribution combines sharper theoretical control of fluctuations with an application to network analysis; the high-temperature assumption is part of the stated scope of the concentration guarantees.
summary.tldr: Under high temperature, sharper concentration bounds for Ising-model polynomials support statistics for testing interactions in social networks.

title: Concentration of Multilinear Functions of the Ising Model with Applications to Network Data

abstract: Recently, there has been a growing research interest in the analysis of dynamic regret, which measures the performance of an online learner against a sequence of local minimizers. By exploiting the strong convexity, previous studies have shown that the dynamic regret can be upper bounded by the path-length of the comparator sequence. In this paper, we illustrate that the dynamic regret can be further improved by allowing the learner to query the gradient of the function multiple times, and meanwhile the strong convexity can be weakened to other non-degenerate conditions. Specifically, we introduce the squared path-length, which could be much smaller than the path-length, as a new regularity of the comparator sequence. When multiple gradients are accessible to the learner, we first demonstrate that the dynamic regret of strongly convex functions can be upper bounded by the minimum of the path-length and the squared path-length. We then extend our theoretical guarantee to functions that are semi-strongly convex or self-concordant. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that semi-strong convexity and self-concordance are utilized to tighten the dynamic regret.
