paragraphs: Dynamic regret measures how an online learner performs relative to a sequence of local minimizers that may move over time. Earlier results used strong convexity to bound this regret by the path-length of that sequence. Path-length describes accumulated movement, linking the difficulty of tracking a changing optimum to how much it shifts.

The paper introduces squared path-length as another measure of movement and shows how to obtain tighter guarantees when the learner can query a function's gradient multiple times. For strongly convex functions, the resulting regret bound depends on the smaller of ordinary path-length and squared path-length. Squared path-length can be much smaller, so the new guarantee can improve substantially.

The authors extend their theoretical guarantee to semi-strongly convex and self-concordant functions, broadening the structural conditions used in the analysis. The additional gradient access is a substantive requirement behind the improvement. The result explains how extra information about each function can improve tracking guarantees, while showing that strong convexity is not the only structure under which tighter dynamic regret is possible.
summary.tldr: With multiple gradient queries, dynamic regret can depend on the smaller of path-length and squared path-length under the analyzed function conditions.

title: Improved Dynamic Regret for Non-degenerate Functions

abstract: We prove that, under low noise assumptions, the support vector machine with $N\ll m$ random features (RFSVM) can achieve the learning rate faster than $O(1/\sqrt{m})$ on a training set with $m$ samples when an optimized feature map is used. Our work extends the previous fast rate analysis of random features method from least square loss to 0-1 loss. We also show that the reweighted feature selection method, which approximates the optimized feature map, helps improve the performance of RFSVM in experiments on a synthetic data set.
originalAbstract: We prove that, under low noise assumptions, the support vector machine with $N\ll m$ random features (RFSVM) can achieve the learning rate faster than $O(1/\sqrt{m})$ on a training set with $m$ samples when an optimized feature map is used. Our work extends the previous fast rate analysis of random features method from least square loss to 0-1 loss. We also show that the reweighted feature selection method, which approximates the optimized feature map, helps improve the performance of RFSVM in experiments on a synthetic data set.

paragraphs: This paper studies the statistical performance of support vector machines built with random features. The central question is whether a classifier can learn quickly while using far fewer random features than training examples. The authors analyze this question using classification error, connecting the random-feature representation directly to the quality of the resulting predictions.

They prove that, under low-noise assumptions and with an optimized feature map, the learning rate can be faster than one divided by the square root of the number of training examples. The result allows the number of random features to be much smaller than the sample size. It extends earlier fast-rate analysis for least-squares loss to the zero-one loss associated with classification mistakes.

The paper also examines a reweighted feature selection method that approximates the optimized feature map. Experiments on a synthetic dataset show improved classifier performance with this selection method. The theoretical conclusion depends on the stated noise and feature-map conditions, while the experiment supports a practical way to approximate the feature construction used in that analysis.
summary.tldr: Under low-noise assumptions, an optimized random-feature SVM can achieve fast classification learning rates with far fewer features than training examples.

title: But How Does It Work in Theory? Linear SVM with Random Features

abstract: We introduce Spike-and-Slab Deep Learning (SS-DL), a fully Bayesian alternative to dropout for improving generalizability of deep ReLU networks. This new type of regularization enables provable recovery of smooth input-output maps with {\sl unknown} levels of smoothness. Indeed, we show that the posterior distribution concentrates at the near minimax rate for alpha-Holder smooth maps, performing as well as if we knew the smoothness level alpha ahead of time. Our result sheds light on architecture design for deep neural networks, namely the choice of depth, width and sparsity level. These network attributes typically depend on unknown smoothness in order to be optimal. We obviate this constraint with the fully Bayes construction. As an aside, we show that SS-DL does not overfit in the sense that the posterior concentrates on smaller networks with fewer (up to the optimal number of) nodes and links. Our results provide new theoretical justifications for deep ReLU networks from a Bayesian point of view.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Spike-and-Slab Deep Learning, a fully Bayesian alternative to dropout for regularizing deep ReLU networks. Its central question is whether a network can recover a smooth input-output relationship without knowing in advance how smooth that relationship is. That unknown smoothness normally affects the architecture needed for optimal performance.

The authors prove that the posterior concentrates around alpha-Hölder smooth maps at a near-minimax rate. In other words, the uncertainty represented by the posterior narrows around the target at a rate close to the best achievable for the smoothness class. The construction adapts to unknown smoothness, performing as well as if its level had been supplied beforehand.

The analysis also informs the choice of network depth, width, and sparsity. Rather than requiring these attributes to be tuned using known smoothness, the Bayesian construction addresses that dependence. The paper further shows that the posterior favors smaller networks with up to the optimal number of nodes and links, giving a specific theoretical sense in which the method avoids overfitting.
summary.tldr: Spike-and-Slab Deep Learning provides near-minimax Bayesian recovery of smooth functions while adapting to unknown smoothness and favoring appropriately sparse networks.

title: Posterior Concentration for Sparse Deep Learning

abstract: Classical anomaly detection is principally concerned with point-based anomalies, those anomalies that occur at a single point in time. Yet, many real-world anomalies are range-based, meaning they occur over a period of time. Motivated by this observation, we present a new mathematical model to evaluate the accuracy of time series classification algorithms. Our model expands the well-known Precision and Recall metrics to measure ranges, while simultaneously enabling customization support for domain-specific preferences.

Yet, many real-world anomalies are range-based, meaning they occur over a period of time. Our model expands the well-known Precision and Recall metrics to measure ranges, while simultaneously enabling customization support for domain-specific preferences.

paragraphs: Classical anomaly detection often treats an anomaly as something that occurs at a single time point. The paper starts from a different observation: many real anomalies persist over an interval. In those cases, the object being detected has duration, so evaluating predictions requires a way to account for ranges of time.

The authors introduce a mathematical evaluation model that extends precision and recall to ranges. These familiar metrics provide the starting point, while the extension makes them applicable to events spanning multiple observations. The contribution concerns measuring the accuracy of time-series classification algorithms, rather than introducing a new algorithm for producing their predictions.

The model also allows customization for domain-specific preferences. This matters because an evaluation measure needs to reflect what counts as useful detection in the application where it is used. By combining range-based evaluation with configurable preferences, the framework offers a way to assess predictions in terms suited to sustained events. Its stated contribution is the evaluation model itself and its support for representing application-specific priorities.
summary.tldr: The paper extends precision and recall to anomalies that span time intervals, with customization for application-specific evaluation preferences.

title: Precision and Recall for Time Series

abstract: Visual attention, derived from cognitive neuroscience, facilitates human perception on the most pertinent subset of the sensory data. Recently, significant efforts have been made to exploit attention schemes to advance computer vision systems. For visual tracking, it is often challenging to track target objects undergoing large appearance changes. Attention maps facilitate visual tracking by selectively paying attention to temporal robust features. Existing tracking-by-detection approaches mainly use additional attention modules to generate feature weights as the classifiers are not equipped with such mechanisms. In this paper, we propose a reciprocative learning algorithm to exploit visual attention for training deep classifiers. The proposed algorithm consists of feed-forward and backward operations to generate attention maps, which serve as regularization terms coupled with the original classification loss function for training. The deep classifier learns to attend to the regions of target objects robust to appearance changes. Extensive experiments on large-scale benchmark datasets show that the proposed attentive tracking method performs favorably against the state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Tracking an object becomes difficult when its appearance changes substantially over time. Visual attention can help by emphasizing features that remain useful across those changes. The paper focuses on training the classifier used for tracking to attend to such regions, addressing a capability that existing tracking-by-detection systems often obtain through additional attention modules.

The proposed reciprocative learning algorithm uses both forward and backward operations to produce attention maps. These maps become regularization terms that are combined with the classifier's original classification loss. Attention therefore influences the training objective itself, giving the classifier a reason to develop features associated with more stable parts of the target.

The intended result is a classifier that concentrates on target regions robust to appearance variation, rather than relying equally on all available visual evidence. Extensive experiments on large-scale tracking benchmarks show favorable performance relative to state-of-the-art approaches. The reported evidence supports attention-guided classifier training as a useful tracking strategy, with the central contribution lying in how attention maps are coupled to the learning process.
summary.tldr: Reciprocative learning uses attention maps to regularize tracking classifiers toward object regions that remain reliable as appearance changes.

title: Deep Attentive Tracking via Reciprocative Learning

abstract: We examine the question of when and how parametric models are most useful in reinforcement learning. In particular, we look at commonalities and differences between parametric models and experience replay. Replay-based learning algorithms share important traits with model-based approaches, including the ability to plan: to use more computation without additional data to improve predictions and behaviour. We discuss when to expect benefits from either approach, and interpret prior work in this context. We hypothesise that, under suitable conditions, replay-based algorithms should be competitive to or better than model-based algorithms if the model is used only to generate fictional transitions from observed states for an update rule that is otherwise model-free. We validated this hypothesis on Atari 2600 video games. The replay-based algorithm attained state-of-the-art data efficiency, improving over prior results with parametric models. Additionally, we discuss different ways to use models. We show that it can be better to plan backward than to plan forward when using models to perform credit assignment (e.g., to directly learn a value or policy), even though the latter seems more common. Finally, we argue and demonstrate that it can be beneficial to plan forward for immediate behaviour, rather than for credit assignment.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning agent can spend extra computation learning from stored experiences or from a learned environment model. This paper compares these options and emphasizes that experience replay also supports planning: it can improve predictions and behavior without collecting additional data. The question becomes what a parametric model adds beyond that capability.

The authors hypothesize that replay can match or outperform model-based learning under suitable conditions when the model only generates fictional transitions from observed states for an otherwise model-free update. Atari experiments support this hypothesis. The replay-based method achieves state-of-the-art data efficiency and improves on prior results using parametric models in the comparison described.

The paper also examines other uses of models. For credit assignment, backward planning can work better than forward planning. For choosing immediate behavior, forward planning can be beneficial. These findings make the model’s role central to the comparison: the value of learning an environment model depends partly on how its predictions are used to support learning or action selection.
summary.tldr: The benefits of learned reinforcement-learning models depend on their use, with replay competitive under suitable conditions and planning direction affecting results.

title: When to use parametric models in reinforcement learning?

abstract: Convolutions are a fundamental building block of modern computer vision systems. Recent approaches have argued for going beyond convolutions in order to capture long-range dependencies. These efforts focus on augmenting convolutional models with content-based interactions, such as self-attention and non-local means, to achieve gains on a number of vision tasks. The natural question that arises is whether attention can be a stand-alone primitive for vision models instead of serving as just an augmentation on top of convolutions. In developing and testing a pure self-attention vision model, we verify that self-attention can indeed be an effective stand-alone layer. A simple procedure of replacing all instances of spatial convolutions with a form of self-attention to ResNet-50 produces a fully self-attentional model that outperforms the baseline on ImageNet classification with 12% fewer FLOPS and 29% fewer parameters. On COCO object detection, a fully self-attention model matches the mAP of a baseline RetinaNet while having 39% fewer FLOPS and 34% fewer parameters. Detailed ablation studies demonstrate that self-attention is especially impactful when used in later layers. These results establish that stand-alone self-attention is an important addition to the vision practitioner's toolbox.

This paper asks a more direct architectural question: can self-attention serve as the main spatial processing layer, rather than only supplementing convolutions?

On ImageNet classification, the resulting model exceeds the baseline’s performance while using 12% fewer floating-point operations and 29% fewer parameters. This demonstrates that the tested attention architecture can supply effective spatial processing while reducing both computation and model size in that comparison.

For COCO object detection, a fully self-attention model matches a baseline RetinaNet’s mean average precision with 39% fewer floating-point operations and 34% fewer parameters. Ablation studies find that attention is especially impactful in later layers. Together, these results establish stand-alone self-attention as a useful option for vision architecture design, with benefits demonstrated in classification and detection rather than a universal advantage across all tasks.
summary.tldr: Replacing spatial convolutions with self-attention matches or improves tested vision baselines while reducing computation and parameter counts.

title: Stand-Alone Self-Attention in Vision Models

abstract: In the last decade, it has been shown that many hard AI tasks, especially in NLP, can be naturally modeled as extreme classification problems leading to improved precision. However, such models are prohibitively expensive to train due to the memory bottleneck in the last layer. For example, a reasonable softmax layer for the dataset of interest in this paper can easily reach well beyond 100 billion parameters (> 400 GB memory). To alleviate this problem, we present Merged-Average Classifiers via Hashing (MACH), a generic $K$-classification algorithm where memory provably scales at $O(\log K)$ without any assumption on the relation between classes. MACH is subtly a count-min sketch structure in disguise, which uses universal hashing to reduce classification with a large number of classes to few embarrassingly parallel and independent classification tasks with a small (constant) number of classes. MACH naturally provides a technique for zero communication model parallelism. We experiment with 6 datasets; some multiclass and some multilabel, and show consistent improvement in precision and recall metrics compared to respective baselines. In particular, we train an end-to -end deep classifier on a private product search dataset sampled from Amazon Search Engine with 70 million queries and 49.46 million documents. MACH outperforms, by a significant margin, the state-of-the-art extreme classification models deployed on commercial search engines: Parabel and dense embedding models. Our largest model has 6.4 billion parameters and trains in less than 35 hrs on a single p3.16x machine. Our training times are 7-10x faster, and our memory footprints are 2-4x smaller than the best baselines. This training time is also significantly lower than the one reported by Google’s mixture of experts (MoE) language model on a comparable model size and hardware.

Its structure is connected to a count-min sketch.

Reported training is 7–10 times faster, with memory footprints 2–4 times smaller, than the best baselines.
summary.tldr: MACH uses hashing to split massive classification tasks into small independent classifiers, reducing memory and training costs.

title: Extreme Classification in Log Memory using Count-Min Sketch: A Case Study of Amazon Search with 50M Products

abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

This paper uses brain recordings from people reading complex natural text as a reference for interpretation. It compares word and sequence representations from ELMo, USE, BERT, and Transformer-XL with those recordings.

The analysis examines how representations vary with network depth, available context, and attention type. The results reveal differences among models in their context-related representations. For transformer models, layer depth interacts with both context length and attention type, indicating that these architectural and input choices need to be considered together when interpreting the learned representations.

The authors then hypothesize that making BERT more aligned with brain recordings could improve its language abilities. An altered BERT with greater brain alignment performs better than the original on syntactic probing tasks. This finding supports the proposed connection in the evaluated tasks, while the broader language-understanding claim remains a hypothesis. The work uses neuroscience both to interpret language models and to guide a tested model modification.
summary.tldr: Brain recordings reveal differences among language-model representations, and a more brain-aligned BERT improves on the reported syntactic probes.

title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)

abstract: Deep neural networks as image priors have been recently introduced for problems such as denoising, super-resolution and inpainting with promising performance gains over hand-crafted image priors such as sparsity. Unlike learned generative priors they do not require any training over large datasets. However, few theoretical guarantees exist in the scope of using untrained network priors for inverse imaging problems. We explore new applications and theory for untrained neural network priors. Specifically, we consider the problem of solving linear inverse problems, such as compressive sensing, as well as non-linear problems, such as compressive phase retrieval. We model images to lie in the range of an untrained deep generative network with a fixed seed. We further present a projected gradient descent scheme that can be used for both compressive sensing and phase retrieval and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees for its convergence. We also show both theoretically as well as empirically that with deep neural network priors, one can achieve better compression rates for the same image quality as compared to when hand crafted priors are used.

paragraphs: Recovering an image from incomplete measurements requires assumptions about what plausible images look like. This paper studies an assumption supplied by an untrained neural network, rather than a handcrafted rule such as sparsity or a generative model trained on a large image collection. The image is modeled as belonging to the outputs of an untrained deep generative network with a fixed seed.

The authors consider both linear and nonlinear reconstruction problems. Their examples are compressive sensing and compressive phase retrieval. They introduce a projected gradient descent method that can be used in both settings and establish rigorous convergence guarantees. This connects a promising image reconstruction approach with an analysis of how an associated optimization algorithm behaves.

The paper also reports theoretical and empirical evidence that deep network priors can achieve better compression rates than handcrafted priors at the same image quality. The contribution therefore combines a reconstruction method, convergence theory, and evidence about measurement efficiency, within the stated network-based image model.
summary.tldr: An untrained network image model supports a reconstruction algorithm with convergence guarantees and evidence of improved compression at matched image quality.

title: Algorithmic Guarantees for Inverse Imaging with Untrained Network Priors

abstract: We consider the problem of minimizing the composition of a smooth (nonconvex) function and a smooth vector mapping, where the inner mapping is in the form of an expectation over some random variable or a finite sum. We propose a stochastic composite gradient method that employs incremental variance-reduced estimators for both the inner vector mapping and its Jacobian. We show that this method achieves the same orders of complexity as the best known first-order methods for minimizing expected-value and finite-sum nonconvex functions, despite the additional outer composition which renders the composite gradient estimator biased. This finding enables a much broader range of applications in machine learning to benefit from the low complexity of incremental variance-reduction methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies an objective formed by applying a smooth, possibly nonconvex function to another smooth vector-valued mapping. The inner mapping is an expectation or a finite sum. This nesting makes stochastic gradients more complicated than those of an ordinary expected-value objective.

The proposed stochastic composite-gradient method incrementally reduces variance in estimates of both the inner mapping and its Jacobian. The outer composition still makes the resulting composite-gradient estimator biased, so the analysis must account for more than ordinary sampling variance.

The authors show complexity orders matching the best known first-order methods for corresponding expected-value and finite-sum nonconvex optimization problems, despite that additional composition. The contribution is a theoretical extension of efficient variance-reduction methods to a broader objective class. The abstract does not provide experimental benchmarks or the detailed smoothness constants, and its guarantees apply to the stated smooth composite setting.
summary.tldr: Incremental variance reduction extends efficient stochastic optimization to smooth composite objectives.

title: A Stochastic Composite Gradient Method with Incremental Variance Reduction

abstract: In this paper, we propose three online algorithms for submodular maximization. The first one, Mono-Frank-Wolfe, reduces the number of per-function gradient evaluations from $T^{1/2}$ [Chen2018Online] and $T^{3/2}$ [chen2018projection] to 1, and achieves a $(1-1/e)$-regret bound of $O(T^{4/5})$. The second one, Bandit-Frank-Wolfe, is the first bandit algorithm for continuous DR-submodular maximization, which achieves a $(1-1/e)$-regret bound of $O(T^{8/9})$. Finally, we extend Bandit-Frank-Wolfe to a bandit algorithm for discrete submodular maximization, Responsive-Frank-Wolfe, which attains a $(1-1/e)$-regret bound of $O(T^{8/9})$ in the responsive bandit setting.

The second one, Bandit-Frank-Wolfe, is the first bandit algorithm for continuous DR-submodular maximization, which achieves a $(1-1/e)$-regret bound of $O(T^{8/9})$. Finally, we extend Bandit-Frank-Wolfe to a bandit algorithm for discrete submodular maximization, Responsive-Frank-Wolfe, which attains a $(1-1/e)$-regret bound of $O(T^{8/9})$ in the responsive bandit setting.

paragraphs: This paper introduces three algorithms for online submodular maximization, covering both richer information and bandit feedback. The central issues are how much work an algorithm performs on each arriving function and how well its cumulative decisions compare with a benchmark. The reported guarantees use a 1−1/e approximation-adjusted notion of regret.

Mono-Frank-Wolfe reduces gradient evaluations per function to one, compared with the T^(1/2) and T^(3/2) requirements of the cited approaches, where T is the number of rounds. It achieves an O(T^(4/5)) regret bound. This result pairs a sharply reduced per-function gradient requirement with a sublinear cumulative regret guarantee, so the guaranteed average adjusted regret decreases with more rounds.

Bandit-Frank-Wolfe is presented as the first bandit algorithm for continuous DR-submodular maximization and achieves O(T^(8/9)) adjusted regret. Responsive-Frank-Wolfe extends it to discrete submodular maximization under responsive bandit feedback with the same rate. Together, the results establish guarantees across distinct information settings, with explicit differences in the regret rates and feedback requirements.
summary.tldr: Three Frank-Wolfe algorithms provide sublinear approximation-adjusted regret for online submodular maximization under full-information and bandit feedback.

title: Online Continuous Submodular Maximization: From Full-Information to Bandit Feedback

abstract: We study the problem of recovering a structured signal from independently and identically drawn linear measurements. A convex penalty function $f(\cdot)$ is considered which penalizes deviations from the desired structure, and signal recovery is performed by minimizing $f(\cdot)$ subject to the linear measurement constraints. The main question of interest is to determine the minimum number of measurements that is necessary and sufficient for the perfect recovery of the unknown signal with high probability. Our main result states that, under some mild conditions on $f(\cdot)$ and on the distribution from which the linear measurements are drawn, the minimum number of measurements required for perfect recovery depends only on the first and second order statistics of the measurement vectors. As a result, the required of number of measurements can be determining by studying measurement vectors that are Gaussian (and have the same mean vector and covariance matrix) for which a rich literature and comprehensive theory exists. As an application, we show that the minimum number of random quadratic measurements (also known as rank-one projections) required to recover a low rank positive semi-definite matrix is $3nr$, where $n$ is the dimension of the matrix and $r$ is its rank. As a consequence, we settle the long standing open question of determining the minimum number of measurements required for perfect signal recovery in phase retrieval using the celebrated PhaseLift algorithm, and show it to be $3n$.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a structured signal from independently and identically drawn linear measurements. Recovery minimizes a convex penalty that favors the desired structure while satisfying the measurement constraints. The central question is how many measurements are necessary and sufficient for perfect recovery with high probability.

Under mild conditions on the penalty and measurement distribution, the authors show that this threshold depends only on the measurement vectors' first and second moments. Consequently, one can study Gaussian measurements with the same mean and covariance to determine the required count. This transfers existing Gaussian recovery theory to other measurement distributions covered by the result.

As an application, the paper obtains a threshold of 3nr random quadratic measurements for recovering a positive semidefinite matrix of dimension n and rank r. It also establishes a threshold of 3n for phase retrieval using PhaseLift. These applications illustrate how the universality result resolves specific recovery thresholds through a shared statistical characterization of measurements.
summary.tldr: Under stated conditions, exact-recovery measurement thresholds depend only on measurement means and covariances, enabling analysis through matching Gaussian measurements.

title: Universality in Learning from Linear Measurements

abstract: While we would like agents that can coordinate with humans, current algorithms such as self-play and population-based training create agents that can coordinate with themselves. Agents that assume their partner to be optimal or similar to them can converge to coordination protocols that fail to understand and be understood by humans. To demonstrate this, we introduce a simple environment that requires challenging coordination, based on the popular game Overcooked, and learn a simple model that mimics human play. We evaluate the performance of agents trained via self-play and population-based training. These agents perform very well when paired with themselves, but when paired with our human model, they are significantly worse than agents designed to play with the human model. An experiment with a planning algorithm yields the same conclusion, though only when the human-aware planner is given the exact human model that it is playing with. A user study with real humans shows this pattern as well, though less strongly. Qualitatively, we find that the gains come from having the agent adapt to the human's gameplay. Given this result, we suggest several approaches for designing agents that learn about humans in order to better coordinate with them. Code is available at https://github.com/HumanCompatibleAI/overcooked_ai.

paragraphs: Agents trained to cooperate with copies of themselves may develop coordination habits that people do not share. This paper investigates whether learning about human behavior helps address that mismatch. The authors introduce an Overcooked-inspired environment that demands coordination and train a simple model to imitate human play.

Agents trained through self-play or population-based training coordinate very well with themselves. When paired with the human model, however, they perform significantly worse than agents designed to cooperate with that model. This separates success with familiar artificial partners from success with a partner whose behavior reflects human play.

A planning experiment supports the same conclusion only when the human-aware planner receives the exact human model it faces. A study with real people shows a similar but weaker pattern. Qualitative observations attribute the gains to agents adapting to human gameplay. The findings therefore support incorporating human behavior into coordination training, while showing that the strength of the benefit depends on the evaluation and partner-model match.
summary.tldr: Agents trained with a human behavior model coordinate better with that model, with a weaker corresponding benefit observed with real people.

title: On the Utility of Learning about Humans for Human-AI Coordination

abstract: State-of-the-art approaches to causal discovery usually assume a fixed underlying causal model. However, it is often the case that causal models vary across domains or subjects, due to possibly omitted factors that affect the quantitative causal effects. As a typical example, causal connectivity in the brain network has been reported to vary across individuals, with significant differences across groups of people, such as autistics and typical controls. In this paper, we develop a unified framework for causal discovery and mechanism-based group identification. In particular, we propose a specific and shared causal model (SSCM), which takes into account the variabilities of causal relations across individuals/groups and leverages their commonalities to achieve statistically reliable estimation. The learned SSCM gives the specific causal knowledge for each individual as well as the general trend over the population. In addition, the estimated model directly provides the group information of each individual. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Causal discovery methods commonly assume that one underlying causal model applies across the data. This paper addresses settings where causal relationships differ across individuals, groups, or domains. Such variation can arise from omitted factors that change the strength of causal effects, making a single fixed model an inadequate description of the population.

The authors propose a specific and shared causal model, or SSCM. It represents individual and group variation while using common structure to support statistically reliable estimation. The resulting model provides both individual-specific causal information and a population-level trend. This connects the need to preserve meaningful differences with the statistical value of learning from shared patterns.

The framework also identifies groups directly from the estimated model, unifying causal discovery with mechanism-based clustering. Group information is therefore connected to the modeled causal relationships. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the method's efficacy. The contribution is a joint approach to learning what causal structure is shared, how it varies, and which individuals belong to groups characterized through that structure.
summary.tldr: SSCM jointly learns shared and individual causal relationships while identifying groups through their estimated causal mechanisms.

title: Specific and Shared Causal Relation Modeling and Mechanism-Based Clustering

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) excel at learning representations when trained on large-scale datasets. Pre-trained DNNs also show strong transferability when fine-tuned to other labeled datasets. However, such transferability becomes weak when the target dataset is fully unlabeled as in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA). We envision that the loss of transferability may stem from the intrinsic limitation of the architecture design of DNNs. In this paper, we delve into the components of DNN architectures and propose Transferable Normalization (TransNorm) in place of existing normalization techniques. TransNorm is an end-to-end trainable layer to make DNNs more transferable across domains. As a general method, TransNorm can be easily applied to various deep neural networks and domain adaption methods, without introducing any extra hyper-parameters or learnable parameters. Empirical results justify that TransNorm not only improves classification accuracies but also accelerates convergence for mainstream DNN-based domain adaptation methods.

paragraphs: A pretrained neural network can transfer well to a new labeled dataset, but adaptation becomes harder when the target dataset has no labels. This paper investigates whether part of that difficulty comes from network architecture. It focuses on normalization as a component that could be changed to improve transfer between domains.

The authors introduce Transferable Normalization, or TransNorm, as a replacement for existing normalization techniques. It is a layer trained together with the rest of the network and is intended for use across different neural architectures and domain adaptation methods. The proposed replacement introduces neither extra hyperparameters nor additional learnable parameters, making its contribution an architectural change without expanding those sets of choices.

Empirical results show improved classification accuracy and faster convergence for mainstream deep learning domain adaptation methods. These findings support normalization design as a useful way to improve transfer in the tested settings. The paper presents architectural limitations as a possible source of weak transfer, rather than establishing them as the sole explanation.
summary.tldr: TransNorm replaces normalization layers to improve unlabeled-target domain adaptation accuracy and convergence without adding learnable parameters or hyperparameters.

title: Transferable Normalization: Towards Improving Transferability of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Adversarial training is a popular defense strategy against attack threat models with bounded Lp norms. However, it often degrades the model performance on normal images and more importantly, the defense does not generalize well to novel attacks. Given the success of deep generative models such as GANs and VAEs in characterizing the underlying manifold of images, we investigate whether or not the aforementioned deficiencies of adversarial training can be remedied by exploiting the underlying manifold information. To partially answer this question, we consider the scenario when the manifold information of the underlying data is available. We use a subset of ImageNet natural images where an approximate underlying manifold is learned using StyleGAN. We also construct an ``On-Manifold ImageNet'' (OM-ImageNet) dataset by projecting the ImageNet samples onto the learned manifold. For OM-ImageNet, the underlying manifold information is exact. Using OM-ImageNet, we first show that on-manifold adversarial training improves both standard accuracy and robustness to on-manifold attacks. However, since no out-of-manifold perturbations are realized, the defense can be broken by Lp adversarial attacks. We further propose Dual Manifold Adversarial Training (DMAT) where adversarial perturbations in both latent and image spaces are used in robustifying the model. Our DMAT improves performance on normal images, and achieves comparable robustness to the standard adversarial training against Lp attacks. In addition, we observe that models defended by DMAT achieve improved robustness against novel attacks which manipulate images by global color shifts or various types of image filtering. Interestingly, similar improvements are also achieved when the defended models are tested on (out-of-manifold) natural images. These results demonstrate the potential benefits of using manifold information in enhancing robustness of deep learning models against various types of novel adversarial attacks.

We use a subset of ImageNet natural images where an approximate underlying manifold is learned using StyleGAN. We also construct an ``On-Manifold ImageNet'' (OM-ImageNet) dataset by projecting the ImageNet samples onto the learned manifold. For OM-ImageNet, the underlying manifold information is exact. Using OM-ImageNet, we first show that on-manifold adversarial training improves both standard accuracy and robustness to on-manifold attacks. However, since no out-of-manifold perturbations are realized, the defense can be broken by Lp adversarial attacks. Our DMAT improves performance on normal images, and achieves comparable robustness to the standard adversarial training against Lp attacks. In addition, we observe that models defended by DMAT achieve improved robustness against novel attacks which manipulate images by global color shifts or various types of image filtering. Interestingly, similar improvements are also achieved when the defended models are tested on (out-of-manifold) natural images. paragraphs: The paper investigates whether information about the image manifold can improve adversarial defenses. It considers a setting where this information is available, learning an approximate manifold with StyleGAN on an ImageNet subset. Projecting images onto it creates OM-ImageNet, where the manifold information is exact by construction.

Training against attacks restricted to that manifold improves normal accuracy and robustness to on-manifold attacks. However, this leaves perturbations outside the manifold unrepresented, and Lp attacks can still break the defense. The proposed Dual Manifold Adversarial Training addresses both directions by using adversarial perturbations in the model's latent space and in image space.

The authors report improved normal-image performance and robustness comparable to standard adversarial training against Lp attacks. They also observe better resistance to novel attacks involving global color shifts and image filtering, with similar improvements on natural images outside the learned manifold. These results support the potential value of manifold information under the studied conditions, rather than establishing protection against arbitrary attacks.
summary.tldr: Combining latent-space and image-space adversarial training improves accuracy and resistance to several attack types in the studied manifold-informed setting.

title: Dual Manifold Adversarial Robustness: Defense against Lp and non-Lp Adversarial Attacks

abstract: This work studies the problem of learning episodic Markov Decision Processes with known transition and bandit feedback. We develop the first algorithm with a ``best-of-both-worlds'' guarantee: it achieves O(log T) regret when the losses are stochastic, and simultaneously enjoys worst-case robustness with \tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}) regret even when the losses are adversarial, where T is the number of episodes. More generally, it achieves \tilde{O}(\sqrt{C}) regret in an intermediate setting where the losses are corrupted by a total amount of C. Our algorithm is based on the Follow-the-Regularized-Leader method from Zimin and Neu (2013), with a novel hybrid regularizer inspired by recent works of Zimmert et al. (2019a, 2019b) for the special case of multi-armed bandits. Crucially, our regularizer admits a non-diagonal Hessian with a highly complicated inverse. Analyzing such a regularizer and deriving a particular self-bounding regret guarantee is our key technical contribution and might be of independent interest.

paragraphs: This paper studies episodic decision-making when state-transition rules are known but loss feedback is limited to bandit feedback. The goal is an algorithm that performs especially well when losses are stochastic while retaining guarantees when losses are adversarial. These demands are combined in one best-of-both-worlds result.

The algorithm achieves O(log T) regret for stochastic losses and a worst-case regret bound of roughly O(√T), with logarithmic factors suppressed, for adversarial losses. Here T is the number of episodes. For an intermediate setting with total loss corruption C, the authors give a bound expressed as roughly O(√C), again suppressing logarithmic factors. These guarantees connect performance to the loss regime.

The method uses Follow-the-Regularized-Leader with a new hybrid regularizer. Its Hessian is non-diagonal and has a complicated inverse, making the analysis challenging. The central technical contribution is analyzing this regularizer and deriving a particular self-bounding regret guarantee. The results establish adaptability across loss conditions within the specified setting of known transitions and bandit feedback.
summary.tldr: One episodic MDP algorithm combines logarithmic stochastic regret with adversarial robustness when transitions are known.

title: Simultaneously Learning Stochastic and Adversarial Episodic MDPs with Known Transition

abstract: Recent years have seen the rise of statistical program learning based on neural models as an alternative to traditional rule-based systems for programming by example. Rule-based approaches offer correctness guarantees in an unsupervised way as they inherently capture logical rules, while neural models are more realistically scalable to raw, high-dimensional input, and provide resistance to noisy I/O specifications. We introduce PLANS (Program LeArning from Neurally inferred Specifications), a hybrid model for program synthesis from visual observations that gets the best of both worlds, relying on (i) a neural architecture trained to extract abstract, high-level information from each raw individual input (ii) a rule-based system using the extracted information as I/O specifications to synthesize a program capturing the different observations. In order to address the key challenge of making PLANS resistant to noise in the network's output, we introduce a dynamic filtering algorithm for I/O specifications based on selective classification techniques. We obtain state-of-the-art performance at program synthesis from diverse demonstration videos in the Karel and ViZDoom environments, while requiring no ground-truth program for training.

paragraphs: Learning a program from demonstration videos requires interpreting visual observations and finding logical behavior that explains them. Neural models can handle raw, high-dimensional inputs and noisy specifications, while rule-based synthesis explicitly captures logical rules. PLANS combines these capabilities by using a neural model to prepare the information consumed by a symbolic program synthesizer.

The neural component extracts abstract, high-level information from individual visual inputs. A rule-based system then treats that information as input-output specifications and synthesizes a program consistent with the observations. Because errors in neural perception can corrupt those specifications, the authors introduce a dynamic filtering algorithm based on selective classification to make the overall system more resistant to noisy network outputs.

PLANS achieves state-of-the-art program-synthesis performance from diverse demonstration videos in the Karel and ViZDoom environments. Training does not require ground-truth programs. The result shows the value of an intermediate specification layer: visual interpretation and logical synthesis can cooperate, provided the system also addresses uncertainty in the information passed between them. Filtering is therefore a central part of connecting learned perception to rule-based reasoning.
summary.tldr: PLANS combines neural video interpretation, noise-aware specification filtering, and rule-based synthesis to learn programs without ground-truth program supervision.

title: PLANS: Neuro-Symbolic Program Learning from Videos

abstract: We present an efficient low-rank approximation algorithm for non-negative tensors. The algorithm is derived from our two findings: First, we show that rank-1 approximation for tensors can be viewed as a mean-field approximation by treating each tensor as a probability distribution. Second, we theoretically provide a sufficient condition for distribution parameters to reduce Tucker ranks of tensors; interestingly, this sufficient condition can be achieved by iterative application of the mean-field approximation. Since the mean-field approximation is always given as a closed formula, our findings lead to a fast low-rank approximation algorithm without using a gradient method. We empirically demonstrate that our algorithm is faster than the existing non-negative Tucker rank reduction methods and achieves competitive or better approximation of given tensors.

paragraphs: This paper develops a fast way to approximate non-negative tensors with lower Tucker ranks. A tensor is a multidimensional array, and reducing its ranks seeks a simpler representation that still captures the original values well. The authors approach this problem by interpreting a tensor as a probability distribution.

Two findings connect that probabilistic view to an algorithm. First, a rank-one tensor approximation can be understood as a mean-field approximation. Second, the authors derive a sufficient condition on distribution parameters for reducing Tucker ranks. Repeated mean-field approximations can achieve that condition. Because each mean-field approximation has a closed-form expression, the resulting method avoids gradient-based optimization.

Experiments show that the algorithm runs faster than existing non-negative Tucker rank reduction methods while producing competitive or better approximations. The theoretical condition establishes one route to lower ranks, rather than claiming that all successful reductions must follow it. The practical significance is that the authors turn a probabilistic approximation into explicit computational steps that deliver favorable speed and reconstruction quality in the reported tests.
summary.tldr: Repeated closed-form mean-field approximations enable fast non-negative tensor rank reduction without gradient optimization.

title: Fast Tucker Rank Reduction for Non-Negative Tensors Using Mean-Field Approximation

abstract: Both the design and control of a robot play equally important roles in its task performance. However, while optimal control is well studied in the machine learning and robotics community, less attention is placed on finding the optimal robot design. This is mainly because co-optimizing design and control in robotics is characterized as a challenging problem, and more importantly, a comprehensive evaluation benchmark for co-optimization does not exist. In this paper, we propose Evolution Gym, the first large-scale benchmark for co-optimizing the design and control of soft robots. In our benchmark, each robot is composed of different types of voxels (e.g., soft, rigid, actuators), resulting in a modular and expressive robot design space. Our benchmark environments span a wide range of tasks, including locomotion on various types of terrains and manipulation. Furthermore, we develop several robot co-evolution algorithms by combining state-of-the-art design optimization methods and deep reinforcement learning techniques. Evaluating the algorithms on our benchmark platform, we observe robots exhibiting increasingly complex behaviors as evolution progresses, with the best evolved designs solving many of our proposed tasks. Additionally, even though robot designs are evolved autonomously from scratch without prior knowledge, they often grow to resemble existing natural creatures while outperforming hand-designed robots. Nevertheless, all tested algorithms fail to find robots that succeed in our hardest environments. This suggests that more advanced algorithms are required to explore the high-dimensional design space and evolve increasingly intelligent robots -- an area of research in which we hope Evolution Gym will accelerate progress. Our website with code, environments, documentation, and tutorials is available at http://evogym.csail.mit.edu/.

paragraphs: A robot’s performance depends on both its physical design and the controller that makes it move. Evolution Gym provides a large-scale benchmark for optimizing these together. The paper addresses the difficulty of comparing methods for this joint problem, where changing a robot’s body also changes what an effective controller must learn.

Robots are assembled from modular voxels with different properties, including soft material, rigid material, and actuators. Tasks cover movement across different terrains and manipulation. The authors combine design-optimization methods with deep reinforcement learning to create and evaluate several algorithms that evolve robot bodies alongside their control strategies.

As evolution progresses, the evaluated robots develop more complex behavior, and the best designs solve many tasks. Designs created from scratch often resemble natural creatures and outperform hand-designed robots. However, every tested algorithm fails on the hardest environments. The benchmark therefore supplies both evidence that joint optimization can produce effective designs and concrete challenges that remain unsolved by the evaluated methods.
summary.tldr: Evolution Gym benchmarks joint robot-body and controller optimization, producing capable evolved robots while exposing tasks that defeat all tested algorithms.

title: Evolution Gym: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Evolving Soft Robots

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have dominated the field of Computer Vision and achieved great success due to their built-in translation equivariance. Group equivariant CNNs (G-CNNs) that incorporate more equivariance can significantly improve the performance of conventional CNNs. However, G-CNNs are faced with two major challenges: \emph{spatial-agnostic problem} and \emph{expensive computational cost}. In this work, we propose a general framework of previous equivariant models, which includes G-CNNs and equivariant self-attention layers as special cases. Under this framework, we explicitly decompose the feature aggregation operation into a kernel generator and an encoder, and decouple the spatial and extra geometric dimensions in the computation. Therefore, our filters are essentially dynamic rather than being spatial-agnostic. We further show that our \emph{E}quivariant model is parameter \emph{E}fficient and computation \emph{E}fficient by complexity analysis, and also data \emph{E}fficient by experiments, so we call our model $E^4$-Net. Extensive experiments verify that our model can significantly improve previous works with smaller model size.Especially, under the setting of training on $1/5$ data of CIFAR10, our model improves G-CNNs by $5\%+$ accuracy,while using only $56\%$ parameters and $68\%$ FLOPs.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks encode how their features should respond to geometric transformations. Ordinary convolutional networks already incorporate translation equivariance, while group-equivariant networks extend this idea. The paper addresses two challenges in those extensions: feature aggregation that is insensitive to spatial context and high computational cost.

The authors introduce a common framework containing both group-equivariant convolutions and equivariant self-attention. They split feature aggregation into a kernel generator and an encoder, and separate computation over spatial dimensions from computation over additional geometric dimensions. This produces dynamic filters. Their model, E⁴-Net, combines equivariance with parameter, computational, and data efficiency; complexity analysis supports the first two efficiency claims, while experiments support the third.

The experiments show improvements over earlier approaches with smaller models. In the specific setting of training on one fifth of CIFAR10, the authors report an accuracy improvement of more than 5% over group-equivariant CNNs while using 56% of their parameters and 68% of their floating-point operations. This example demonstrates the reported benefits under a restricted training-data budget.
summary.tldr: E⁴-Net uses dynamic equivariant feature aggregation to improve accuracy while reducing parameters and computation in the reported experiments.

title: Efficient Equivariant Network

abstract: Ensembles of neural networks achieve superior performance compared to standalone networks in terms of accuracy, uncertainty calibration and robustness to dataset shift. Deep ensembles, a state-of-the-art method for uncertainty estimation, only ensemble random initializations of a fixed architecture. Instead, we propose two methods for automatically constructing ensembles with varying architectures, which implicitly trade-off individual architectures’ strengths against the ensemble’s diversity and exploit architectural variation as a source of diversity. On a variety of classification tasks and modern architecture search spaces, we show that the resulting ensembles outperform deep ensembles not only in terms of accuracy but also uncertainty calibration and robustness to dataset shift. Our further analysis and ablation studies provide evidence of higher ensemble diversity due to architectural variation, resulting in ensembles that can outperform deep ensembles, even when having weaker average base learners. To foster reproducibility, our code is available: https://github.com/automl/nes

paragraphs: Combining neural networks can improve prediction accuracy, confidence calibration, and robustness when evaluation data differ from training data. Conventional deep ensembles build this combination from separate random initializations of one fixed architecture. This paper investigates architectural variation as another source of useful diversity among ensemble members.

The authors propose two methods that automatically construct ensembles containing different architectures. Their selection implicitly balances each architecture’s individual predictive strength against what it contributes to the group’s diversity. This matters because the strongest collection need not consist of the individually strongest models: the ensemble also depends on how well its members complement one another.

Across several classification tasks and modern architecture search spaces, the resulting ensembles outperform deep ensembles in accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and robustness to dataset shift. Further analyses and ablations provide evidence that changing architectures increases diversity. Some resulting ensembles outperform deep ensembles even though their average individual member is weaker. The findings therefore support evaluating architectures as potential collaborators within an ensemble, alongside judging their standalone predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Automatically combining different neural architectures improves ensemble accuracy, calibration, and robustness in the reported classification experiments.

title: Neural Ensemble Search for Uncertainty Estimation and Dataset Shift

abstract: The recent success of transformer models in language, such as BERT, has motivated the use of such architectures for multi-modal feature learning and tasks. However, most multi-modal variants (e.g., ViLBERT) have limited themselves to visual-linguistic data. Relatively few have explored its use in audio-visual modalities, and none, to our knowledge, illustrate them in the context of granular audio-visual detection or segmentation tasks such as sound source separation and localization. In this work, we introduce TriBERT -- a transformer-based architecture, inspired by ViLBERT, which enables contextual feature learning across three modalities: vision, pose, and audio, with the use of flexible co-attention. The use of pose keypoints is inspired by recent works that illustrate that such representations can significantly boost performance in many audio-visual scenarios where often one or more persons are responsible for the sound explicitly (e.g., talking) or implicitly (e.g., sound produced as a function of human manipulating an object). From a technical perspective, as part of the TriBERT architecture, we introduce a learned visual tokenization scheme based on spatial attention and leverage weak-supervision to allow granular cross-modal interactions for visual and pose modalities. Further, we supplement learning with sound-source separation loss formulated across all three streams. We pre-train our model on the large MUSIC21 dataset and demonstrate improved performance in audio-visual sound source separation on that dataset as well as other datasets through fine-tuning. In addition, we show that the learned TriBERT representations are generic and significantly improve performance on other audio-visual tasks such as cross-modal audio-visual-pose retrieval by as much as 66.7% in top-1 accuracy.

paragraphs: TriBERT learns jointly from visual information, human pose, and audio. Human pose is relevant because people can produce sound directly, as in speech, or through actions involving objects. The model uses a transformer architecture with flexible co-attention to learn contextual relationships among these three streams.

Its visual tokenization is learned through spatial attention. Weak supervision supports detailed interactions involving visual and pose information, while a sound-source separation loss trains across all three modalities. Together, these components connect representation learning to the task of separating sounds, giving the model a reason to associate visible activity and body configuration with audio.

The authors pretrain TriBERT on MUSIC21 and report improved audiovisual sound separation there and on other datasets after fine-tuning. They also evaluate the learned representations on other audiovisual tasks. Cross-modal audio-visual-pose retrieval improves by as much as 66.7% in top-1 accuracy. These results support the usefulness of including pose in human-centered audiovisual learning and show that the resulting representations can benefit tasks beyond separation.
summary.tldr: TriBERT combines vision, human pose, and audio through co-attention, improving reported sound separation and cross-modal retrieval.

title: TriBERT: Human-centric Audio-visual Representation Learning

abstract: Most existing temporal action localization (TAL) methods rely on a transfer learning pipeline: by first optimizing a video encoder on a large action classification dataset (i.e., source domain), followed by freezing the encoder and training a TAL head on the action localization dataset (i.e., target domain). This results in a task discrepancy problem for the video encoder – trained for action classification, but used for TAL. Intuitively, joint optimization with both the video encoder and TAL head is a strong baseline solution to this discrepancy. However, this is not operable for TAL subject to the GPU memory constraints, due to the prohibitive computational cost in processing long untrimmed videos. In this paper, we resolve this challenge by introducing a novel low-fidelity (LoFi) video encoder optimization method. Instead of always using the full training configurations in TAL learning, we propose to reduce the mini-batch composition in terms of temporal, spatial, or spatio-temporal resolution so that jointly optimizing the video encoder and TAL head becomes operable under the same memory conditions of a mid-range hardware budget. Crucially, this enables the gradients to flow backwards through the video encoder conditioned on a TAL supervision loss, favourably solving the task discrepancy problem and providing more effective feature representations. Extensive experiments show that the proposed LoFi optimization approach can significantly enhance the performance of existing TAL methods. Encouragingly, even with a lightweight ResNet18 based video encoder in a single RGB stream, our method surpasses two-stream (RGB + optical-flow) ResNet50 based alternatives, often by a good margin. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/saic-fi/lofi_action_localization.

paragraphs: Temporal action localization identifies where actions occur within a video. Many systems first train a video encoder for action classification, freeze it, and then train a localization head. This creates a mismatch: the encoder's training task differs from its eventual use. Joint training could address the mismatch, but processing long untrimmed videos can exceed the available GPU memory.

LoFi makes joint optimization practical by reducing the temporal resolution, spatial resolution, or both in the training mini-batches. Under the same mid-range hardware memory budget, the encoder and localization head can then be updated together. Crucially, localization errors send gradients back through the encoder, allowing its features to adapt to the target task.

The reported experiments show substantial improvements to existing localization methods. Even a lightweight ResNet18 encoder using only RGB video surpasses the compared ResNet50 alternatives using both RGB and optical flow, often by a substantial margin. These results demonstrate the value of adapting the encoder with localization supervision when lower-fidelity training makes that adaptation computationally feasible.
summary.tldr: LoFi lowers video training resolution to enable joint encoder and localization-head optimization within a modest memory budget, improving reported localization performance.

title: Low-Fidelity Video Encoder Optimization for Temporal Action Localization

abstract: We present a variational method for online state estimation and parameter learning in state-space models (SSMs), a ubiquitous class of latent variable models for sequential data. As per standard batch variational techniques, we use stochastic gradients to simultaneously optimize a lower bound on the log evidence with respect to both model parameters and a variational approximation of the states' posterior distribution. However, unlike existing approaches, our method is able to operate in an entirely online manner, such that historic observations do not require revisitation after being incorporated and the cost of updates at each time step remains constant, despite the growing dimensionality of the joint posterior distribution of the states. This is achieved by utilizing backward decompositions of this joint posterior distribution and of its variational approximation, combined with Bellman-type recursions for the evidence lower bound and its gradients. We demonstrate the performance of this methodology across several examples, including high-dimensional SSMs and sequential Variational Auto-Encoders.

paragraphs: State-space models describe sequential observations through hidden states. Learning with these models can require estimating both the hidden states and the parameters governing the sequence. This paper develops a variational method that performs both tasks online, incorporating each new observation without needing to revisit earlier observations afterward.

The method uses stochastic gradients to optimize a lower bound on the data's log evidence with respect to model parameters and an approximate posterior over states. Its distinctive property is constant update cost per time step even as the joint posterior includes an increasing number of states. Here, constant cost refers to growth over time as observations accumulate.

The authors achieve this using backward decompositions of the posterior and its approximation, together with Bellman-type recursions for the objective and gradients. These recursions make it possible to carry the needed calculations forward incrementally. Demonstrations include high-dimensional state-space models and sequential variational autoencoders, showing the method's application across several sequential modeling examples.
summary.tldr: A variational method learns hidden states and model parameters online without revisiting observations or increasing per-step update cost over time.

title: Online Variational Filtering and Parameter Learning

abstract: Optimization is a key component for training machine learning models and has a strong impact on their generalization. In this paper, we consider a particular optimization method---the stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) algorithm---and investigate the generalization of models trained by SGLD. We derive a new generalization bound by connecting SGLD with Gaussian channels found in information and communication theory. Our bound can be computed from the training data and incorporates the variance of gradients for quantifying a particular kind of "sharpness" of the loss landscape. We also consider a closely related algorithm with SGLD, namely differentially private SGD (DP-SGD). We prove that the generalization capability of DP-SGD can be amplified by iteration. Specifically, our bound can be sharpened by including a time-decaying factor if the DP-SGD algorithm outputs the last iterate while keeping other iterates hidden. This decay factor enables the contribution of early iterations to our bound to reduce with time and is established by strong data processing inequalities---a fundamental tool in information theory. We demonstrate our bound through numerical experiments, showing that it can predict the behavior of the true generalization gap.

title: Analyzing the Generalization Capability of SGLD Using Properties of Gaussian Channels

abstract: To tackle interpretability in deep learning, we present a novel framework to jointly learn a predictive model and its associated interpretation model. The interpreter provides both local and global interpretability about the predictive model in terms of human-understandable high level attribute functions, with minimal loss of accuracy. This is achieved by a dedicated architecture and well chosen regularization penalties. We seek for a small-size dictionary of high level attribute functions that take as inputs the outputs of selected hidden layers and whose outputs feed a linear classifier. We impose strong conciseness on the activation of attributes with an entropy-based criterion while enforcing fidelity to both inputs and outputs of the predictive model. A detailed pipeline to visualize the learnt features is also developed. Moreover, besides generating interpretable models by design, our approach can be specialized to provide post-hoc interpretations for a pre-trained neural network. We validate our approach against several state-of-the-art methods on multiple datasets and show its efficacy on both kinds of tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a framework that learns a prediction model together with a model that explains its behavior. The explanations use high-level attributes intended to be understandable to people. They describe both individual predictions and the predictor more broadly, while aiming to preserve predictive accuracy.

The interpreter builds a small dictionary of attribute functions from the outputs of selected hidden layers. These attributes then feed a linear classifier, creating a relatively direct connection between the learned attributes and the interpretation model's decisions. An entropy-based penalty encourages concise attribute activations, while additional requirements keep the interpretation faithful to the predictor's inputs and outputs.

The authors also develop a visualization pipeline for inspecting the learned features. The framework can train interpretable models jointly or be adapted to explain an already trained network. Evaluations against several leading methods across multiple datasets support its effectiveness in both settings. The contribution is a way to make explanation learning part of the modeling process while also supporting explanations after training.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained interpreter explains neural-network predictions through concise high-level attributes with minimal accuracy loss.

title: A Framework to Learn with Interpretation

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) is an effective means to leverage unlabeled data to improve a model’s performance. Typical SSL methods like FixMatch assume that labeled and unlabeled data share the same label space. However, in practice, unlabeled data can contain categories unseen in the labeled set, i.e., outliers, which can significantly harm the performance of SSL algorithms. To address this problem, we propose a novel Open-set Semi-Supervised Learning (OSSL) approach called OpenMatch.Learning representations of inliers while rejecting outliers is essential for the success of OSSL. To this end, OpenMatch unifies FixMatch with novelty detection based on one-vs-all (OVA) classifiers. The OVA-classifier outputs the confidence score of a sample being an inlier, providing a threshold to detect outliers. Another key contribution is an open-set soft-consistency regularization loss, which enhances the smoothness of the OVA-classifier with respect to input transformations and greatly improves outlier detection. \ours achieves state-of-the-art performance on three datasets, and even outperforms a fully supervised model in detecting outliers unseen in unlabeled data on CIFAR10. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/VisionLearningGroup/OP_Match}.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled examples to supplement labeled training data. Many methods assume both sources contain the same categories. OpenMatch addresses a more difficult situation: the unlabeled collection also contains examples from unfamiliar categories. These outliers can harm training if the method treats them as examples of the known classes.

OpenMatch combines FixMatch with novelty detection based on one-vs-all classifiers. Their outputs provide confidence that a sample belongs to the known categories, enabling threshold-based outlier detection. An additional soft-consistency loss encourages the detector’s outputs to vary smoothly under input transformations. The authors report that this regularization substantially improves outlier detection.

The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on three evaluated datasets. On CIFAR10, it also surpasses a fully supervised model at detecting outliers from categories absent even from the unlabeled training data. That specific result suggests the learned detector can extend beyond the outliers encountered during training. Overall, the approach links learning useful known-class representations with rejecting unfamiliar examples from the unlabeled pool.
summary.tldr: OpenMatch combines semi-supervised learning with novelty detection and consistency regularization to learn from unlabeled data containing unknown categories.

title: OpenMatch: Open-Set Semi-supervised Learning with Open-set Consistency Regularization

abstract: We propose a new approach to automated theorem proving where an AlphaZero-style agent is self-training to refine a generic high-level expert strategy expressed as a nondeterministic program. An analogous teacher agent is self-training to generate tasks of suitable relevance and difficulty for the learner. This allows leveraging minimal amounts of domain knowledge to tackle problems for which training data is unavailable or hard to synthesize. As a specific illustration, we consider loop invariant synthesis for imperative programs and use neural networks to refine both the teacher and solver strategies.
