An analogous teacher agent is self-training to generate tasks of suitable relevance and difficulty for the learner. This allows leveraging minimal amounts of domain knowledge to tackle problems for which training data is unavailable or hard to synthesize. As a specific illustration, we consider loop invariant synthesis for imperative programs and use neural networks to refine both the teacher and solver strategies.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an approach to automated theorem proving for settings where training examples are unavailable or difficult to generate. It starts with a generic expert strategy expressed as a nondeterministic program: a high-level procedure that leaves choices open. Learning then refines how those choices are made during search.

An AlphaZero-style learner trains itself to improve that strategy. Alongside it, a teacher agent also self-trains, generating tasks intended to have suitable relevance and difficulty for the learner. Task generation and proof search thus both become learning problems, while the high-level strategy provides a way to incorporate a small amount of domain knowledge.

The authors illustrate the approach with loop invariant synthesis for imperative programs. In this application, neural networks refine both the teacher's strategy and the solver's strategy. The contribution is the combination of structured expert guidance, self-training search, and an adaptive source of tasks. It offers a route to working on proof-related problems without first assembling a conventional collection of training examples.
summary.tldr: Self-training teacher and solver agents refine high-level search strategies for theorem proving, illustrated through loop invariant synthesis.

title: Learning to Find Proofs and Theorems by Learning to Refine Search Strategies: The Case of Loop Invariant Synthesis

abstract: The Gaussian homotopy (GH) method is a popular approach to finding better stationary points for non-convex optimization problems by gradually reducing a parameter value $t$, which changes the problem to be solved from an almost convex one to the original target one. Existing GH-based methods repeatedly call an iterative optimization solver to find a stationary point every time $t$ is updated, which incurs high computational costs. We propose a novel single loop framework for GH methods (SLGH) that updates the parameter $t$ and the optimization decision variables at the same. Computational complexity analysis is performed on the SLGH algorithm under various situations: either a gradient or gradient-free oracle of a GH function can be obtained for both deterministic and stochastic settings. The convergence rate of SLGH with a tuned hyperparameter becomes consistent with the convergence rate of gradient descent, even though the problem to be solved is gradually changed due to $t$. In numerical experiments, our SLGH algorithms show faster convergence than an existing double loop GH method while outperforming gradient descent-based methods in terms of finding a better solution.

paragraphs: Gaussian homotopy tackles a nonconvex objective by starting with an almost convex version and gradually changing it back toward the original problem. A parameter controls this progression. Existing methods repeatedly solve an optimization problem whenever that parameter changes, creating an expensive loop of inner solves within an outer schedule.

The proposed single-loop framework updates the optimization variables and the homotopy parameter together. This removes the need to complete a separate stationary-point search at every parameter update. The authors analyze computational complexity for deterministic and stochastic settings, considering access either to gradients or to gradient-free information about the homotopy function.

With an appropriately tuned hyperparameter, the convergence rate matches that of gradient descent even though the objective changes during optimization. Numerical experiments show faster convergence than an existing double-loop homotopy method and better solutions than gradient-descent-based methods. The theoretical rate and empirical solution quality answer different questions: the method maintains favorable convergence behavior while retaining the practical motivation for gradually transforming a difficult objective.
summary.tldr: Updating the homotopy parameter and optimization variables together reduces nested computation while matching gradient-descent convergence rates with suitable tuning.

title: Single Loop Gaussian Homotopy Method for Non-convex Optimization

abstract: Development of transformer-based text-to-image models is impeded by its slow generation and complexity, for high-resolution images. In this work, we put forward a solution based on hierarchical transformers and local parallel autoregressive generation. We pretrain a 6B-parameter transformer with a simple and flexible self-supervised task, a cross-modal general language model (CogLM), and fine-tune it for fast super-resolution. The new text-to-image system, CogView2, shows very competitive generation compared to concurrent state-of-the-art DALL-E-2, and naturally supports interactive text-guided editing on images.

paragraphs: Generating high-resolution images with transformers can be slow and computationally complicated. CogView2 addresses this problem through a hierarchical transformer design and local parallel autoregressive generation. The approach combines a hierarchy for image generation with a mechanism for carrying out local generation work in parallel, targeting the difficulty of producing detailed images efficiently.

The system begins with CogLM, a transformer containing six billion parameters. It is pretrained using a self-supervised task that brings text and images into a cross-modal language-modeling framework. The authors then fine-tune this model for fast super-resolution, the stage concerned with increasing image resolution. This connects broad cross-modal pretraining with a more specialized image-generation capability.

The resulting system is reported to produce images that are highly competitive with the contemporary DALL-E-2 system. It also supports interactive editing in which text guides changes to an image. The stated contribution therefore combines an efficiency-oriented generation design with competitive image generation and a text-based editing capability, without claiming universal superiority over the comparison system.
summary.tldr: CogView2 combines hierarchical transformers, local parallel generation, and super-resolution training for competitive text-to-image generation and interactive editing.

title: CogView2: Faster and Better Text-to-Image Generation via Hierarchical Transformers

abstract: Few-shot image generation (FSIG) aims to learn to generate new and diverse samples given an extremely limited number of samples from a domain, e.g., 10 training samples. Recent work has addressed the problem using transfer learning approach, leveraging a GAN pretrained on a large-scale source domain dataset and adapting that model to the target domain based on very limited target domain samples. Central to recent FSIG methods are knowledge preserving criteria, which aim to select a subset of source model's knowledge to be preserved into the adapted model. However, a major limitation of existing methods is that their knowledge preserving criteria consider only source domain/source task, and they fail to consider target domain/adaptation task in selecting source model's knowledge, casting doubt on their suitability for setups of different proximity between source and target domain. Our work makes two contributions. As our first contribution, we re-visit recent FSIG works and their experiments. Our important finding is that, under setups which assumption of close proximity between source and target domains is relaxed, existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods which consider only source domain/source task in knowledge preserving perform no better than a baseline fine-tuning method. To address the limitation of existing methods, as our second contribution, we propose Adaptation-Aware kernel Modulation (AdAM) to address general FSIG of different source-target domain proximity. Extensive experimental results show that the proposed method consistently achieves SOTA performance across source/target domains of different proximity, including challenging setups when source and target domains are more apart. Project Page: https://yunqing-me.github.io/AdAM/

paragraphs: Few-shot image generation adapts a pretrained generator to a domain represented by very few examples, such as ten images. Existing approaches often decide which source knowledge to preserve using information about the source task alone. This paper investigates whether that choice remains appropriate when the source and target domains are less closely related.

The authors revisit earlier methods and their experimental setups. When the assumption of close source–target proximity is relaxed, they find that leading methods using source-only preservation criteria perform no better than ordinary fine-tuning. This result makes domain proximity central to evaluating whether a knowledge-preservation strategy is useful.

To address the issue, the paper introduces Adaptation-Aware kernel Modulation, or AdAM. Its approach makes the adaptation task relevant to how source-model knowledge is handled. Across the tested source and target domains, the method consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, including more distant domain pairs. The findings support considering the destination task when adapting a generator from limited examples, especially where source similarity cannot be assumed.
summary.tldr: AdAM improves few-shot generator adaptation across different domain distances by accounting for the adaptation task in handling source knowledge.

title: Few-shot Image Generation via Adaptation-Aware Kernel Modulation

abstract: The proportional fair resource allocation problem is a major problem studied in flow control of networks, operations research, and economic theory, where it has found numerous applications. This problem, defined as the constrained maximization of $\sum_i \log x_i$, is known as the packing proportional fairness problem when the feasible set is defined by positive linear constraints and $x \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^n$. In this work, we present a distributed accelerated first-order method for this problem which improves upon previous approaches. We also design an algorithm for the optimization of its dual problem. Both algorithms are width-independent.

paragraphs: Proportional fairness is a resource allocation objective used in network flow control, operations research, and economics. It chooses allocation quantities by maximizing the sum of their logarithms. In the packing version studied here, allocation variables are nonnegative and must satisfy positive linear constraints describing the feasible use of resources.

The paper introduces an accelerated first-order method for solving this problem in a distributed way. First-order optimization works with gradient information, while the distributed formulation allows the computation to be organized across participants or components. The authors state that their method improves on previous approaches to the packing proportional fairness problem.

They also develop an algorithm for the dual optimization problem, providing a second route for working with the same allocation structure. Both algorithms are width-independent, a shared property of their computational guarantees. The contribution is thus algorithmic on both sides of the formulation: a faster distributed method for the allocation objective and an accompanying method for its dual.
summary.tldr: The paper develops improved width-independent algorithms for packing proportional fairness and its dual.

title: Fast Algorithms for Packing Proportional Fairness and its Dual

abstract: Causal discovery aims to recover causal structures generating the observational data. Despite its success in certain problems, in many real-world scenarios the observed variables are not the target variables of interest, but the imperfect measures of the target variables. Causal discovery under measurement error aims to recover the causal graph among unobserved target variables from observations made with measurement error. We consider a specific formulation of the problem, where the unobserved target variables follow a linear non-Gaussian acyclic model, and the measurement process follows the random measurement error model. Existing methods on this formulation rely on non-scalable over-complete independent component analysis (OICA). In this work, we propose the Transformed Independent Noise (TIN) condition, which checks for independence between a specific linear transformation of some measured variables and certain other measured variables. By leveraging the non-Gaussianity and higher-order statistics of data, TIN is informative about the graph structure among the unobserved target variables. By utilizing TIN, the ordered group decomposition of the causal model is identifiable. In other words, we could achieve what once required OICA to achieve by only conducting independence tests. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of our method.

paragraphs: Causal discovery is complicated when recorded measurements are imperfect versions of the variables whose causal relationships matter. This paper studies recovering structure among those unobserved target variables. Its formulation assumes that the targets follow a linear, non-Gaussian model without causal cycles and that observations follow a random measurement-error model.

Existing methods for this formulation use over-complete independent component analysis, which the authors describe as difficult to scale. They propose the Transformed Independent Noise condition instead. It tests whether a particular linear transformation of some measured variables is independent of other measured variables. Non-Gaussianity and higher-order statistics make these tests informative about the underlying causal structure.

Using this condition, the authors establish identifiability of the causal model's ordered group decomposition. This is the specific structural result claimed, rather than unrestricted recovery of every causal detail. Independence tests can therefore recover a decomposition previously obtained through the more demanding analysis. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the method's effectiveness and reliability under the studied formulation.
summary.tldr: Under linear non-Gaussian and measurement-error assumptions, transformed independence tests identify an ordered decomposition of hidden causal structure.

title: Independence Testing-Based Approach to Causal Discovery under Measurement Error and Linear Non-Gaussian Models

abstract: As we collect additional samples from a data population for which a known density function estimate may have been previously obtained by a black box method, the increased complexity of the data set may result in the true density being deviated from the known estimate by a mixture distribution. To model this phenomenon, we consider the \emph{deviating mixture model} $(1-\lambda^{*})h_0 + \lambda^{*} (\sum_{i = 1}^{k} p_{i}^{*} f(x|\theta_{i}^{*}))$, where $h_0$ is a known density function, while the deviated proportion $\lambda^{*}$ and latent mixing measure $G_{*} = \sum_{i = 1}^{k} p_{i}^{*} \delta_{\theta_i^{*}}$ associated with the mixture distribution are unknown. Via a novel notion of distinguishability between the known density $h_{0}$ and the deviated mixture distribution, we establish rates of convergence for the maximum likelihood estimates of $\lambda^{*}$ and $G^{*}$ under Wasserstein metric. Simulation studies are carried out to illustrate the theory.

paragraphs: The paper considers a population for which a density estimate already exists, possibly from a black-box method. As more samples arrive, that estimate may no longer describe the full distribution adequately. The authors model the difference by combining the known density with an additional mixture distribution, making the new structure an explicit object of statistical estimation.

Two kinds of quantities are unknown: the proportion assigned to the deviating mixture and the mixture's component parameters and weights. Estimating them goes beyond producing another overall density estimate. It asks how much of the population is associated with the deviation and how the components within that deviation are organized.

The authors introduce a notion of distinguishability between the known density and the added mixture. Using it, they establish convergence rates for maximum-likelihood estimates of the deviation proportion and latent mixing measure, with Wasserstein distance used in the analysis. Simulations illustrate the theory. The contribution is a parameter-learning framework whose guarantees explicitly account for distinguishing the new mixture from the existing density.
summary.tldr: A deviating-mixture framework estimates new mixture structure around a known density and provides convergence rates based on distinguishability.

title: Beyond black box densities: Parameter learning for the deviated components

abstract: Knowledge-intensive language tasks require NLP systems to both provide the correct answer and retrieve supporting evidence for it in a given corpus. Autoregressive language models are emerging as the de-facto standard for generating answers, with newer and more powerful systems emerging at an astonishing pace. In this paper we argue that all this (and future) progress can be directly applied to the retrieval problem with minimal intervention to the models' architecture. Previous work has explored ways to partition the search space into hierarchical structures and retrieve documents by autoregressively generating their unique identifier. In this work we propose an alternative that doesn't force any structure in the search space: using all ngrams in a passage as its possible identifiers. This setup allows us to use an autoregressive model to generate and score distinctive ngrams, that are then mapped to full passages through an efficient data structure. Empirically, we show this not only outperforms prior autoregressive approaches but also leads to an average improvement of at least 10 points over more established retrieval solutions for passage-level retrieval on the KILT benchmark, establishing new state-of-the-art downstream performance on some datasets, while using a considerably lighter memory footprint than competing systems. Code available in the supplementary materials. Pre-trained models will be made available.

paragraphs: Knowledge-intensive language systems need to retrieve evidence as well as generate answers. This paper applies autoregressive language models directly to retrieval by letting them generate text that identifies relevant passages. Instead of assigning each passage a unique identifier within a hierarchy, the method treats all of its ngrams, or contiguous text sequences, as possible identifiers. The model generates and scores distinctive sequences, and an efficient data structure maps those sequences back to complete passages. A passage can therefore be reached through multiple pieces of its own text, without imposing a hierarchical organization on the search space.

On KILT passage retrieval, the method outperforms earlier autoregressive approaches and reports an average improvement of at least ten points over established retrieval solutions. It also reaches new best downstream results on some datasets while using substantially less memory than competing systems. These findings support passage text itself as a useful retrieval identifier.
summary.tldr: Generating distinctive passage substrings gives autoregressive models an effective, memory-efficient way to retrieve supporting documents.

title: Autoregressive Search Engines: Generating Substrings as Document Identifiers

abstract: Supervised learning aims to train a classifier under the assumption that training and test data are from the same distribution. To ease the above assumption, researchers have studied a more realistic setting: out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, where test data may come from classes that are unknown during training (i.e., OOD data). Due to the unavailability and diversity of OOD data, good generalization ability is crucial for effective OOD detection algorithms. To study the generalization of OOD detection, in this paper, we investigate the probably approximately correct (PAC) learning theory of OOD detection, which is proposed by researchers as an open problem. First, we find a necessary condition for the learnability of OOD detection. Then, using this condition, we prove several impossibility theorems for the learnability of OOD detection under some scenarios. Although the impossibility theorems are frustrating, we find that some conditions of these impossibility theorems may not hold in some practical scenarios. Based on this observation, we next give several necessary and sufficient conditions to characterize the learnability of OOD detection in some practical scenarios. Lastly, we also offer theoretical supports for several representative OOD detection works based on our OOD theory.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks a model to recognize test examples belonging to classes unknown during training. This creates a generalization problem because the unfamiliar data can be diverse and unavailable in advance. The paper investigates when learning such a detector is theoretically possible using the probably approximately correct learning framework.

The authors first establish a necessary condition for learnability. They use it to prove several impossibility results for particular scenarios. These results identify settings in which the desired learning guarantees cannot be achieved; they do not establish that out-of-distribution detection is impossible in every setting.

The analysis then examines practical scenarios where assumptions underlying those impossibility results may fail. For some of these scenarios, the paper gives necessary and sufficient conditions characterizing learnability. It also uses the resulting theory to support several representative detection methods. The contribution is a conditional account of what makes the problem learnable, connecting negative results with positive characterizations instead of treating detection success as a single unrestricted question.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when out-of-distribution detection is learnable, proving impossibility results and positive conditions for specific scenarios.

title: Is Out-of-Distribution Detection Learnable?

abstract: In the stochastic contextual bandit setting, regret-minimizing algorithms have been extensively researched, but their instance-minimizing best-arm identification counterparts remain seldom studied. In this work, we focus on the stochastic bandit problem in the $(\epsilon,\delta)$-PAC setting: given a policy class $\Pi$ the goal of the learner is to return a policy $\pi\in \Pi$ whose expected reward is within $\epsilon$ of the optimal policy with probability greater than $1-\delta$. We characterize the first instance-dependent PAC sample complexity of contextual bandits through a quantity $\rho_{\Pi}$, and provide matching upper and lower bounds in terms of $\rho_{\Pi}$ for the agnostic and linear contextual best-arm identification settings. We show that no algorithm can be simultaneously minimax-optimal for regret minimization and instance-dependent PAC for best-arm identification. Our main result is a new instance-optimal and computationally efficient algorithm that relies on a polynomial number of calls to a cost-sensitive classification oracle.

paragraphs: This paper studies contextual bandits with the goal of identifying a good policy after collecting data. Given a policy class, the learner must return a policy whose expected reward is within ε of the best in that class, with probability greater than 1−δ. The focus is the number of samples needed for this guarantee.

The authors introduce an instance-dependent quantity, ρΠ, that characterizes this sample requirement. Matching upper and lower bounds are established for agnostic and linear contextual best-arm identification settings. Accounting for the particular problem instance makes the analysis sensitive to how difficult that instance is, rather than describing only worst-case difficulty.

The main algorithm achieves instance-optimal sample complexity and computational efficiency through a polynomial number of calls to a cost-sensitive classification oracle. The paper also proves that one algorithm cannot simultaneously attain the stated minimax optimality for regret minimization and instance-dependent PAC optimality for identification. This separates two objectives that might otherwise appear interchangeable in bandit learning.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes instance-dependent policy-identification complexity and gives an efficient optimal algorithm, separating this goal from regret minimization.

title: Instance-optimal PAC Algorithms for Contextual Bandits

abstract: Recently cloud-based graph convolutional network (GCN) has demonstrated great success and potential in many privacy-sensitive applications such as personal healthcare and financial systems. Despite its high inference accuracy and performance on the cloud, maintaining data privacy in GCN inference, which is of paramount importance to these practical applications, remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we take an initial attempt towards this and develop CryptoGCN--a homomorphic encryption (HE) based GCN inference framework. A key to the success of our approach is to reduce the tremendous computational overhead for HE operations, which can be orders of magnitude higher than its counterparts in the plaintext space. To this end, we develop a solution that can effectively take advantage of the sparsity of matrix operations in GCN inference to significantly reduce the encrypted computational overhead. Specifically, we propose a novel Adjacency Matrix-Aware (AMA) data formatting method along with the AMA assisted patterned sparse matrix partitioning, to exploit the complex graph structure and perform efficient matrix-matrix multiplication in HE computation. In this way, the number of HE operations can be significantly reduced. We also develop a co-optimization framework that can explore the trade-offs among the accuracy, security level, and computational overhead by judicious pruning and polynomial approximation of activation modules in GCNs. Based on the NTU-XVIEW skeleton joint dataset, i.e., the largest dataset evaluated homomorphically by far as we are aware of, our experimental results demonstrate that CryptoGCN outperforms state-of-the-art solutions in terms of the latency and number of homomorphic operations, i.e., achieving as much as a 3.10$\times$ speedup on latency and reduces the total Homomorphic Operation Count (HOC) by 77.4\% with a small accuracy loss of 1-1.5$\%$. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ranran0523/CryptoGCN.

This allows computation on encrypted data, but the required operations can be much more expensive than their unencrypted counterparts. The paper targets that overhead so graph-based prediction can become more practical in privacy-sensitive applications.

Its main technique organizes encrypted data around the graph's adjacency matrix. Adjacency Matrix-Aware formatting and patterned sparse matrix partitioning exploit sparse graph operations to reduce the number of homomorphic computations needed for matrix multiplication. summary.tldr: CryptoGCN exploits graph sparsity to accelerate encrypted inference, reporting up to 3.10-fold lower latency with a small accuracy loss.

title: CryptoGCN: Fast and Scalable Homomorphically Encrypted Graph Convolutional Network Inference

abstract: Cascades are a classical strategy to enable inference cost to vary adaptively across samples, wherein a sequence of classifiers are invoked in turn. A deferral rule determines whether to invoke the next classifier in the sequence, or to terminate prediction. One simple deferral rule employs the confidence of the current classifier, e.g., based on the maximum predicted softmax probability. Despite being oblivious to the structure of the cascade --- e.g., not modelling the errors of downstream models --- such confidence-based deferral often works remarkably well in practice. In this paper, we seek to better understand the conditions under which confidence-based deferral may fail, and when alternate deferral strategies can perform better. We first present a theoretical characterisation of the optimal deferral rule, which precisely characterises settings under which confidence-based deferral may suffer. We then study post-hoc deferral mechanisms, and demonstrate they can significantly improve upon confidence-based deferral in settings where (i) downstream models are specialists that only work well on a subset of inputs, (ii) samples are subject to label noise, and (iii) there is distribution shift between the train and test set.

paragraphs: A classifier cascade adjusts prediction cost by deciding whether each input needs another model’s attention. A common rule stops when the current classifier is confident and otherwise passes the input onward. This can work well, but the current model’s confidence does not explicitly describe how useful the next model will be.

The paper characterizes the optimal deferral rule theoretically and uses that result to identify settings where confidence-based decisions may perform poorly. The key issue is that deciding whether to continue depends on the structure of the cascade, including downstream model errors. Confidence in the current answer can leave out information relevant to that decision.

The authors then study post-hoc deferral mechanisms and demonstrate significant improvements in three settings: downstream specialists that work well only on some inputs, noisy labels, and shifts between training and test distributions. These findings clarify when simple confidence rules deserve closer scrutiny. They support alternative deferral strategies in the studied conditions without implying that confidence-based cascades generally fail.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal cascade deferral and shows when post-hoc alternatives can outperform rules based only on current-model confidence.

title: When Does Confidence-Based Cascade Deferral Suffice?

abstract: One of the central questions in the theory of deep learning is to understand how neural networks learn hierarchical features. The ability of deep networks to extract salient features is crucial to both their outstanding generalization ability and the modern deep learning paradigm of pretraining and finetuneing. However, this feature learning process remains poorly understood from a theoretical perspective, with existing analyses largely restricted to two-layer networks. In this work we show that three-layer neural networks have provably richer feature learning capabilities than two-layer networks. We analyze the features learned by a three-layer network trained with layer-wise gradient descent, and present a general purpose theorem which upper bounds the sample complexity and width needed to achieve low test error when the target has specific hierarchical structure. We instantiate our framework in specific statistical learning settings -- single-index models and functions of quadratic features -- and show that in the latter setting three-layer networks obtain a sample complexity improvement over all existing guarantees for two-layer networks. Crucially, this sample complexity improvement relies on the ability of three-layer networks to efficiently learn *nonlinear* features. We then establish a concrete optimization-based depth separation by constructing a function which is efficiently learnable via gradient descent on a three-layer network, yet cannot be learned efficiently by a two-layer network. Our work makes progress towards understanding the provable benefit of three-layer neural networks over two-layer networks in the feature learning regime.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why an additional neural-network layer can help a model learn useful features. Much existing theory focuses on two-layer networks, leaving hierarchical feature learning less understood. The authors analyze three-layer networks trained by layer-wise gradient descent and establish richer feature-learning capabilities in the settings studied.

Their general theorem bounds the number of samples and network width sufficient for low test error when the target has a specified hierarchical structure. They apply the framework to single-index models and functions of quadratic features. For the quadratic-feature setting, their sample-complexity guarantee improves on existing guarantees for two-layer networks, with the improvement depending on efficient learning of nonlinear features.

The authors also construct a function that gradient descent can learn efficiently with a three-layer network but that a two-layer network cannot learn efficiently. This gives a concrete optimization-based separation between the depths. The result supplies a provable benefit of depth under the analyzed structure and training procedure, rather than a general claim that three layers always outperform two.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that three-layer networks can efficiently learn nonlinear features that yield advantages over two-layer networks in specified settings.

title: Provable Guarantees for Nonlinear Feature Learning in Three-Layer Neural Networks

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) can provide a principled approach to uncertainty quantification with easy-to-interpret kernel hyperparameters, such as the lengthscale, which controls the correlation distance of function values.However, selecting an appropriate kernel can be challenging.Deep GPs avoid manual kernel engineering by successively parameterizing kernels with GP layers, allowing them to learn low-dimensional embeddings of the inputs that explain the output data.Following the architecture of deep neural networks, the most common deep GPs warp the input space layer-by-layer but lose all the interpretability of shallow GPs. An alternative construction is to successively parameterize the lengthscale of a kernel, improving the interpretability but ultimately giving away the notion of learning lower-dimensional embeddings. Unfortunately, both methods are susceptible to particular pathologies which may hinder fitting and limit their interpretability.This work proposes a novel synthesis of both previous approaches: {Thin and Deep GP} (TDGP). Each TDGP layer defines locally linear transformations of the original input data maintaining the concept of latent embeddings while also retaining the interpretation of lengthscales of a kernel. Moreover, unlike the prior solutions, TDGP induces non-pathological manifolds that admit learning lower-dimensional representations.We show with theoretical and experimental results that i) TDGP is, unlike previous models, tailored to specifically discover lower-dimensional manifolds in the input data, ii) TDGP behaves well when increasing the number of layers, and iii) TDGP performs well in standard benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer uncertainty estimates and interpretable kernel parameters, such as a lengthscale describing how far correlations extend. Choosing the kernel can nevertheless be difficult. Deep Gaussian processes learn more flexible structures, but common constructions sacrifice either this interpretability or the ability to learn lower-dimensional embeddings, and can develop problematic behavior.

Thin and Deep Gaussian Processes combine these two approaches. Each layer defines locally linear transformations of the original inputs. This retains latent embeddings while preserving the interpretation of kernel lengthscales. The construction is designed to discover lower-dimensional structure without the manifold pathologies associated with the prior approaches discussed by the authors.

Theoretical and experimental results support three claims: the model is specifically suited to finding lower-dimensional manifolds, behaves well as layers are added, and performs well on standard benchmark datasets. The contribution is a particular architecture that joins representation learning with interpretable correlation structure. Its reported behavior with increasing depth also addresses a difficulty that can make deeper probabilistic models harder to fit and interpret.
summary.tldr: Thin and Deep Gaussian Processes learn lower-dimensional structure while retaining interpretable lengthscales and favorable behavior with depth.

title: Thin and deep Gaussian processes

abstract: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a powerful medical imaging modality that offers diagnostic information without harmful ionizing radiation. Unlike optical imaging, MRI sequentially samples the spatial Fourier domain (k-space) of the image. Measurements are collected in multiple shots, or readouts, and in each shot, data along a smooth trajectory is sampled.Conventional MRI data acquisition relies on sampling k-space row-by-row in short intervals, which is slow and inefficient. More efficient, non-Cartesian sampling trajectories (e.g., Spirals) use longer data readout intervals, but are more susceptible to magnetic field inhomogeneities, leading to off-resonance artifacts. Spiral trajectories cause off-resonance blurring in the image, and the mathematics of this blurring resembles that of optical blurring, where magnetic field variation corresponds to depth and readout duration to aperture size. Off-resonance blurring is a system issue with a physics-based, accurate forward model. We present a physics-informed deep learning framework for off-resonance correction in MRI, which is trained exclusively on synthetic, noise-like data with representative marginal statistics. Our approach allows for fat/water separation and is compatible with parallel imaging acceleration. Through end-to-end training using synthetic randomized data (i.e., noise-like images, coil sensitivities, field maps), we train the network to reverse off-resonance effects across diverse anatomies and contrasts without retraining. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through results on phantom and in-vivo data. This work has the potential to facilitate the clinical adoption of non-Cartesian sampling trajectories, enabling efficient, rapid, and motion-robust MRI scans. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/mikgroup/ResoNet.

summary.tldr: ResoNet learns MRI off-resonance correction entirely from synthetic noise-like data and works across anatomies and contrasts without retraining.

title: ResoNet: Noise-Trained Physics-Informed MRI Off-Resonance Correction

abstract: The Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (SLTH) states that randomly-initialised neural networks likely contain subnetworks that perform well without any training. Although unstructured pruning has been extensively studied in this context, its structured counterpart, which can deliver significant computational and memory efficiency gains, has been largely unexplored. One of the main reasons for this gap is the limitations of the underlying mathematical tools used in formal analyses of the SLTH.In this paper, we overcome these limitations: we leverage recent advances in the multidimensional generalisation of the Random Subset-Sum Problem and obtain a variant that admits the stochastic dependencies that arise when addressing structured pruning in the SLTH. We apply this result to prove, for a wide class of random Convolutional Neural Networks, the existence of structured subnetworks that can approximate any sufficiently smaller network.This result provides the first sub-exponential bound around the SLTH for structured pruning, opening up new avenues for further research on the hypothesis and contributing to the understanding of the role of over-parameterization in deep learning.

paragraphs: The Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis proposes that a randomly initialized neural network is likely to contain useful subnetworks that require no weight training. Much of the existing analysis concerns unstructured pruning. Structured pruning is particularly interesting because it can offer computational and memory savings, but its mathematical analysis has been constrained by tools that do not handle the relevant dependencies.

This paper develops a suitable variant of a multidimensional random subset-sum result. The key extension accommodates stochastic dependencies that arise when analyzing structured pruning. The authors apply this mathematical tool to a broad class of random convolutional neural networks, proving that they contain structured subnetworks capable of approximating any sufficiently smaller target network.

The result establishes a sub-exponential bound for the structured version of the hypothesis, with polynomial over-parameterization highlighted in the paper’s title. Its significance is an existence guarantee about what random networks can contain. The claim concerns approximation of sufficiently smaller networks, preserving the size relationship central to the theorem. It strengthens the theoretical account of how over-parameterization can support useful structured subnetworks.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that a broad class of over-parameterized random convolutional networks contains structured subnetworks approximating sufficiently smaller networks.

title: Polynomially Over-Parameterized Convolutional Neural Networks Contain Structured Strong Winning Lottery Tickets

abstract: We present an efficient algorithm for regularized optimal transport. In contrast toprevious methods, we use the Douglas-Rachford splitting technique to developan efficient solver that can handle a broad class of regularizers. The algorithmhas strong global convergence guarantees, low per-iteration cost, and can exploitGPU parallelization, making it considerably faster than the state-of-the-art formany problems. We illustrate its competitiveness in several applications, includingdomain adaptation and learning of generative models.

In contrast toprevious methods, we use the Douglas-Rachford splitting technique to developan efficient solver that can handle a broad class of regularizers. The algorithmhas strong global convergence guarantees, low per-iteration cost, and can exploitGPU parallelization, making it considerably faster than the state-of-the-art formany problems. paragraphs: This paper introduces a solver for regularized optimal transport, focusing on both computational efficiency and flexibility in the choice of regularizer. Its central design uses Douglas-Rachford splitting. The authors develop this technique into an algorithm that can handle a broad class of regularizers, making the solver applicable across multiple versions of the optimization problem.

The method combines strong global convergence guarantees with inexpensive iterations and support for GPU parallelization. These properties address complementary concerns: the convergence analysis establishes the algorithm's behavior, while the iteration cost and parallel execution affect how quickly it can run. The reported advantage therefore involves both mathematical guarantees and a computational design suited to GPU hardware.

The authors report that the solver is considerably faster than leading methods on many problems and demonstrate its competitiveness in domain adaptation and generative-model learning. The scope of that speed claim is many problems, rather than every possible use. Together, the results support a practical solver that combines regularizer flexibility, convergence guarantees, and efficient computation.
summary.tldr: A GPU-friendly Douglas-Rachford solver supports a broad class of regularized optimal transport problems with global convergence guarantees and reported speed improvements.

title: Bringing regularized optimal transport to lightspeed: a splitting method adapted for GPUs

abstract: The MineRL BASALT competition has served to catalyze advances in learning from human feedback through four hard-to-specify tasks in Minecraft, such as create and photograph a waterfall. Given the completion of two years of BASALT competitions, we offer to the community a formalized benchmark through the BASALT Evaluation and Demonstrations Dataset (BEDD), which serves as a resource for algorithm development and performance assessment. BEDD consists of a collection of 26 million image-action pairs from nearly 14,000 videos of human players completing the BASALT tasks in Minecraft. It also includes over 3,000 dense pairwise human evaluations of human and algorithmic agents. These comparisons serve as a fixed, preliminary leaderboard for evaluating newly-developed algorithms. To enable this comparison, we present a streamlined codebase for benchmarking new algorithms against the leaderboard. In addition to presenting these datasets, we conduct a detailed analysis of the data from both datasets to guide algorithm development and evaluation. The released code and data are available at https://github.com/minerllabs/basalt-benchmark.

To enable this comparison, we present a streamlined codebase for benchmarking new algorithms against the leaderboard. In addition to presenting these datasets, we conduct a detailed analysis of the data from both datasets to guide algorithm development and evaluation. The released code and data are available at https://github.com/minerllabs/basalt-benchmark.

paragraphs: Some tasks are easy for people to recognize as successful but difficult to specify precisely for an algorithm. The BASALT Minecraft tasks explore this problem through activities such as creating and photographing a waterfall. BEDD turns material from two years of these competitions into a formal benchmark for developing and assessing agents that tackle such loosely specified goals.

The dataset contains 26 million image-action pairs drawn from nearly 14,000 videos of human players completing the tasks. These demonstrations record both what players saw and what they did. A separate evaluation collection supplies more than 3,000 dense pairwise human judgments comparing human and algorithmic agents, providing evidence about how people assess task performance.

The comparisons form a fixed, preliminary leaderboard, and an accompanying codebase supports benchmarking new algorithms against it. The paper also analyzes both collections to help researchers use them for training and evaluation. Its contribution is a shared resource connecting demonstrations with human assessments, making progress on tasks with difficult-to-formalize success criteria easier to compare.
summary.tldr: BEDD combines Minecraft demonstrations and human comparisons into a benchmark for agents solving hard-to-specify tasks.

title: BEDD: The MineRL BASALT Evaluation and Demonstrations Dataset for Training and Benchmarking Agents that Solve Fuzzy Tasks

abstract: Uncertainty quantification is crucial for the deployment of image restoration models in safety-critical domains, like autonomous driving and biological imaging. To date, methods for uncertainty visualization have mainly focused on per-pixel estimates. Yet, a heatmap of per-pixel variances is typically of little practical use, as it does not capture the strong correlations between pixels. A more natural measure of uncertainty corresponds to the variances along the principal components (PCs) of the posterior distribution. Theoretically, the PCs can be computed by applying PCA on samples generated from a conditional generative model for the input image. However, this requires generating a very large number of samples at test time, which is painfully slow with the current state-of-the-art (diffusion) models. In this work, we present a method for predicting the PCs of the posterior distribution for any input image, in a single forward pass of a neural network. Our method can either wrap around a pre-trained model that was trained to minimize the mean square error (MSE), or can be trained from scratch to output both a predicted image and the posterior PCs. We showcase our method on multiple inverse problems in imaging, including denoising, inpainting, super-resolution, and biological image-to-image translation. Our method reliably conveys instance-adaptive uncertainty directions, achieving uncertainty quantification comparable with posterior samplers while being orders of magnitude faster. Code and examples are available on our [webpage](https://eliasnehme.github.io/NPPC/).

abstract: Deployed language models decay over time due to shifting inputs, changing user needs, or emergent world-knowledge gaps. When such problems are identified, we want to make targeted edits while avoiding expensive retraining. However, current model editors, which modify such behaviors of pre-trained models, degrade model performance quickly across multiple, sequential edits. We propose GRACE, a \textit{lifelong} model editing method, which implements spot-fixes on streaming errors of a deployed model, ensuring minimal impact on unrelated inputs. GRACE writes new mappings into a pre-trained model's latent space, creating a discrete, local codebook of edits without altering model weights. This is the first method enabling thousands of sequential edits using only streaming errors. Our experiments on T5, BERT, and GPT models show GRACE's state-of-the-art performance in making and retaining edits, while generalizing to unseen inputs. Our code is available at [github.com/thartvigsen/grace](https://www.github.com/thartvigsen/grace}).

paragraphs: GRACE addresses the problem of repeatedly correcting a deployed language model as its inputs, user requirements, and knowledge needs change. Retraining can be expensive, while existing editing methods can lose performance after many successive corrections. The aim is therefore to accumulate targeted repairs while keeping unrelated behavior largely intact.

The method stores new mappings inside the model's latent representation space without changing its original weights. These mappings form a discrete, local codebook of edits: corrections are represented as localized additions to the model's behavior. GRACE builds this codebook from errors arriving over time, allowing the editing process to continue as new problems are discovered.

The authors report thousands of sequential edits using only this stream of errors. Experiments with T5, BERT, and GPT models show state-of-the-art performance at applying and retaining corrections, together with generalization to unseen inputs. The findings matter because successful continual editing requires both remembering earlier fixes and extending them beyond the exact examples that prompted them.
summary.tldr: GRACE stores localized corrections in a model's latent space, enabling thousands of sequential edits without changing its pretrained weights.

title: Aging with GRACE: Lifelong Model Editing with Discrete Key-Value Adaptors

abstract: The adversarial attacks have attracted increasing attention in various fields including natural language processing. The current textual attacking models primarily focus on fooling models by adding character-/word-/sentence-level perturbations, ignoring their influence on human perception. In this paper, for the first time in the community, we propose a novel mode of textual attack, punctuation-level attack. With various types of perturbations, including insertion, displacement, deletion, and replacement, the punctuation-level attack achieves promising fooling rates against SOTA models on typical textual tasks and maintains minimal influence on human perception and understanding of the text by mere perturbation of single-shot single punctuation. Furthermore, we propose a search method named Text Position Punctuation Embedding and Paraphrase (TPPEP) to accelerate the pursuit of optimal position to deploy the attack, without exhaustive search, and we present a mathematical interpretation of TPPEP. Thanks to the integrated Text Position Punctuation Embedding (TPPE), the punctuation attack can be applied at a constant cost of time. Experimental results on public datasets and SOTA models demonstrate the effectiveness of the punctuation attack and the proposed TPPE. We additionally apply the single punctuation attack to summarization, semantic-similarity-scoring, and text-to-image tasks, and achieve encouraging results.

paragraphs: Text models can be vulnerable to small changes in their inputs. This paper investigates attacks that alter a single punctuation mark, aiming to disrupt model behavior while minimally affecting how people perceive and understand the text. The considered edits include inserting, moving, deleting, and replacing punctuation.

The authors also introduce Text Position Punctuation Embedding and Paraphrase, or TPPEP, to find a useful attack position without exhaustively checking every possibility. They provide a mathematical interpretation of this search method. Its integrated Text Position Punctuation Embedding component enables the punctuation attack to be applied at constant time cost, according to the paper.

Experiments on public datasets and state-of-the-art models show promising fooling rates and support the effectiveness of the proposed position embedding. Additional applications to summarization, semantic similarity scoring, and text-to-image tasks yield encouraging results. The findings highlight a mismatch between human and model sensitivity: a punctuation edit with little perceived effect can still substantially alter a model's behavior.
summary.tldr: Single-punctuation edits can fool text models, and a proposed search method finds attack positions without exhaustive evaluation.

title: Punctuation-level Attack: Single-shot and Single Punctuation Can Fool Text Models

abstract: This paper presents a case study on the design, administration, post-processing, and evaluation of surveys on large language models (LLMs). It comprises two components:(1) A statistical method for eliciting beliefs encoded in LLMs. We introduce statistical measures and evaluation metrics that quantify the probability of an LLM "making a choice", the associated uncertainty, and the consistency of that choice.(2) We apply this method to study what moral beliefs are encoded in different LLMs, especially in ambiguous cases where the right choice is not obvious.We design a large-scale survey comprising 680 high-ambiguity moral scenarios (e.g., "Should I tell a white lie?") and 687 low-ambiguity moral scenarios (e.g., "Should I stop for a pedestrian on the road?"). Each scenario includes a description, two possible actions, and auxiliary labels indicating violated rules (e.g., "do not kill"). We administer the survey to 28 open- and closed-source LLMs.We find that (a) in unambiguous scenarios, most models ``choose" actions that align with commonsense. In ambiguous cases, most models express uncertainty.(b) Some models are uncertain about choosing the commonsense action because their responses are sensitive to the question-wording.(c) Some models reflect clear preferences in ambiguous scenarios. Specifically, closed-source models tend to agree with each other.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to survey language models about moral choices while measuring more than the action appearing in a single response. Its statistical method estimates the probability of choosing an action, uncertainty about that choice, and consistency. These distinctions matter when responses vary with how a scenario is presented.

The authors construct 680 highly ambiguous moral scenarios and 687 less ambiguous scenarios, each with two possible actions and labels identifying relevant rule violations. They administer the survey to 28 open- and closed-source models. The design allows them to compare response patterns where a commonsense answer is relatively clear and where competing considerations make the choice less obvious.

Most models select commonsense actions in unambiguous cases and express uncertainty in ambiguous ones. Some uncertainty about commonsense choices arises from sensitivity to wording. Other models show clear preferences even in ambiguous scenarios, with closed-source models tending to agree. These findings characterize elicited response patterns and their stability, giving a more detailed picture than treating every model answer as an equally firm preference.
summary.tldr: A statistical survey of 28 language models measures moral-choice preferences, uncertainty, and wording sensitivity across ambiguous and clearer scenarios.

title: Evaluating the Moral Beliefs Encoded in LLMs

abstract: Domain generalization (DG) is a fundamental yet challenging topic in machine learning. Recently, the remarkable zero-shot capabilities of the large pre-trained vision-language model (e.g., CLIP) have made it popular for various downstream tasks. However, the effectiveness of this capacity often degrades when there are shifts in data distribution during testing compared to the training data. In this paper, we propose a novel method, known as CLIPCEIL, a model that utilizes Channel rEfinement and Image-text aLignment to facilitate the CLIP to the inaccessible $\textit{out-of-distribution}$ test datasets that exhibit domain shifts. Specifically, we refine the feature channels in the visual domain to ensure they contain domain-invariant and class-relevant features by using a lightweight adapter. This is achieved by minimizing the inter-domain variance while maximizing the inter-class variance. In the meantime, we ensure the image-text alignment by aligning text embeddings of the class descriptions and their corresponding image embedding while further removing the domain-specific features. Moreover, our model integrates multi-scale CLIP features by utilizing a self-attention fusion module, technically implemented through one Transformer layer. Extensive experiments on five widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate that CLIPCEIL outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/yuxi120407/CLIPCEIL}.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can recognize categories without task-specific examples yet still struggle when test images differ from its training data. CLIPCEIL addresses this domain generalization problem by adapting CLIP to emphasize information that identifies classes across domains. The target test datasets are unavailable during this adaptation.

Its first component is a lightweight adapter that refines visual feature channels. Training reduces variation between domains while increasing variation between classes, encouraging features that remain useful despite changes in the data source. A second component aligns image representations with text descriptions of their classes while further suppressing domain-specific information. These objectives connect visual robustness with the class meaning provided by language.

CLIPCEIL also combines CLIP features at multiple scales through a self-attention module implemented as one Transformer layer. The authors report better performance than existing state-of-the-art methods across five benchmark datasets. These results support the combined strategy of refining visual channels, preserving image-text correspondence, and integrating multiple feature scales for the evaluated distribution shifts.
summary.tldr: CLIPCEIL improves domain generalization by refining CLIP’s visual channels, aligning images with class descriptions, and combining features across scales.

title: CLIPCEIL: Domain Generalization through CLIP via Channel rEfinement and Image-text aLignment

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) often suffer from the overconfidence issue, where incorrect predictions are made with high confidence scores, hindering the applications in critical systems. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Typicalness-Aware Learning (TAL) to address this issue and improve failure detection performance. We observe that, with the cross-entropy loss, model predictions are optimized to align with the corresponding labels via increasing logit magnitude or refining logit direction. However, regarding atypical samples, the image content and their labels may exhibit disparities. This discrepancy can lead to overfitting on atypical samples, ultimately resulting in the overconfidence issue that we aim to address.To address this issue, we have devised a metric that quantifies the typicalness of each sample, enabling the dynamic adjustment of the logit magnitude during the training process. By allowing relatively atypical samples to be adequately fitted while preserving reliable logit direction, the problem of overconfidence can be mitigated. TAL has been extensively evaluated on benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing failure detection methods. Specifically, TAL achieves a more than 5\% improvement on CIFAR100 in terms of the Area Under the Risk-Coverage Curve (AURC) compared to the state-of-the-art. Code is available at https://github.com/liuyijungoon/TAL.

paragraphs: Failure detection becomes difficult when a neural network gives an incorrect prediction a high confidence score. This paper links that problem to how cross-entropy training fits atypical examples. Predictions can be aligned with labels by increasing logit magnitude or refining logit direction, but atypical image content may fit its label less naturally and encourage overfitting.

Typicalness-Aware Learning assigns each sample a typicalness measure and uses it to adjust logit magnitude dynamically during training. The aim is to fit relatively atypical examples adequately while retaining reliable logit direction. This targets the training behavior that can make confidence excessive, rather than simply treating every example’s fit in the same way.

The authors evaluate the method on benchmark datasets and report stronger failure detection than existing methods. On CIFAR100, they report more than a 5% improvement in Area Under the Risk-Coverage Curve relative to the state of the art. The findings support sample typicalness as a useful signal for mitigating overconfidence and making prediction failures easier to identify.
summary.tldr: Typicalness-Aware Learning adjusts logit magnitude using sample typicalness to reduce overconfidence and improve reported failure-detection performance.

title: Typicalness-Aware Learning for Failure Detection

abstract: Real-world image denoising remains a challenge task. This paper studies self-supervised image denoising, requiring only noisy images captured in a single shot. We revamping the blind-spot technique by leveraging the transformer’s capability for long-range pixel interactions, which is crucial for effectively removing noise dependence in relating pixel–a requirement for achieving great performance for the blind-spot technique. The proposed method integrates these elements with two key innovations: a directional self-attention (DSA) module using a half-plane grid for self-attention, creating a sophisticated blind-spot structure, and a Siamese architecture with mutual learning to mitigate the performance impactsfrom the restricted attention grid in DSA. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing self-supervised and clean-image-free methods. This combination of blind-spot and transformer techniques provides a natural synergy for tackling real-world image denoising challenges.

paragraphs: This paper develops self-supervised image denoising using only noisy images captured in a single shot. It revisits the blind-spot approach through transformers, emphasizing their ability to connect pixels over long distances. The authors identify dependence between noise in related pixels as an important obstacle to strong blind-spot denoising performance.

The proposed directional self-attention module restricts attention using a half-plane grid, creating the model's blind-spot structure. That restriction shapes which image information can interact, but also affects performance by narrowing the attention pattern. A Siamese architecture with mutual learning is introduced to mitigate those effects, pairing the attention constraint with a mechanism for improving learning.

Benchmark experiments show better performance than existing self-supervised and clean-image-free denoising methods. The findings support combining long-range transformer interactions with deliberately constrained attention and mutual learning. The contribution is a coordinated architecture for learning from noisy observations, with each component addressing a different aspect of making blind-spot denoising work on real-world images.
summary.tldr: Directional attention and Siamese mutual learning improve blind-spot transformer denoising using only single-shot noisy images.

title: Pseudo-Siamese Blind-spot Transformers for Self-Supervised Real-World Denoising

abstract: Large language models can memorize and repeat their training data, causing privacy and copyright risks. To mitigate memorization, we introduce a subtle modification to the next-token training objective that we call the goldfish loss. During training, a randomly sampled subsets of tokens are excluded from the loss computation. These dropped tokens are not memorized by the model, which prevents verbatim reproduction of a complete chain of tokens from the training set. We run extensive experiments training billion-scale LLaMA-2 models, both pre-trained and trained from scratch, and demonstrate significant reductions in extractable memorization with little to no impact on downstream benchmarks._Code and checkpoints: https://github.com/ahans30/goldfish-loss_

paragraphs: Language models can reproduce passages from their training data, creating privacy and copyright concerns. This paper addresses that behavior by changing the objective used during training. The proposed goldfish loss keeps the next-token prediction setting but leaves a randomly selected subset of tokens out of the loss calculation.

The central idea is to interrupt the learning signal that supports exact reproduction of a complete passage. According to the authors, the omitted tokens are not memorized, breaking the chain needed to repeat an entire training sequence verbatim. The intervention therefore operates at the level of which token predictions contribute to training, targeting memorization through a small change to the objective.

The authors test the method with billion-scale LLaMA-2 models, including models that were already pretrained and models trained from scratch. They report substantial reductions in extractable memorization with little or no effect on the downstream benchmarks evaluated. These findings support goldfish loss as a way to reduce recoverable training text while retaining measured task performance.
summary.tldr: Goldfish loss omits randomly selected tokens from training loss to reduce extractable memorization with little measured downstream impact.

title: Be like a Goldfish, Don't Memorize! Mitigating Memorization in Generative LLMs

abstract: Existing image-text modality alignment in Vision Language Models (VLMs) treats each text token equally in an autoregressive manner. Despite being simple and effective, this method results in sub-optimal cross-modal alignment by over-emphasizing the text tokens that are less correlated with or even contradictory with the input images. In this paper, we advocate for distinct contributions for each text token based on its visual correlation. Specifically, we present by contrasting image inputs, the difference in prediction logits on each text token provides strong guidance of visual correlation. We therefore introduce Contrastive Alignment (CAL), a simple yet effective re-weighting strategy that prioritizes training visually correlated tokens. Our experimental results demonstrate that CAL consistently improves different types of VLMs across different resolutions and model sizes on various benchmark datasets. Importantly, our method incurs minimal additional computational overhead, rendering it highly efficient compared to alternative data scaling strategies.

paragraphs: Vision-language models commonly learn image-text alignment by giving every text token equal treatment during autoregressive training. The paper argues that this can place too much emphasis on words that have little connection to the image, or even contradict it. Equal weighting can therefore weaken the connection between visual evidence and the language being learned.

Contrastive Alignment, or CAL, assigns different training weights according to each token’s visual correlation. To estimate that correlation, the method contrasts image inputs and examines how the prediction logits for each token change. Those differences provide a signal for identifying tokens whose predictions are more closely connected to the visual input.

Experiments show consistent improvements across different types of vision-language models, image resolutions, model sizes, and benchmark datasets. The authors also report minimal additional computational overhead, making the method efficient relative to alternative data-scaling strategies. The finding supports improving alignment through a more selective training signal: the method changes which tokens receive emphasis based on their relationship to the image.
summary.tldr: CAL improves vision-language alignment by weighting text tokens according to how strongly their predictions depend on the image.

title: Seeing the Image: Prioritizing Visual Correlation by Contrastive Alignment

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel conceptual framework to detect outliers using optimal transport with a concave cost function. Conventional outlier detection approaches typically use a two-stage procedure: first, outliers are detected and removed, and then estimation is performed on the cleaned data. However, this approach does not inform outlier removal with the estimation task, leaving room for improvement. To address this limitation, we propose an automatic outlier rectification mechanism that integrates rectification and estimation within a joint optimization framework. We take the first step to utilize the optimal transport distance with a concave cost function to construct a rectification set in the space of probability distributions. Then, we select the best distribution within the rectification set to perform the estimation task. Notably, the concave cost function we introduced in this paper is the key to making our estimator effectively identify the outlier during the optimization process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach over conventional approaches in simulations and empirical analyses for mean estimation, least absolute regression, and the fitting of option implied volatility surfaces.

paragraphs: Outlier handling often happens before the main estimation task: suspicious observations are removed, and an estimate is then fitted to what remains. This separation means the estimation objective cannot help determine which observations should be treated as outliers. The paper instead makes correction and estimation parts of one optimization problem.

The method uses an optimal transport distance with a concave cost to define a set of possible corrected probability distributions. It then chooses a distribution from that set according to the estimation task. This changes the central decision from simply deleting individual observations to selecting a suitable distribution for the quantity being estimated. The authors identify the concave transport cost as essential to detecting outliers during optimization.

The approach is evaluated through simulations and empirical analyses involving mean estimation, least absolute regression, and option implied volatility surface fitting. These results demonstrate effectiveness relative to conventional approaches in the studied tasks. The broader methodological contribution is a way to let the purpose of an analysis guide outlier treatment, rather than making that treatment an independent preprocessing decision.
summary.tldr: The paper jointly optimizes outlier correction and estimation using a concave-cost optimal transport framework.

title: Automatic Outlier Rectification via Optimal Transport

abstract: Pre-training plays a vital role in various vision tasks, such as object recognition and detection. Commonly used pre-training methods, which typically rely on randomized approaches like uniform or Gaussian distributions to initialize model parameters, often fall short when confronted with long-tailed distributions, especially in detection tasks. This is largely due to extreme data imbalance and the issue of simplicity bias. In this paper, we introduce a novel pre-training framework for object detection, called Dynamic Rebalancing Contrastive Learning with Dual Reconstruction (2DRCL). Our method builds on a Holistic-Local Contrastive Learning mechanism, which aligns pre-training with object detection by capturing both global contextual semantics and detailed local patterns. To tackle the imbalance inherent in long-tailed data, we design a dynamic rebalancing strategy that adjusts the sampling of underrepresented instances throughout the pre-training process, ensuring better representation of tail classes. Moreover, Dual Reconstruction addresses simplicity bias by enforcing a reconstruction task aligned with the self-consistency principle, specifically benefiting underrepresented tail classes. Experiments on COCO and LVIS v1.0 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, particularly in improving the mAP/AP scores for tail classes.

These findings connect the method's design to its intended outcome: better detection of categories that receive relatively little data. The contribution is the combined pretraining framework, addressing feature scale, sampling imbalance, and reconstruction together.
summary.tldr: 2DRCL combines global-local contrastive learning, dynamic sampling, and dual reconstruction to improve detection of underrepresented object categories.

title: Long-tailed Object Detection Pretraining: Dynamic Rebalancing Contrastive Learning with Dual Reconstruction

abstract: Conventional notions of generalization often fail to describe the ability of learned models to capture meaningful information from dynamical data. A neural network that learns complex dynamics with a small test error may still fail to reproduce its \emph{physical} behavior, including associated statistical moments and Lyapunov exponents. To address this gap, we propose an ergodic theoretic approach to generalization of complex dynamical models learned from time series data. Our main contribution is to define and analyze generalization of a broad suite of neural representations of classes of ergodic systems, including chaotic systems, in a way that captures emulating underlying invariant, physical measures. Our results provide theoretical justification for why regression methods for generators of dynamical systems (Neural ODEs) fail to generalize, and why their statistical accuracy improves upon adding Jacobian information during training. We verify our results on a number of ergodic chaotic systems and neural network parameterizations, including MLPs, ResNets, Fourier Neural layers, and RNNs.

paragraphs: A model can predict dynamical data with low test error yet fail to reproduce the system’s physical behavior. The paper highlights statistical moments and Lyapunov exponents as examples of properties that ordinary prediction accuracy can miss. It develops an alternative view of generalization for learned dynamics that explicitly addresses these longer-term statistical characteristics.

The proposed framework uses ergodic theory to define and analyze whether neural representations emulate underlying invariant physical measures. It covers classes of ergodic systems, including chaotic ones. This shifts attention toward the statistical behavior generated by the learned system, providing a way to assess physical fidelity beyond conventional test error.

The authors verify their results on several ergodic chaotic systems with MLPs, ResNets, Fourier Neural layers, and recurrent networks. The contribution connects a more physically meaningful notion of generalization with a specific training ingredient that helps learned dynamics reproduce the statistics examined in the work.
summary.tldr: An ergodic-theory framework explains why low prediction error can miss physical statistics and why Jacobian information improves learned dynamics.

title: When are dynamical systems learned from time series data statistically accurate?

abstract: World models constitute a promising approach for training reinforcement learning agents in a safe and sample-efficient manner. Recent world models predominantly operate on sequences of discrete latent variables to model environment dynamics. However, this compression into a compact discrete representation may ignore visual details that are important for reinforcement learning. Concurrently, diffusion models have become a dominant approach for image generation, challenging well-established methods modeling discrete latents. Motivated by this paradigm shift, we introduce DIAMOND (DIffusion As a Model Of eNvironment Dreams), a reinforcement learning agent trained in a diffusion world model. We analyze the key design choices that are required to make diffusion suitable for world modeling, and demonstrate how improved visual details can lead to improved agent performance. DIAMOND achieves a mean human normalized score of 1.46 on the competitive Atari 100k benchmark; a new best for agents trained entirely within a world model. We further demonstrate that DIAMOND's diffusion world model can stand alone as an interactive neural game engine by training on static *Counter-Strike: Global Offensive* gameplay. To foster future research on diffusion for world modeling, we release our code, agents, videos and playable world models at https://diamond-wm.github.io.
