paragraphs: This paper examines where reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards changes a language model's reasoning. The authors analyze token entropy, which reflects uncertainty about the next token, throughout chains of thought. They observe that roughly 20% of tokens have high entropy and often correspond to decision points that send reasoning along different paths.

Moderately increasing the entropy of these tokens through decoding temperature adjustments improves performance in their experiments. Motivated by this finding, the authors restrict policy gradient updates to these reasoning forks. The approach concentrates the learning signal on positions where the model faces meaningful alternatives, rather than distributing updates across every token in a response.

Using only these tokens matches full-gradient performance on Qwen3-8B. On Qwen3-32B, the reported improvements are 11.04 on AIME'25 and 7.71 on AIME'24. Updating only the lowest-entropy 80% instead substantially harms performance. Together, these findings indicate that optimizing uncertain decision points accounts for much of RLVR's effectiveness in the studied models and suggests a more selective training strategy.
summary.tldr: Updating the roughly 20% of tokens that mark uncertain reasoning decisions matches or improves full-token reinforcement learning in the studied Qwen models.

title: Beyond the 80/20 Rule: High-Entropy Minority Tokens Drive Effective Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning

abstract: Multi-modal contrastive learning as a self-supervised representation learning technique has achieved great success in foundation model training, such as CLIP~\citep{radford2021learning}. In this paper, we study the theoretical properties of the learned representations from multi-modal contrastive learning beyond linear representations and specific data distributions. Our analysis reveals that, enabled by temperature optimization, multi-modal contrastive learning not only maximizes mutual information between modalities but also adapts to intrinsic dimensions of data, which can be much lower than user-specified dimensions for representation vectors. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the ability of contrastive learning to learn low-dimensional and informative representations, bridging theoretical insights and practical performance.

paragraphs: Multimodal contrastive learning trains representations by connecting information across modalities. A representation vector may contain many coordinates, but the shared information in the underlying data can have far fewer effective dimensions. This paper studies whether contrastive learning can adapt to that smaller structure, rather than simply using the dimensionality chosen by the model designer.

The theoretical analysis goes beyond linear representations and specific data distributions. It finds that optimizing the temperature enables multimodal contrastive learning both to maximize mutual information between modalities and to adapt to intrinsic data dimensions. These are related but distinct properties: retaining shared information does not by itself describe how compactly that information is represented.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate representations that are informative and low-dimensional, connecting the theoretical account to observed learning behavior. The role of temperature optimization is central to the stated result, so the conclusion should not be read as an unconditional property of every contrastive setup. The work helps explain how a large representation space can accommodate learned structure whose effective dimensionality is substantially smaller.
summary.tldr: With temperature optimization, multimodal contrastive learning can preserve shared information while adapting to its lower intrinsic dimensionality.

title: Multi-modal contrastive learning adapts to intrinsic dimensions of shared latent variables

abstract: Autoregressive (AR) image generation models are capable of producing high-fidelity images but often suffer from slow inference due to their inherently sequential, token-by-token decoding process. Speculative decoding, which employs a lightweight draft model to approximate the output of a larger AR model, has shown promise in accelerating text generation without compromising quality. However, its application to image generation remains largely underexplored. The challenges stem from a significantly larger sampling space, which complicates the alignment between the draft and target model outputs, coupled with the inadequate use of the two-dimensional spatial structure inherent in images, thereby limiting the modeling of local dependencies. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Hawk, a new approach that harnesses the spatial structure of images to guide the speculative model toward more accurate and efficient predictions. Experimental results on multiple text-to-image benchmarks demonstrate a 1.71× speedup over standard AR models, while preserving both image fidelity and diversity.

paragraphs: Autoregressive image models produce high-quality images but generate tokens sequentially, making inference slow. Speculative decoding uses a smaller draft model to approximate a larger model's output and offers a possible route to acceleration. Applying it to images is challenging because the sampling space is much larger and image content has an inherently two-dimensional structure.

Hawk uses that spatial structure to guide the speculative model's predictions. The motivation is that nearby image content contains useful local dependencies, but an approach that inadequately uses spatial context misses this information. Better spatial guidance is intended to improve agreement between the draft and target models, addressing a central difficulty in image speculation.

Across multiple text-to-image benchmarks, Hawk achieves a reported 1.71-fold speedup over standard autoregressive models while preserving image fidelity and diversity. The results show that spatially informed speculative prediction can reduce generation time in the evaluated setting. Preserving both reported qualities matters because acceleration should retain image quality as well as variation among generated images.
summary.tldr: Hawk uses image spatial structure to improve speculative decoding, achieving a reported 1.71-fold speedup while preserving fidelity and diversity.

title: Hawk: Leveraging Spatial Context for Faster Autoregressive Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) aims to infer human emotions by integrating complementary signals from diverse modalities. However, in real-world scenarios, missing modalities are common due to data corruption, sensor failure, or privacy concerns, which can significantly degrade model performance. To tackle this challenge, we propose Hyper-Modality Enhancement (HME), a novel framework that avoids explicit modality reconstruction by enriching each observed modality with semantically relevant cues retrieved from other samples. This cross-sample enhancement reduces reliance on fully observed data during training, making the method better suited to scenarios with inherently incomplete inputs. In addition, we introduce an uncertainty-aware fusion mechanism that adaptively balances original and enriched representations to improve robustness. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks show that HME consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods under various missing modality conditions, demonstrating its practicality in real-world MSA applications.

paragraphs: Multimodal sentiment analysis combines complementary signals to infer human emotion, but some inputs may be unavailable because of corruption, sensor failure, or privacy concerns. Hyper-Modality Enhancement, or HME, addresses this incomplete-input setting. It enriches the modalities that are available, giving the model additional relevant information without explicitly reconstructing the missing modalities.

The framework retrieves semantically relevant cues from other samples and uses them to enhance each observed modality. This cross-sample strategy reduces dependence on fully observed examples during training, which matters when incomplete inputs are a feature of the available data itself. An uncertainty-aware fusion mechanism then adaptively balances the original representation with its enriched version, accounting for uncertainty when combining the two.

Across three public benchmarks, the authors report that HME consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods under various missing-modality conditions. These results support retrieval-based enrichment as a practical approach to sentiment analysis with incomplete inputs. They also show the value of pairing additional contextual cues with an adaptive mechanism for deciding how strongly those cues should influence the representation.
summary.tldr: HME enriches available modalities with cues from other samples and uncertainty-aware fusion to improve sentiment analysis when inputs are missing.

title: Hyper-Modality Enhancement for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Missing Modalities

abstract: The increasing emphasis on privacy and data security has driven the adoption of federated learning (FL). Prompt learning (PL), which fine-tunes prompt embeddings of pretrained models, has gained a surge of interest in FL community, marked by the emergence of an influx of federated prompt learning (FPL) algorithms. Despite recent advancements, a systematic understanding of their underlying mechanisms and principled guidelines for deploying these techniques in different FL scenarios remain absent. Moreover, inconsistent experimental protocols, limited evaluation scenarios, and the lack of the proper assessment of centralized PL methods in existing works have obscured the essence of these algorithms. To close these gaps, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark, named F LIP, to achieve standardized FPL evaluation. F LIP assesses the performance of 13 centralized and FPL methods across 3 FL protocols and 12 open datasets, considering 6 distinct evaluation scenarios. Our findings demonstrate that PL maintains strong generalization performance in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings with minimal resource consumption, but there is no silver bullet found for diverse FPL scenarios. The results (1) pinpoint the suitable application scenarios of each FPL algorithm, (2) demonstrate the competitiveness of adapted centralized PL methods, and (3) offer notable insights to interpret their effectiveness and remaining challenges. All benchmarks and code are available to facilitate further research in this domain.

paragraphs: Federated prompt learning adapts pretrained models by learning prompt embeddings across a federated setting. Many algorithms have appeared, but inconsistent protocols and narrow evaluations make their strengths hard to compare. FLiP provides a standardized benchmark intended to clarify which methods suit different scenarios and how much specialized federated designs contribute.

The benchmark evaluates 13 centralized and federated prompt-learning methods across three federated protocols, 12 open datasets, and six evaluation scenarios. Including centralized methods adapted to the setting is an important part of the comparison: it tests whether existing prompt-learning approaches remain competitive alongside algorithms designed specifically for federation.

The results show strong prompt-learning generalization within and outside the training distribution while using few resources. They also show that no single method works best across the diverse scenarios, and that adapted centralized methods can be competitive. FLiP therefore supports scenario-specific choices and a clearer interpretation of algorithm effectiveness, with released benchmarks and code enabling further evaluation under shared conditions.
summary.tldr: FLiP standardizes federated prompt-learning evaluation and finds strong efficiency and generalization, but no universally best method.

title: FLiP: Towards Comprehensive and Reliable Evaluation of Federated Prompt Learning

abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) object detection faces significant challenges due to complex environmental conditions and different imaging conditions. These factors introduce significant changes in scale and appearance, particularly for small objects that occupy limited pixels and exhibit limited information, complicating detection tasks. To address these challenges, we propose a Multimodel Causal Reasoning framework based on YOLO backbone for UAV Object Detection (MCR-UOD). The key idea is to use the backdoor adjustment to discover the condition-invariant object representation for easy detection. Specifically, the YOLO backbone is first adjusted to incorporate the pre-trained vision-language model. The original category labels are replaced with semantic text prompts, and the detection head is replaced with text-image contrastive learning. Based on this backbone, our method consists of two parts. The first part, named language guided region exploration, discovers the regions with high probability of object existence using text embeddings based on vision-language model such as CLIP. Another part is the backdoor adjustment casual reasoning module, which constructs a confounder dictionary tailored to different imaging conditions to capture global image semantics and derives a prior probability distribution of shooting conditions. During causal inference, we use the confounder dictionary and the prior to intervene on local instance features, disentangling condition variations, and obtaining condition-invariant representations. Experimental results on several public datasets confirm the state-of-the-art performance of our approach. The code, data and models will be released upon publication of this paper.

paragraphs: Object detection from UAV imagery is difficult when environmental and imaging conditions change how objects look. Small objects are especially challenging because they occupy few pixels. MCR-UOD aims to separate these condition-related variations from the information needed to identify objects, using a combination of language guidance and causal reasoning.

The framework adapts a YOLO backbone to include a pretrained vision-language model. Semantic text prompts replace category labels, and text-image contrastive learning replaces the detection head. A language-guided exploration component uses text embeddings to identify promising object regions. A second component builds a dictionary representing imaging-condition confounders and estimates a prior distribution over shooting conditions.

During causal inference, the dictionary and prior support backdoor adjustment of local instance features to obtain representations invariant to those conditions. The authors report state-of-the-art detection performance on several public datasets. The approach matters because it explicitly models imaging conditions as a source of variation to disentangle, while using language-image alignment to help locate and represent objects.
summary.tldr: MCR-UOD combines language-guided region discovery with causal adjustment to improve UAV object detection across imaging conditions.

title: Multimodal Causal Reasoning for UAV Object Detection

abstract: In segmentation models, the number of change-points is typically chosen using a penalized cost function. In this work, we propose to learn the penalty and its constants in databases of signals with weak change-point annotations. We propose a convex relaxation for the resulting interval regression problem, and solve it using accelerated proximal gradient methods. We show that this method achieves state-of-the-art change-point detection in a database of annotated DNA copy number profiles from neuroblastoma tumors.

paragraphs: Change-point detection divides a signal into segments by locating positions where its behavior changes. Segmentation models commonly choose the number of changes through a cost function that penalizes additional change-points. The penalty therefore affects the segmentation directly: it controls how readily the model introduces another boundary in the signal.

This paper proposes learning the penalty and its constants from a database of signals with weak change-point annotations. The approach uses available annotations to guide a choice that otherwise must be supplied to the segmentation model. It formulates the learning task as an interval regression problem and introduces a convex relaxation, making the resulting optimization amenable to accelerated proximal gradient methods.

The method achieves state-of-the-art change-point detection on an annotated database of DNA copy-number profiles from neuroblastoma tumors. This finding supports learning segmentation penalties from weak supervision in that application. The broader methodological contribution is to make penalty selection itself a learnable component, connecting annotated examples to the rule used to choose how many changes a signal contains.
summary.tldr: Learning segmentation penalties from weak annotations improves change-point detection on a database of tumor DNA copy-number profiles.

title: Learning Sparse Penalties for Change-point Detection using Max Margin Interval Regression

abstract: Total variation (TV) models are among the most popular and successful tools in signal processing. However, due to the complex nature of the TV term, it is challenging to efficiently compute a solution for large-scale problems. State-of-the-art algorithms that are based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) often involve solving large-size linear systems. In this paper, we propose a highly scalable parallel algorithm for TV models that is based on a novel decomposition strategy of the problem domain. As a result, the TV models can be decoupled into a set of small and independent subproblems, which admit closed form solutions. This makes our approach particularly suitable for parallel implementation. Our algorithm is guaranteed to converge to its global minimum. With N variables and n_p processes, the time complexity is O(N/(εn_p)) to reach an epsilon-optimal solution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms, especially in dealing with high-resolution, mega-size images.

paragraphs: Total variation models are widely used in signal processing, but solving them becomes difficult as the number of variables grows. The paper targets a computational bottleneck in leading approaches based on the alternating direction method of multipliers: they often require solving large linear systems. That work can make large signal and image problems expensive.

The proposed algorithm divides the problem domain using a new decomposition strategy. This turns the original optimization problem into small, independent subproblems with closed-form solutions. Independence is the key practical feature: separate processes can solve these pieces in parallel, while closed-form solutions simplify the work required for each piece.

Experiments report better performance than existing leading algorithms, particularly for very large, high-resolution images.
summary.tldr: A domain decomposition makes total variation optimization parallelizable through small, closed-form subproblems, with global convergence guarantees.

title: A Highly Scalable Parallel Algorithm for Isotropic Total Variation Models

abstract: In this paper we propose an efficient, scalable non-parametric Gaussian process model for inference on Poisson point processes. Our model does not resort to gridding the domain or to introducing latent thinning points. Unlike competing models that scale as O(n^3) over n data points, our model has a complexity O(nk^2) where k << n. We propose a MCMC sampler and show that the model obtained is faster, more accurate and generates less correlated samples than competing approaches on both synthetic and real-life data. Finally, we show that our model easily handles data sizes not considered thus far by alternate approaches.

paragraphs: The paper develops a Gaussian process model for Bayesian inference on Poisson point processes. These models concern observed event locations, and the computational challenge grows with the number of observations. The proposed approach aims to retain a nonparametric model while making inference practical for substantially larger datasets.

The model avoids dividing the domain into a grid and avoids introducing latent thinning points. Its stated computational complexity is O(nk squared), with k much smaller than the number of observations n, compared with cubic scaling for competing models. The authors also propose a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler to carry out inference under the model.

On synthetic and real data, the method is reported to be faster and more accurate than the competing approaches, with less correlation among generated samples. These results address both computational expense and sampling behavior. The authors additionally demonstrate handling dataset sizes not previously considered by alternative methods, supporting the claim that the formulation expands the practical scale of point-process inference.
summary.tldr: A scalable Gaussian-process point-process model avoids gridding and thinning points while improving runtime, accuracy, and sampling behavior in experiments.

title: Scalable Nonparametric Bayesian Inference on Point Processes with Gaussian Processes

abstract: As the number of ad exchanges has grown, publishers have turned to low regret learning algorithms to decide which exchange offers the best price for their inventory. This in turn opens the following question for the exchange: how to set prices to attract as many sellers as possible and maximize revenue. In this work we formulate this precisely as a learning problem, and present algorithms showing that by simply knowing that the counterparty is using a low regret algorithm is enough for the exchange to have its own low regret learning algorithm to find the optimal price.

paragraphs: Publishers selling advertising inventory can use low-regret learning algorithms to choose among ad exchanges. Their choices evolve as they learn which exchange offers favorable prices. This creates a pricing problem for an exchange: it must attract sellers and maximize revenue while interacting with counterparties whose decisions are themselves produced by learning algorithms.

The paper formulates this interaction as a learning problem and develops pricing algorithms for the exchange. Its central result is that knowing the seller uses a low-regret algorithm is enough for the exchange to obtain its own low-regret algorithm for finding the optimal price. The seller’s learning behavior supplies the key assumption supporting that result.

This matters because the pricing decision is linked to an adaptive counterparty, rather than treated as an isolated choice against fixed behavior. The result shows that a broad performance property of the seller’s algorithm can support a learning guarantee for the exchange as well. The stated conclusion remains conditional on low-regret behavior by the counterparty in the formulated problem.
summary.tldr: Knowing that sellers use low-regret learning is sufficient for an exchange to develop its own low-regret pricing algorithm.

title: Pricing a Low-regret Seller

abstract: Very often features come with their own vectorial descriptions which provide detailed information about their properties. We refer to these vectorial descriptions as feature side-information. In the standard learning scenario, input is represented as a vector of features and the feature side-information is most often ignored or used only for feature selection prior to model fitting. We believe that feature side-information which carries information about features intrinsic property will help improve model prediction if used in a proper way during learning process. In this paper, we propose a framework that allows for the incorporation of the feature side-information during the learning of very general model families to improve the prediction performance. We control the structures of the learned models so that they reflect features’ similarities as these are defined on the basis of the side-information. We perform experiments on a number of benchmark datasets which show significant predictive performance gains, over a number of baselines, as a result of the exploitation of the side-information.

paragraphs: A feature can have its own description in addition to the values it takes across training examples. The paper calls these vector descriptions feature side-information. Such descriptions may capture intrinsic properties of features, yet standard learning often ignores them or uses them only to choose features before fitting a model.

The proposed framework incorporates this information during learning across very general model families. It controls the structure of the learned model so that the model reflects similarities among features, with those similarities defined using the side-information. Descriptions of the inputs therefore influence how the predictive model is organized.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets show significant predictive gains over multiple baselines when the side-information is used. The findings support treating information about features as a resource for model fitting itself. The contribution is especially relevant to nonlinear modeling because it offers a framework for connecting feature relationships to learned structure, rather than leaving those descriptions outside the prediction-learning process.
summary.tldr: Using descriptions of features to guide model structure improves prediction across the reported benchmark experiments.

title: Regularising Non-linear Models Using Feature Side-information

abstract: We introduce a new framework for training deep generative models for high-dimensional conditional density estimation. The Bottleneck Conditional Density Estimator (BCDE) is a variant of the conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) that employs layer(s) of stochastic variables as the bottleneck between the input x and target y, where both are high-dimensional. Crucially, we propose a new hybrid training method that blends the conditional generative model with a joint generative model. Hybrid blending is the key to effective training of the BCDE, which avoids overfitting and provides a novel mechanism for leveraging unlabeled data. We show that our hybrid training procedure enables models to achieve competitive results in the MNIST quadrant prediction task in the fully-supervised setting, and sets new benchmarks in the semi-supervised regime for MNIST, SVHN, and CelebA.

paragraphs: Conditional density estimation models the distribution of a target given an input. This paper addresses the case where both are high-dimensional, introducing the Bottleneck Conditional Density Estimator, or BCDE. The model is a variant of a conditional variational autoencoder, with layers of stochastic variables forming a bottleneck between input and target.

The central training contribution combines a conditional generative model with a joint generative model. This hybrid procedure brings together modeling the target given the input and modeling the variables jointly. The authors identify this blending as essential to effective BCDE training, describing it as a way to avoid overfitting and incorporate unlabeled data.

In fully supervised MNIST quadrant prediction, the hybrid training procedure produces competitive results. In semi-supervised experiments on MNIST, SVHN, and CelebA, it establishes new reported benchmarks. These findings support the combination of the stochastic bottleneck architecture and hybrid training, especially when unlabeled examples are available alongside labeled data. The contribution concerns learning distributions over high-dimensional targets rather than only producing individual predictions.
summary.tldr: BCDE combines a stochastic bottleneck with hybrid generative training to improve high-dimensional conditional density estimation.

title: Bottleneck Conditional Density Estimation

abstract: Alternating direction method of multiplier (ADMM) is a popular method used to design distributed versions of a machine learning algorithm, whereby local computations are performed on local data with the output exchanged among neighbors in an iterative fashion. During this iterative process the leakage of data privacy arises. A differentially private ADMM was proposed in prior work (Zhang & Zhu, 2017) where only the privacy loss of a single node during one iteration was bounded, a method that makes it difficult to balance the tradeoff between the utility attained through distributed computation and privacy guarantees when considering the total privacy loss of all nodes over the entire iterative process. We propose a perturbation method for ADMM where the perturbed term is correlated with the penalty parameters; this is shown to improve the utility and privacy simultaneously. The method is based on a modified ADMM where each node independently determines its own penalty parameter in every iteration and decouples it from the dual updating step size. The condition for convergence of the modified ADMM and the lower bound on the convergence rate are also derived.

paragraphs: Distributed ADMM algorithms let nodes compute on local data and repeatedly exchange outputs with neighbors. Those exchanges can reveal private information. The paper highlights a difficulty with earlier privacy analysis: bounding the loss for one node in one iteration does not readily explain the privacy and utility tradeoff across the entire network and iterative process.

The authors modify ADMM so that each node independently chooses its penalty parameter at every iteration. They also separate that parameter from the step size used for dual updates. On top of this modification, they introduce a perturbation method whose added term is correlated with the penalty parameters.

The proposed construction is shown to improve utility and privacy simultaneously. The paper also derives a convergence condition for the modified algorithm and a lower bound on its convergence rate. These results connect the design of privacy-preserving perturbations with the underlying optimization procedure, treating parameter choice as part of how distributed learning balances useful computation and privacy.
summary.tldr: An ADMM modification links privacy perturbations to locally chosen penalty parameters, improving privacy and utility together.

title: Improving the Privacy and Accuracy of ADMM-Based Distributed Algorithms

abstract: We propose infinite mixture prototypes to adaptively represent both simple and complex data distributions for few-shot learning. Infinite mixture prototypes combine deep representation learning with Bayesian nonparametrics, representing each class by a set of clusters, unlike existing prototypical methods that represent each class by a single cluster. By inferring the number of clusters, infinite mixture prototypes interpolate between nearest neighbor and prototypical representations in a learned feature space, which improves accuracy and robustness in the few-shot regime. We show the importance of adaptive capacity for capturing complex data distributions such as super-classes (like alphabets in character recognition), with 10-25% absolute accuracy improvements over prototypical networks, while still maintaining or improving accuracy on standard few-shot learning benchmarks. By clustering labeled and unlabeled data with the same rule, infinite mixture prototypes achieve state-of-the-art semi-supervised accuracy, and can perform purely unsupervised clustering, unlike existing fully- and semi-supervised prototypical methods.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning must recognize classes from very limited labeled data. Prototypical approaches summarize each class with one cluster in a learned feature space, which can be restrictive when a class contains several distinct kinds of examples. Infinite mixture prototypes instead let each class have an inferred number of clusters.

The method combines deep representation learning with Bayesian nonparametrics to adapt its capacity to the data. Depending on the inferred clustering, its representation can fall between a single class prototype and a nearest-neighbor style representation. This flexibility is especially relevant for complex classes such as whole alphabets, whose constituent characters need not form one simple cluster.

The authors report absolute accuracy improvements of 10–25% over prototypical networks on complex distributions such as super-classes, while maintaining or improving accuracy on standard few-shot benchmarks. The method also applies the same clustering rule to labeled and unlabeled examples. That supports state-of-the-art semi-supervised accuracy in the reported results and permits purely unsupervised clustering, extending the approach beyond classification with a fixed labeled support set.
summary.tldr: Infinite mixture prototypes infer multiple clusters per class, improving few-shot learning on complex distributions and supporting semi-supervised and unsupervised clustering.

title: Infinite Mixture Prototypes for Few-shot Learning

abstract: We give the first dimensionality reduction methods for the overconstrained Tukey regression problem. The Tukey loss function $\|y\|_M = \sum_i M(y_i)$ has $M(y_i) \approx |y_i|^p$ for residual errors $y_i$ smaller than a prescribed threshold $\tau$, but $M(y_i)$ becomes constant for errors $|y_i| > \tau$. Our results depend on a new structural result, proven constructively, showing that for any $d$-dimensional subspace $L \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, there is a fixed bounded-size subset of coordinates containing, for every $y \in L$, all the large coordinates, with respect to the Tukey loss function, of $y$. Our methods reduce a given Tukey regression problem to a smaller weighted version, whose solution is a provably good approximate solution to the original problem. Our reductions are fast, simple and easy to implement, and we give empirical results demonstrating their practicality, using existing heuristic solvers for the small versions. We also give exponential-time algorithms giving provably good solutions, and hardness results suggesting that a significant speedup in the worst case is unlikely.

paragraphs: Tukey regression uses a loss that grows approximately as a power of the residual for smaller errors, then becomes constant beyond a chosen threshold. Thus, making an already large residual even larger does not keep increasing its contribution. This paper introduces dimensionality reduction methods for overconstrained regression problems using this loss.

The key mathematical result concerns a fixed low-dimensional subspace. The authors construct a bounded-size set of coordinates that contains all coordinates considered large under the Tukey loss for every vector in that subspace. This shared structural property supports reducing the original regression task to a smaller, weighted problem while preserving a provably good approximation.

The reductions are described as fast and simple, and experiments demonstrate their practicality when existing heuristic solvers handle the smaller problems. The paper separately provides exponential-time algorithms with provable solution quality. Its hardness results suggest that substantially faster worst-case algorithms are unlikely. The practical contribution is therefore a smaller problem with approximation guarantees, alongside a theoretical account of the remaining computational difficulty.
summary.tldr: Tukey regression can be reduced to smaller weighted problems with approximation guarantees using a new structural property of subspaces.

title: Dimensionality Reduction for Tukey Regression

abstract: Due to the ease of modern data collection, applied statisticians often have access to a large set of covariates that they wish to relate to some observed outcome. Generalized linear models (GLMs) offer a particularly interpretable framework for such an analysis. In these high-dimensional problems, the number of covariates is often large relative to the number of observations, so we face non-trivial inferential uncertainty; a Bayesian approach allows coherent quantification of this uncertainty. Unfortunately, existing methods for Bayesian inference in GLMs require running times roughly cubic in parameter dimension, and so are limited to settings with at most tens of thousand parameters. We propose to reduce time and memory costs with a low-rank approximation of the data in an approach we call LR-GLM. When used with the Laplace approximation or Markov chain Monte Carlo, LR-GLM provides a full Bayesian posterior approximation and admits running times reduced by a full factor of the parameter dimension. We rigorously establish the quality of our approximation and show how the choice of rank allows a tunable computational–statistical trade-off. Experiments support our theory and demonstrate the efficacy of LR-GLM on real large-scale datasets.

paragraphs: Generalized linear models offer an interpretable way to relate many covariates to an outcome. When the number of covariates is large relative to the number of observations, uncertainty becomes an important part of inference. Combined with either a Laplace approximation or Markov chain Monte Carlo, it produces an approximation to the full Bayesian posterior. The authors rigorously analyze approximation quality and show how rank controls a tradeoff between computational cost and statistical accuracy. Experiments support the theory and demonstrate effectiveness on large real datasets. The central contribution is therefore a tunable way to reduce the cost of uncertainty quantification, with theoretical support for the approximation being introduced.
summary.tldr: LR-GLM uses low rank data approximations to accelerate Bayesian inference in generalized linear models with a tunable computational–statistical tradeoff.

title: LR-GLM: High-Dimensional Bayesian Inference Using Low-Rank Data Approximations

abstract: Responding to user data deletion requests, removing noisy examples, or deleting corrupted training data are just a few reasons for wanting to delete instances from a machine learning (ML) model. However, efficiently removing this data from an ML model is generally difficult. In this paper, we introduce data removal-enabled (DaRE) forests, a variant of random forests that enables the removal of training data with minimal retraining. Model updates for each DaRE tree in the forest are exact, meaning that removing instances from a DaRE model yields exactly the same model as retraining from scratch on updated data. DaRE trees use randomness and caching to make data deletion efficient. The upper levels of DaRE trees use random nodes, which choose split attributes and thresholds uniformly at random. These nodes rarely require updates because they only minimally depend on the data. At the lower levels, splits are chosen to greedily optimize a split criterion such as Gini index or mutual information. DaRE trees cache statistics at each node and training data at each leaf, so that only the necessary subtrees are updated as data is removed. For numerical attributes, greedy nodes optimize over a random subset of thresholds, so that they can maintain statistics while approximating the optimal threshold. By adjusting the number of thresholds considered for greedy nodes, and the number of random nodes, DaRE trees can trade off between more accurate predictions and more efficient updates. In experiments on 13 real-world datasets and one synthetic dataset, we find DaRE forests delete data orders of magnitude faster than retraining from scratch while sacrificing little to no predictive power.

paragraphs: Removing a training example from a learned model usually requires more than deleting its stored record. DaRE forests modify random forests so that examples can be removed with minimal retraining. Their updates are exact: deleting data produces the same DaRE model as training from scratch on the remaining data.

The design combines randomness with cached information. Upper tree levels use random splits that depend only minimally on the data and rarely need updating. Lower levels choose splits greedily. Statistics stored at nodes and training examples stored at leaves allow the method to update only affected subtrees. For numerical features, greedy splits consider a random subset of thresholds.

The number of random nodes and candidate thresholds provides a tradeoff between predictive accuracy and update efficiency. Across 13 real-world datasets and one synthetic dataset, DaRE forests remove data orders of magnitude faster than full retraining with little or no loss of predictive performance. Exactness concerns the deletion result; the configurable tree design governs the efficiency and prediction tradeoff.
summary.tldr: DaRE forests combine random splits and caching to delete training examples exactly, achieving much faster updates than retraining in the reported experiments.

title: Machine Unlearning for Random Forests

abstract: Existing work on privacy-preserving machine learning with Secure Multiparty Computation (MPC) is almost exclusively focused on model training and on inference with trained models, thereby overlooking the important data pre-processing stage. In this work, we propose the first MPC based protocol for private feature selection based on the filter method, which is independent of model training, and can be used in combination with any MPC protocol to rank features. We propose an efficient feature scoring protocol based on Gini impurity to this end. To demonstrate the feasibility of our approach for practical data science, we perform experiments with the proposed MPC protocols for feature selection in a commonly used machine-learning-as-a-service configuration where computations are outsourced to multiple servers, with semi-honest and with malicious adversaries. Regarding effectiveness, we show that secure feature selection with the proposed protocols improves the accuracy of classifiers on a variety of real-world data sets, without leaking information about the feature values or even which features were selected. Regarding efficiency, we document runtimes ranging from several seconds to an hour for our protocols to finish, depending on the size of the data set and the security settings.

paragraphs: Privacy-preserving machine learning often concentrates on training and prediction, even though preprocessing also handles sensitive data. This paper addresses feature selection: deciding which input variables to keep. It proposes a secure multiparty computation protocol for filter-based selection, so features can be assessed independently of a particular model's training procedure.

The method uses an efficient secure scoring protocol based on Gini impurity. Its separation from training allows it to work with other MPC protocols for feature ranking. The authors evaluate an outsourced service configuration in which multiple servers perform the computation, considering both semi-honest and malicious adversaries. This places the preprocessing step within explicit security settings rather than assuming trusted computation.

On a variety of real-world datasets, the proposed secure selection improves classifier accuracy while revealing neither feature values nor the identities of selected features. Reported runtimes range from seconds to an hour, depending on dataset size and security settings. The findings show practical feasibility across the tested configurations, while also making clear that the computational cost varies substantially with the workload and protection requirements.
summary.tldr: Secure multiparty computation enables feature selection that hides both feature values and selected features while improving accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Privacy-Preserving Feature Selection with Secure Multiparty Computation

abstract: Data poisoning and backdoor attacks manipulate training data in order to cause models to fail during inference. A recent survey of industry practitioners found that data poisoning is the number one concern among threats ranging from model stealing to adversarial attacks. However, it remains unclear exactly how dangerous poisoning methods are and which ones are more effective considering that these methods, even ones with identical objectives, have not been tested in consistent or realistic settings. We observe that data poisoning and backdoor attacks are highly sensitive to variations in the testing setup. Moreover, we find that existing methods may not generalize to realistic settings. While these existing works serve as valuable prototypes for data poisoning, we apply rigorous tests to determine the extent to which we should fear them. In order to promote fair comparison in future work, we develop standardized benchmarks for data poisoning and backdoor attacks.

This paper asks how dangerous existing methods are when evaluated consistently and realistically. Its starting concern is that even attacks pursuing the same objective had been tested under different conditions, making their apparent effectiveness difficult to compare.

The authors apply rigorous testing and find that attack results are highly sensitive to the evaluation setup. They also find that existing methods may fail to generalize to realistic settings. This means that success in one experimental configuration does not, by itself, establish how well an attack will work under another configuration.

It treats earlier methods as valuable prototypes while examining how far their demonstrated capabilities extend. The central contribution is therefore a better basis for assessing the threat: consistent evaluation can distinguish strong attack performance from results that depend heavily on particular testing choices.
summary.tldr: Standardized testing shows that poisoning and backdoor attack effectiveness depends strongly on evaluation conditions and may not carry over to realistic settings.

title: Just How Toxic is Data Poisoning? A Unified Benchmark for Backdoor and Data Poisoning Attacks

abstract: Existing deep topic models are effective in capturing the latent semantic structures in textual data but usually rely on a plethora of documents. This is less than satisfactory in practical applications when only a limited amount of data is available. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that efficiently solves the problem of topic modeling under the small data regime. Specifically, the framework involves two innovations: a bi-level generative model that aims to exploit the task information to guide the document generation, and a topic meta-learner that strives to learn a group of global topic embeddings so that fast adaptation to the task-specific topic embeddings can be achieved with a few examples. We apply the proposed framework to a hierarchical embedded topic model and achieve better performance than various baseline models on diverse experiments, including few-shot topic discovery and few-shot document classification.

The framework combines two ideas. A generative model with two levels uses task information to guide how documents are modeled. A topic meta-learner learns shared topic embeddings that can be adapted into task-specific embeddings using only a few examples. The shared representations provide reusable topic knowledge, while adaptation allows the model to account for the particular task’s documents.

The authors implement this framework within a hierarchical embedded topic model. Across experiments, it outperforms several baseline models on few-shot topic discovery and few-shot document classification. These results support learning an adaptable foundation for topics when individual tasks have little data, with benefits for both uncovering themes and using text representations to classify documents.
summary.tldr: A topic meta-learner adapts shared topic embeddings to small document collections, improving few-shot topic discovery and classification.

title: Bayesian Deep Embedding Topic Meta-Learner

abstract: Group convolutional neural networks (G-CNNs) have been shown to increase parameter efficiency and model accuracy by incorporating geometric inductive biases. In this work, we investigate the properties of representations learned by regular G-CNNs, and show considerable parameter redundancy in group convolution kernels. This finding motivates further weight-tying by sharing convolution kernels over subgroups. To this end, we introduce convolution kernels that are separable over the subgroup and channel dimensions. In order to obtain equivariance to arbitrary affine Lie groups we provide a continuous parameterisation of separable convolution kernels. We evaluate our approach across several vision datasets, and show that our weight sharing leads to improved performance and computational efficiency. In many settings, separable G-CNNs outperform their non-separable counterpart, while only using a fraction of their training time. In addition, thanks to the increase in computational efficiency, we are able to implement G-CNNs equivariant to the $\mathrm{Sim(2)}$ group; the group of dilations, rotations and translations of the plane. $\mathrm{Sim(2)}$-equivariance further improves performance on all tasks considered, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on rotated MNIST.

They also provide a continuous parameterization for separable kernels to obtain equivariance to arbitrary affine Lie groups. This additional structure improves every evaluated task and achieves state-of-the-art results on rotated MNIST.
summary.tldr: Separable group convolutions reduce redundant parameters and computation while improving performance across the evaluated vision tasks.

title: Exploiting Redundancy: Separable Group Convolutional Networks on Lie Groups

abstract: In this work we propose a batch multimarginal version of the Greenkhorn algorithm for the entropic-regularized optimal transport problem. This framework is general enough to cover, as particular cases, existing Sinkhorn and Greenkhorn algorithms for the bi-marginal setting, and greedy MultiSinkhorn for the general multimarginal case. We provide a comprehensive convergence analysis based on the properties of the iterative Bregman projections method with greedy control. Linear rate of convergence as well as explicit bounds on the iteration complexity are obtained. When specialized to the above mentioned algorithms, our results give new convergence rates or provide key improvements over the state-of-the-art rates. We present numerical experiments showing that the flexibility of the batch can be exploited to improve performance of Sinkhorn algorithm both in bi-marginal and multimarginal settings.

The framework includes several existing methods as special cases: Sinkhorn and Greenkhorn for two marginals, and greedy MultiSinkhorn for the general setting. This provides a common basis for studying algorithms that otherwise appear as separate procedures.

The convergence analysis uses iterative Bregman projections with greedy control. The authors establish a linear convergence rate, describing geometric progress toward the solution, and explicit bounds on the number of iterations required. When applied to the included algorithms, the analysis yields either new convergence rates or substantial improvements to previously available rates.

Batching also gives the method a practical degree of flexibility. Numerical experiments show that this flexibility can improve Sinkhorn’s performance in both two-marginal and multimarginal problems. The contribution therefore combines a unified theoretical treatment with evidence that choices about how updates are grouped can matter computationally, alongside the guarantees governing convergence.
summary.tldr: A batch Greenkhorn framework unifies transport algorithms, strengthens convergence guarantees, and offers empirical performance gains through flexible batching.

title: Batch Greenkhorn Algorithm for Entropic-Regularized Multimarginal Optimal Transport: Linear Rate of Convergence and Iteration Complexity

abstract: In this paper, we propose Nesterov Accelerated Shuffling Gradient (NASG), a new algorithm for the convex finite-sum minimization problems. Our method integrates the traditional Nesterov’s acceleration momentum with different shuffling sampling schemes. We show that our algorithm has an improved rate of $\Ocal(1/T)$ using unified shuffling schemes, where $T$ is the number of epochs. This rate is better than that of any other shuffling gradient methods in convex regime. Our convergence analysis does not require an assumption on bounded domain or a bounded gradient condition. For randomized shuffling schemes, we improve the convergence bound further. When employing some initial condition, we show that our method converges faster near the small neighborhood of the solution. Numerical simulations demonstrate the efficiency of our algorithm.

paragraphs: Many optimization problems minimize a finite sum of component losses. Shuffling gradient methods process those components in an order that can change across passes through the data. This paper introduces Nesterov Accelerated Shuffling Gradient, or NASG, which combines such sampling schemes with Nesterov momentum to improve convergence for convex finite-sum problems.

The authors establish a rate of O(1/T), where T counts epochs, under a unified treatment of shuffling schemes. They report this as an improvement over previous shuffling gradient rates in the convex setting. Their analysis does not require a bounded optimization domain or an assumption that gradients remain bounded, removing two conditions that can constrain convergence arguments.

For randomized shuffling, the convergence bound improves further. The paper also obtains faster convergence near a small neighborhood of the solution when an additional initial condition is satisfied. Numerical simulations demonstrate the algorithm’s efficiency. The results show how momentum and the ordering of component updates can work together, while keeping the stronger local conclusion conditional on the stated initialization requirement.
summary.tldr: NASG combines Nesterov momentum with shuffling to improve convex finite-sum convergence without bounded-domain or bounded-gradient assumptions.

title: Nesterov Accelerated Shuffling Gradient Method for Convex Optimization

abstract: This paper develops a scalable new algorithm, called NysADMM, to minimize a smooth convex loss function with a convex regularizer. NysADMM accelerates the inexact Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) by constructing a preconditioner for the ADMM subproblem from a randomized low-rank Nyström approximation. NysADMM comes with strong theoretical guarantees: it solves the ADMM subproblem in a constant number of iterations when the rank of the Nyström approximation is the effective dimension of the subproblem regularized Gram matrix. In practice, ranks much smaller than the effective dimension can succeed, so NysADMM uses an adaptive strategy to choose the rank that enjoys analogous guarantees. Numerical experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that NysADMM can solve important applications, such as the lasso, logistic regression, and support vector machines, in half the time (or less) required by standard solvers. The breadth of problems on which NysADMM beats standard solvers is a surprise: it suggests that ADMM is a dominant paradigm for numerical optimization across a wide range of statistical learning problems that are usually solved with bespoke methods.

title: NysADMM: faster composite convex optimization via low-rank approximation

abstract: Since their introduction, diffusion models have quickly become the prevailing approach to generative modeling in many domains. They can be interpreted as learning the gradients of a time-varying sequence of log-probability density functions. This interpretation has motivated classifier-based and classifier-free guidance as methods for post-hoc control of diffusion models. In this work, we build upon these ideas using the score-based interpretation of diffusion models, and explore alternative ways to condition, modify, and reuse diffusion models for tasks involving compositional generation and guidance. In particular, we investigate why certain types of composition fail using current techniques and present a number of solutions. We conclude that the sampler (not the model) is responsible for this failure and propose new samplers, inspired by MCMC, which enable successful compositional generation. Further, we propose an energy-based parameterization of diffusion models which enables the use of new compositional operators and more sophisticated, Metropolis-corrected samplers. Intriguingly we find these samplers lead to notable improvements in compositional generation across a wide variety of problems such as classifier-guided ImageNet modeling and compositional text-to-image generation.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can be interpreted as learning gradients of changing log-probability densities. This perspective supports guidance and suggests ways to combine existing models for compositional generation. The paper studies how to condition, modify, and reuse diffusion models, including why some compositions fail under current techniques.

For the failures investigated, the authors identify the sampler as the responsible component. They propose sampling methods inspired by Markov chain Monte Carlo that enable successful composition. This diagnosis matters because combining model information is only part of the generation procedure; the sampling process must also realize the intended combination.

The authors additionally propose an energy-based parameterization that supports new composition operators and more sophisticated samplers with Metropolis corrections. They report notable improvements across problems including classifier-guided ImageNet generation and compositional text-to-image generation. The contribution therefore links a diagnosis of sampling failure with changes to both sampling and model parameterization, expanding how diffusion models can be reused for controlled generation without treating every successful composition as a consequence of model combination alone.
summary.tldr: MCMC-inspired samplers and an energy-based parameterization improve compositional generation with diffusion models.

title: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle: Compositional Generation with Energy-Based Diffusion Models and MCMC

abstract: Having reliable specifications is an unavoidable challenge in achieving verifiable correctness, robustness, and interpretability of AI systems. Existing specifications for neural networks are in the paradigm of data as specification. That is, the local neighborhood centering around a reference input is considered to be correct (or robust). While existing specifications contribute to verifying adversarial robustness, a significant problem in many research domains, our empirical study shows that those verified regions are somewhat tight, and thus fail to allow verification of test set inputs, making them impractical for some real-world applications. To this end, we propose a new family of specifications called neural representation as specification. This form of specifications uses the intrinsic information of neural networks, specifically neural activation patterns (NAPs), rather than input data to specify the correctness and/or robustness of neural network predictions. We present a simple statistical approach to mining neural activation patterns. To show the effectiveness of discovered NAPs, we formally verify several important properties, such as various types of misclassifications will never happen for a given NAP, and there is no ambiguity between different NAPs. We show that by using NAP, we can verify a significant region of the input space, while still recalling 84% of the data on MNIST. Moreover, we can push the verifiable bound to 10 times larger on the CIFAR10 benchmark. Thus, we argue that NAPs can potentially be used as a more reliable and extensible specification for neural network verification.

This paper's empirical study finds those verified regions can be too narrow to cover test inputs, limiting their usefulness in some applications.

The authors propose specifications based on neural activation patterns, using internal network representations to describe regions for verification. The paper presents them as a potentially more reliable and extensible basis for neural verification.
summary.tldr: Specifications built from neural activation patterns enable formal verification over broader regions in the reported MNIST and CIFAR10 evaluations.

title: Towards Reliable Neural Specifications

abstract: Multi-resolution hash encoding has recently been proposed to reduce the computational cost of neural renderings, such as NeRF. This method requires accurate camera poses for the neural renderings of given scenes. However, contrary to previous methods jointly optimizing camera poses and 3D scenes, the naive gradient-based camera pose refinement method using multi-resolution hash encoding severely deteriorates performance. We propose a joint optimization algorithm to calibrate the camera pose and learn a geometric representation using efficient multi-resolution hash encoding. Showing that the oscillating gradient flows of hash encoding interfere with the registration of camera poses, our method addresses the issue by utilizing smooth interpolation weighting to stabilize the gradient oscillation for the ray samplings across hash grids. Moreover, the curriculum training procedure helps to learn the level-wise hash encoding, further increasing the pose refinement. Experiments on the novel-view synthesis datasets validate that our learning frameworks achieve state-of-the-art performance and rapid convergence of neural rendering.

paragraphs: Multi-resolution hash encoding reduces the computational cost of neural rendering, but it depends on accurate camera positions and orientations. Simply applying gradient-based camera refinement alongside this representation can severely degrade performance. This paper investigates that failure and proposes a method that jointly calibrates camera poses and learns scene geometry using the efficient hash representation.

The authors identify oscillating gradient flows in hash encoding as an obstacle to camera registration. Their method uses smooth interpolation weighting to stabilize these oscillations when rays are sampled across hash grids. This targets the optimization signal used to refine the cameras, addressing the interaction between pose estimation and the scene representation.

A curriculum training procedure also helps the model learn the encoding at different levels, further improving pose refinement. Experiments on novel-view synthesis datasets report state-of-the-art performance and rapid convergence. The findings show that retaining an efficient rendering representation requires adapting the joint optimization procedure to its gradient behavior, with interpolation smoothing and curriculum training contributing to the proposed solution.
summary.tldr: Smooth interpolation and curriculum training stabilize joint camera-pose refinement and scene learning with multi-resolution hash encoding.

title: Robust Camera Pose Refinement for Multi-Resolution Hash Encoding

abstract: Although distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) has been widely examined in the past few years, very few studies investigate the validity of the obtained Q-function estimator in the distributional setting. To fully understand how the approximation errors of the Q-function affect the whole training process, we do some error analysis and theoretically show how to reduce both the bias and the variance of the error terms. With this new understanding, we construct a new estimator Quantiled Expansion Mean (QEM) and introduce a new DRL algorithm (QEMRL) from the statistical perspective. We extensively evaluate our QEMRL algorithm on a variety of Atari and Mujoco benchmark tasks and demonstrate that QEMRL achieves significant improvement over baseline algorithms in terms of sample efficiency and convergence performance.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning models a distribution of returns, while action evaluation still involves estimating a Q-function. This paper focuses on the statistical quality of that estimate. The authors ask how approximation errors in the Q-function affect the broader training process, an issue they describe as relatively underexamined in the distributional setting.

They analyze the error terms and theoretically show how to reduce both their bias and their variance. These are distinct aspects of estimation quality: systematic error and variability. Building on that analysis, they construct an estimator called Quantiled Expansion Mean, or QEM, and use it in a new distributional reinforcement-learning algorithm called QEMRL.

The authors evaluate QEMRL on a variety of Atari and Mujoco tasks. They report significant improvements over baseline algorithms in sample efficiency and convergence performance. The findings support the practical value of examining how return distributions are turned into Q-function estimates. The contribution links a statistical error analysis to an estimator and then to observed improvements in learning behavior across the tested environments.
summary.tldr: QEMRL uses a statistically motivated Q-function estimator to improve sample efficiency and convergence on tested Atari and Mujoco tasks.

title: Variance Control for Distributional Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recently, many works studied the expressive power of graph neural networks (GNNs) by linking it to the $1$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm ($1\text{-}\mathsf{WL}$). Here, the $1\text{-}\mathsf{WL}$ is a well-studied heuristic for the graph isomorphism problem, which iteratively colors or partitions a graph’s vertex set. While this connection has led to significant advances in understanding and enhancing GNNs’ expressive power, it does not provide insights into their generalization performance, i.e., their ability to make meaningful predictions beyond the training set. In this paper, we study GNNs’ generalization ability through the lens of Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension theory in two settings, focusing on graph-level predictions. First, when no upper bound on the graphs’ order is known, we show that the bitlength of GNNs’ weights tightly bounds their VC dimension. Further, we derive an upper bound for GNNs’ VC dimension using the number of colors produced by the $1\text{-}\mathsf{WL}$. Secondly, when an upper bound on the graphs’ order is known, we show a tight connection between the number of graphs distinguishable by the $1\text{-}\mathsf{WL}$ and GNNs’ VC dimension. Our empirical study confirms the validity of our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks are often studied through the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman procedure, which repeatedly partitions or colors a graph’s vertices. This connection explains which graphs a network can distinguish, but expressive power alone does not explain generalization. The paper brings VC dimension into the analysis of graph-level predictions to connect these questions more directly.

It separates two settings. When graph size has no known upper bound, the authors show that the bitlength of network weights tightly bounds VC dimension. They also derive an upper bound using the number of colors produced by Weisfeiler-Leman. Thus, both weight precision and graph distinctions enter the capacity analysis.

When an upper bound on graph size is known, the paper establishes a tight connection between VC dimension and the number of graphs distinguishable by Weisfeiler-Leman. An empirical study supports the theoretical findings. The contribution is a mathematical bridge from structural distinguishability to learning capacity, clarifying how a tool used to analyze GNN expressiveness can also inform the study of generalization.
summary.tldr: The paper links Weisfeiler-Leman graph distinguishability and weight precision to GNN VC dimension, connecting expressiveness with generalization theory.

title: WL meet VC

abstract: The use of deep neural networks in real-world applications require well-calibrated networks with confidence scores that accurately reflect the actual probability. However, it has been found that these networks often provide over-confident predictions, which leads to poor calibration. Recent efforts have sought to address this issue by focal loss to reduce over-confidence, but this approach can also lead to under-confident predictions. While different variants of focal loss have been explored, it is difficult to find a balance between over-confidence and under-confidence. In our work, we propose a new loss function by focusing on dual logits. Our method not only considers the ground truth logit, but also take into account the highest logit ranked after the ground truth logit. By maximizing the gap between these two logits, our proposed dual focal loss can achieve a better balance between over-confidence and under-confidence. We provide theoretical evidence to support our approach and demonstrate its effectiveness through evaluations on multiple models and datasets, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Linwei94/DualFocalLoss

paragraphs: A classifier's confidence is useful when it accurately reflects the probability that its prediction is correct. Deep networks often assign excessive confidence, while focal loss, a proposed remedy, can push predictions toward insufficient confidence. This paper targets the difficulty of balancing those two kinds of calibration error during training.

The proposed dual focal loss uses two logits, the scores involved in forming class predictions. It considers the ground-truth logit together with the highest logit ranked after it. By maximizing the gap between this pair, the method changes how training shapes confidence. The authors argue that this can produce a better balance between overconfidence and underconfidence.

The paper supplies theoretical evidence for the approach and evaluates it across multiple models and datasets, reporting state-of-the-art performance in those evaluations. Its contribution is a training loss explicitly designed around the interaction of two scores. The stated outcome is improved calibration performance in the tested settings, supporting the value of addressing both confidence extremes together.
summary.tldr: Dual focal loss uses a pair of logits to better balance overconfidence and underconfidence, improving calibration in the reported evaluations.

title: Dual Focal Loss for Calibration

abstract: In many real-world tasks, some parts of state features, called contexts, are independent of action signals, e.g., customer demand in inventory control, speed of lead car in autonomous driving, etc. One of the challenges of reinforcement learning in these applications is that the true context transitions can be easily exposed some unknown source of contamination, leading to a shift of context transitions between source domains and target domains, which could cause performance degradation for RL algorithms. However, existing methods on robust RL aim at learning robust policies against the deviations of the entire system dynamics. To tackle this problem, this paper proposes the framework of robust situational Markov decision process (RS-MDP) which captures the possible deviations of context transitions explicitly. To scale to large context space, we introduce the softmin smoothed robust Bellman operator to learn the robust Q-value approximately, and apply our RS-MDP framework to existing RL algorithm SAC to learn the desired robust policies. We conduct experiments on several robot control tasks with dynamic contexts and inventory control tasks to demonstrate that our algorithm can generalize better and more robust against deviations of context transitions, and outperform existing robust RL algorithms.

paragraphs: Some parts of an environment’s state evolve independently of the agent’s actions. The paper calls these contexts, with examples including customer demand and the speed of a lead car. Changes in how contexts evolve between training and deployment can degrade reinforcement learning performance, even though the agent does not control those changes.

The proposed robust situational Markov decision process explicitly models possible deviations in context transitions. This focuses robustness on the source of disturbance identified by the problem. To handle large context spaces, the authors introduce a softmin-smoothed robust Bellman operator that approximately learns robust Q-values. They incorporate this framework into the SAC reinforcement learning algorithm.

Experiments cover robot control with changing contexts and inventory control. The authors report better generalization, greater robustness to deviations in context transitions, and improvements over existing robust reinforcement learning methods. These results support explicitly representing action-independent disturbances when designing robust policies. The approximation in the value-learning operator is part of the approach used to make that framework scalable.
summary.tldr: The RS-MDP framework improves robustness by explicitly modeling disturbances in context variables that evolve independently of an agent’s actions.

title: Robust Situational Reinforcement Learning in Face of Context Disturbances

abstract: Real-world graphs generally have only one kind of tendency in their connections. These connections are either homophilic-prone or heterophily-prone. While graphs with homophily-prone edges tend to connect nodes with the same class (i.e., intra-class nodes), heterophily-prone edges tend to build relationships between nodes with different classes (i.e., inter-class nodes). Existing GNNs only take the original graph as input during training. The problem with this approach is that it forgets to take into consideration the ”missing-half” structural information, that is, heterophily-prone topology for homophily-prone graphs and homophily-prone topology for heterophily-prone graphs. In our paper, we introduce Graph cOmplementAry Learning, namely GOAL, which consists of two components: graph complementation and complemented graph convolution. The first component finds the missing-half structural information for a given graph to complement it. The complemented graph has two sets of graphs including both homophily- and heterophily-prone topology. In the latter component, to handle complemented graphs, we design a new graph convolution from the perspective of optimisation. The experiment results show that GOAL consistently outperforms all baselines in eight real-world datasets.

paragraphs: A graph can tend to connect nodes from the same class or nodes from different classes. The paper argues that training only on the observed graph can overlook useful structure associated with the opposite tendency. For a graph dominated by same-class connections, that missing information concerns different-class relationships, and the reverse applies to graphs dominated by different-class connections.

Graph cOmplementAry Learning, or GOAL, addresses this through two components. Graph complementation first identifies the missing kind of structural information and constructs a complemented collection containing both connection tendencies. A specially designed graph convolution then processes this richer structure. The convolution is developed from an optimization perspective.

The approach changes both the structural information supplied to a graph neural network and the way that information is processed. Its motivation is that the dominant pattern in an observed graph need not provide all useful relationships for learning. On eight real-world datasets, GOAL consistently outperforms all evaluated baselines. Those experiments support combining complementary connection structures across the graph settings studied.
summary.tldr: GOAL augments graphs with complementary same-class and different-class connection structure and learns from both using a tailored convolution.

title: Finding the Missing-half: Graph Complementary Learning for Homophily-prone and Heterophily-prone Graphs

abstract: Linkage methods are among the most popular algorithms for hierarchical clustering. Despite their relevance, the current knowledge regarding the quality of the clustering produced by these methods is limited. Here, we improve the currently available bounds on the maximum diameter of the clustering obtained by complete-link for metric spaces. One of our new bounds, in contrast to the existing ones, allows us to separate complete-link from single-link in terms of approximation for the diameter, which corroborates the common perception that the former is more suitable than the latter when the goal is producing compact clusters. We also show that our techniques can be employed to derive upper bounds on the cohesion of a class of linkage methods that includes the quite popular average-link.
