paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering methods are widely used, but their popularity exceeds the available theoretical understanding of the quality of their outputs. This paper studies cluster cohesion, focusing on bounds for the maximum cluster diameter produced by complete-link clustering in metric spaces. Diameter captures how far apart members of a cluster can be.

The authors improve existing bounds and obtain one that separates complete-link from single-link in terms of diameter approximation. This gives theoretical support to the common view that complete-link is better suited to producing compact clusters. The result concerns the stated compactness objective, rather than establishing that complete-link is preferable for every purpose.

The analysis also extends beyond complete-link. The authors show that their techniques yield upper bounds on cohesion for a broader class of linkage methods that includes average-link. The significance is a stronger mathematical account of familiar algorithms: it both distinguishes methods under a concrete quality criterion and supplies techniques for studying the cohesion of additional linkage rules.
summary.tldr: Improved cohesion bounds distinguish complete-link from single-link for diameter approximation and extend to linkage methods including average-link.

title: New Bounds on the Cohesion of Complete-link and Other Linkage Methods for Agglomerative Clustering

abstract: Deep neural networks for image super-resolution (ISR) have shown significant advantages over traditional approaches like the interpolation. However, they are often criticized as ’black boxes’ compared to traditional approaches with solid mathematical foundations. In this paper, we attempt to interpret the behavior of deep neural networks in ISR using theories from the field of signal processing. First, we report an intriguing phenomenon, referred to as ‘the sinc phenomenon.’ It occurs when an impulse input is fed to a neural network. Then, building on this observation, we propose a method named Hybrid Response Analysis (HyRA) to analyze the behavior of neural networks in ISR tasks. Specifically, HyRA decomposes a neural network into a parallel connection of a linear system and a non-linear system and demonstrates that the linear system functions as a low-pass filter while the non-linear system injects high-frequency information. Finally, to quantify the injected high-frequency information, we introduce a metric for image-to-image tasks called Frequency Spectrum Distribution Similarity (FSDS). FSDS reflects the distribution similarity of different frequency components and can capture nuances that traditional metrics may overlook. Code, videos and raw experimental results for this paper can be found in: https://github.com/RisingEntropy/LPFInISR.

paragraphs: Neural networks can perform image super-resolution effectively, but explaining how they transform an image remains difficult. This paper approaches that question using signal processing. The authors begin with an observed response to an impulse input, which they call the sinc phenomenon, and use it as a starting point for analyzing network behavior.

Their method, Hybrid Response Analysis, separates the network into parallel linear and nonlinear systems. The analysis shows that the linear component acts as a low-pass filter, while the nonlinear component adds high-frequency information. This gives a more concrete account of the roles played by different parts of the transformation when producing a higher-resolution image.

The paper also introduces Frequency Spectrum Distribution Similarity, a metric for comparing how different frequency components are distributed in image-to-image tasks. It is intended to quantify the injected high-frequency information and capture nuances that traditional metrics may miss. Together, the decomposition and metric provide tools for interpreting super-resolution through the frequency content of its outputs.
summary.tldr: Hybrid Response Analysis interprets super-resolution networks as a linear low-pass component alongside a nonlinear component that adds high-frequency information.

title: Exploring the Low-Pass Filtering Behavior in Image Super-Resolution

abstract: Identifying and estimating a causal effect is a fundamental task when researchers want to infer a causal effect using an observational study without experiments. A conventional assumption is the strict positivity of the given distribution, or so called positivity (or overlap) under the unconfounded assumption that the probabilities of treatments are positive. However, there exist many environments where neither observational data exhibits strict positivity nor unconfounded assumption holds. Against this background, we examine the graphical counterpart of the conventional positivity condition so as to license the use of identification formula without strict positivity. In particular, we explore various approaches, including analysis in a post-hoc manner, do-calculus, $Q$-decomposition, and algorithmic, to yielding a positivity condition for an identification formula, where we relate them, providing a comprehensive view. We further discuss the design of a positivity-aware identification algorithm based on the theoretical characterization of identification formulas.

paragraphs: Causal inference from observational data requires conditions that make a causal effect recoverable from what was observed. A common requirement is positivity, or overlap: relevant treatment possibilities must have positive probability. The paper examines settings where strict positivity fails and where the usual assumption of no unmeasured confounding may also fail.

The authors investigate graphical conditions that permit a particular identification formula to be used without requiring strict positivity of the entire observed distribution. They study the question through several routes: checking formulas afterward, applying do-calculus, using Q-decomposition, and taking an algorithmic approach. Relating these routes provides a unified view of how positivity requirements arise.

The paper also discusses a positivity-aware identification algorithm grounded in its theoretical characterization of formulas. The central value is a more targeted treatment of overlap: the relevant requirement is tied to the causal graph and identification formula under consideration. This supplies a framework for determining when a formula remains justified despite the failure of the conventional stronger condition.
summary.tldr: The paper develops graphical, formula-specific positivity conditions for causal identification without strict positivity of the full observed distribution.

title: On Positivity Condition for Causal Inference

abstract: We develop theory to understand an intriguing property of diffusion models for image generation that we term critical windows. Empirically, it has been observed that there are narrow time intervals in sampling during which particular features of the final image emerge, e.g. the image class or background color (Ho et al., 2020b; Meng et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2022; Raya & Ambrogioni, 2023; Georgiev et al., 2023; Sclocchi et al., 2024; Biroli et al., 2024). While this is advantageous for interpretability as it implies one can localize properties of the generation to a small segment of the trajectory, it seems at odds with the continuous nature of the diffusion. We propose a formal framework for studying these windows and show that for data coming from a mixture of strongly log-concave densities, these windows can be provably bounded in terms of certain measures of inter- and intra-group separation. We also instantiate these bounds for concrete examples like well-conditioned Gaussian mixtures. Finally, we use our bounds to give a rigorous interpretation of diffusion models as hierarchical samplers that progressively “decide” output features over a discrete sequence of times. We validate our bounds with experiments on synthetic data and show that critical windows may serve as a useful tool for diagnosing fairness and privacy violations in real-world diffusion models.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate images through a continuous sampling process, yet particular features can emerge during surprisingly narrow intervals. This paper calls those intervals critical windows. Understanding them could make generation easier to interpret by connecting an output property, such as image class or background color, to a specific portion of the sampling trajectory.

The authors develop a formal framework and prove bounds on these windows for data drawn from mixtures of strongly log-concave densities. The bounds depend on measures of separation between groups and within groups. They also work out concrete examples involving well-conditioned Gaussian mixtures, connecting the general theory to distributions with explicit structure.

These results support a rigorous interpretation of diffusion models as hierarchical samplers that progressively settle output features at a discrete sequence of times. Experiments on synthetic data validate the bounds. The authors also show that critical windows may help diagnose fairness and privacy violations in real-world diffusion models, extending their possible usefulness beyond understanding when image features emerge.
summary.tldr: Under structured mixture assumptions, the paper bounds narrow sampling intervals when diffusion-model features emerge and interprets generation as hierarchical decision-making.

title: Critical windows: non-asymptotic theory for feature emergence in diffusion models

abstract: We study the problem of full-information online learning in the “bounded recall” setting popular in the study of repeated games. An online learning algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ is $M$-bounded-recall if its output at time $t$ can be written as a function of the $M$ previous rewards (and not e.g. any other internal state of $\mathcal{A}$). We first demonstrate that a natural approach to constructing bounded-recall algorithms from mean-based no-regret learning algorithms (e.g., running Hedge over the last $M$ rounds) fails, and that any such algorithm incurs constant regret per round. We then construct a stationary bounded-recall algorithm that achieves a per-round regret of $\Theta(1/\sqrt{M})$, which we complement with a tight lower bound. Finally, we show that unlike the perfect recall setting, any low regret bound bounded-recall algorithm must be aware of the ordering of the past $M$ losses – any bounded-recall algorithm which plays a symmetric function of the past $M$ losses must incur constant regret per round.

paragraphs: This paper studies online learning when each decision can depend only on the previous M reward observations. The learner cannot carry an additional internal state that preserves older information. This bounded-recall condition makes forgetting part of the mathematical problem and raises the question of how much regret a limited history permits.

A natural approach is to run a familiar mean-based algorithm, such as Hedge, on a sliding window. The authors show that this construction fails to achieve vanishing per-round regret: algorithms of this kind incur constant regret per round. They then construct a stationary bounded-recall algorithm whose per-round regret scales as one over the square root of M.

A matching lower bound establishes that this dependence on memory length is tight. The paper also shows why temporal structure matters: any bounded-recall learner that treats all orderings of the recent losses identically incurs constant per-round regret. Successful learning therefore requires using the order of recent observations, alongside having enough observations available.
summary.tldr: Optimal bounded-recall online learning achieves per-round regret proportional to one over the square root of memory length and must use observation order.

title: Online Learning with Bounded Recall

abstract: It is known that sparsity can improve interpretability for deep neural networks. However, existing methods in the area either require networks that are pre-trained with sparsity constraints, or impose sparsity after the fact, altering the network’s general behavior. In this paper, we demonstrate, for the first time, that sparsity can instead be incorporated into the interpretation process itself, as a sample-specific preprocessing step. Unlike previous work, this approach, which we call SPADE, does not place constraints on the trained model and does not affect its behavior during inference on the sample. Given a trained model and a target sample, SPADE uses sample-targeted pruning to provide a "trace" of the network’s execution on the sample, reducing the network to the most important connections prior to computing an interpretation. We demonstrate that preprocessing with SPADE significantly increases the accuracy of image saliency maps across several interpretability methods. Additionally, SPADE improves the usefulness of neuron visualizations, aiding humans in reasoning about network behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/SPADE.

paragraphs: SPADE uses sparsity to improve explanations of an already trained neural network. Existing approaches may require sparse training or alter the network’s general behavior by pruning afterward. This paper instead makes sparsity a preprocessing step within the interpretation procedure, tailored to the particular sample being explained.

Given a model and a target input, SPADE prunes connections to retain those most important for that sample. The resulting reduced network acts as a trace of the computation used for the input, and an interpretation method is then applied to that trace. The approach imposes no constraints on how the original model was trained and preserves its inference behavior on the target sample.

The authors report significantly more accurate image saliency maps across several interpretation methods after SPADE preprocessing. They also find that neuron visualizations become more useful for people reasoning about network behavior. The contribution is a way to simplify the object being interpreted while retaining the relevant sample behavior, allowing sparsity to support explanation without requiring a generally sparse deployed model.
summary.tldr: SPADE applies sample-specific pruning during interpretation to improve saliency maps and neuron visualizations while preserving the model’s behavior on the target sample.

title: SPADE: Sparsity-Guided Debugging for Deep Neural Networks

abstract: How can we design proteins with desired functions? We are motivated by a chemical intuition that both geometric structure and biochemical properties are critical to a protein’s function. In this paper, we propose SurfPro, a new method to generate functional proteins given a desired surface and its associated biochemical properties. SurfPro comprises a hierarchical encoder that progressively models the geometric shape and biochemical features of a protein surface, and an autoregressive decoder to produce an amino acid sequence. We evaluate SurfPro on a standard inverse folding benchmark CATH 4.2 and two functional protein design tasks: protein binder design and enzyme design. Our SurfPro consistently surpasses previous state-of-the-art inverse folding methods, achieving a recovery rate of 57.78% on CATH 4.2 and higher success rates in terms of protein-protein binding and enzyme-substrate interaction scores

paragraphs: SurfPro generates protein sequences from a desired surface and its biochemical properties. Its motivation is that protein function depends on both geometric shape and chemical characteristics. Supplying both kinds of information gives the model a description of the functional surface it should use to guide sequence generation.

The architecture contains a hierarchical encoder that progressively represents the surface’s geometry and biochemical features. An autoregressive decoder then produces the amino acid sequence. This connects a continuous surface description to a discrete sequence, using the encoded surface information as the basis for designing a protein.

The authors evaluate SurfPro on the CATH 4.2 inverse-folding benchmark and on protein-binder and enzyme-design tasks. It consistently exceeds previous state-of-the-art inverse-folding methods in the reported evaluations, reaching 57.78% sequence recovery on CATH 4.2. It also achieves higher success rates measured through protein–protein binding and enzyme–substrate interaction scores. These findings support surface-conditioned generation across the evaluated tasks, with the functional-design results specifically expressed through those interaction-based scores.
summary.tldr: SurfPro generates protein sequences from surface geometry and biochemical features, improving sequence recovery and interaction-based design scores in its evaluations.

title: SurfPro: Functional Protein Design Based on Continuous Surface

abstract: Hybrid models composing mechanistic ODE-based dynamics with flexible and expressive neural network components have grown rapidly in popularity, especially in scientific domains where such ODE-based modeling offers important interpretability and validated causal grounding (e.g., for counterfactual reasoning). The incorporation of mechanistic models also provides inductive bias in standard blackbox modeling approaches, critical when learning from small datasets or partially observed, complex systems. Unfortunately, as the hybrid models become more flexible, the causal grounding provided by the mechanistic model can quickly be lost. We address this problem by leveraging another common source of domain knowledge: ranking of treatment effects for a set of interventions, even if the precise treatment effect is unknown. We encode this information in a causal loss that we combine with the standard predictive loss to arrive at a hybrid loss that biases our learning towards causally valid hybrid models. We demonstrate our ability to achieve a win-win, state-of-the-art predictive performance and causal validity, in the challenging task of modeling glucose dynamics post-exercise in individuals with type 1 diabetes.

paragraphs: Hybrid models combine mechanistic differential equations with flexible neural networks. The equations bring scientific structure and causal grounding, while the neural components increase expressive power. This paper addresses a tension in that combination: as the learned components become more flexible, the causal grounding supplied by the mechanistic model can be lost, even though prediction remains a central training goal.

The authors add another kind of domain knowledge: rankings of treatment effects across interventions. Such rankings can be available even when the exact size of each effect is unknown. They encode this information in a causal loss and combine it with the usual predictive loss. The combined objective biases training toward hybrid models that respect the supplied causal relationships.

The method is evaluated on glucose dynamics following exercise in people with type 1 diabetes. The authors report state-of-the-art predictive performance together with causal validity in this application. The contribution shows how partial intervention knowledge can guide a flexible scientific model: knowing which effects should be larger can help preserve causal behavior without requiring precise treatment-effect values.
summary.tldr: A loss based on treatment-effect rankings helps hybrid neural ODE models combine strong glucose predictions with causal validity.

title: Hybrid$^2$ Neural ODE Causal Modeling and an Application to Glycemic Response

abstract: Conditional diffusion and flow models are effective for super-resolving small-scale details in natural images. However, in physical sciences such as weather, three major challenges arise: (i) spatially misaligned input-output distributions (PDEs at different resolutions lead to divergent trajectories), (ii) misaligned and distinct input-output channels (channel synthesis), (iii) several channels with diverse stochasticity scales (multiscale). To address these, we propose to first encode inputs into a latent base distribution that is closer to the target, then apply Flow Matching to generate small-scale physics. The encoder captures deterministic components, while Flow Matching adds stochastic details. To handle uncertainty in the deterministic part, we inject noise via an adaptive noise scaling mechanism, dynamically adjusted by maximum-likelihood estimates of the encoder’s predictions. Experiments on real-world weather data (including super-resolution from 25 km to 2 km scales in Taiwan) and in synthetic Kolmogorov flow datasets show that our proposed Adaptive Flow Matching (AFM) framework outperforms existing methods and produces better-calibrated ensembles.

These findings support combining deterministic prediction with adaptively scaled randomness when generating small-scale physical behavior.

title: Adaptive Flow Matching for Resolving Small-Scale Physics

abstract: While denoising diffusion and flow matching have driven major advances in generative modeling, their application to tabular data remains limited, despite its ubiquity in real-world applications. To this end, we develop TabbyFlow, a variational Flow Matching (VFM) method for tabular data generation. To apply VFM to data with mixed continuous and discrete features, we introduce Exponential Family Variational Flow Matching (EF-VFM), which represents heterogeneous data types using a general exponential family distribution. We hereby obtain an efficient, data-driven objective based on moment matching, enabling principled learning of probability paths over mixed continuous and discrete variables. We also establish a connection between variational flow matching and generalized flow matching objectives based on Bregman divergences. Evaluation on tabular data benchmarks demonstrates state-of-the-art performance compared to baselines.

paragraphs: Generating tabular data requires handling columns with different kinds of values, including continuous measurements and discrete categories. The paper introduces TabbyFlow, a method built around variational flow matching specifically for tabular generation.

Its core contribution is Exponential Family Variational Flow Matching. This framework represents heterogeneous variable types through a general exponential-family distribution. From that representation, the authors derive an efficient, data-driven training objective based on matching moments, or statistical summaries. This provides a principled way to learn probability paths involving both continuous and discrete variables within the same framework.

The paper also connects variational flow matching to generalized flow-matching objectives expressed using Bregman divergences. That connection gives the proposed method a broader theoretical context beyond its tabular application. On the evaluated tabular benchmarks, TabbyFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance against the included baselines. The reported results support the usefulness of treating mixed data types explicitly in the generative formulation.
summary.tldr: TabbyFlow unifies continuous and discrete tabular generation through exponential-family variational flow matching and reports state-of-the-art benchmark performance.

title: Exponential Family Variational Flow Matching for Tabular Data Generation

abstract: Fine-tuning LLMs is both computationally and memory-intensive. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, such as QLoRA and DoRA, reduce the number of trainable parameters and lower memory usage, they do not decrease computational cost. In some cases, they may even slow down fine-tuning. In this paper, we introduce SparseLoRA, a method that accelerates LLM fine-tuning through contextual sparsity. We propose a lightweight, training-free SVD sparsity estimator that dynamically selects a sparse subset of weights for loss and gradient computation. Also, we systematically analyze and address sensitivity across layers, tokens, and training steps. Our experimental results show that SparseLoRA reduces computational cost by up to $2.2\times$ and a measured speedup of up to $1.6\times$ while maintaining accuracy across various downstream tasks, including commonsense and arithmetic reasoning, code generation, and instruction following.

paragraphs: Reducing the number of trainable parameters can lower fine-tuning memory requirements without reducing the computation needed to train a language model. The paper notes that parameter-efficient methods can even slow training in some cases. SparseLoRA targets computation directly by selecting which weights participate in loss and gradient calculations.

The selection uses a lightweight estimator based on singular value decomposition that requires no training of its own. It dynamically identifies a sparse subset of weights according to context. The authors also analyze and address differences in sensitivity across layers, tokens, and training steps, making the selection responsive to where and when sparsity is applied.

Experiments report computational cost reductions of up to 2.2 times and measured speedups of up to 1.6 times while maintaining accuracy. The evaluated tasks include commonsense reasoning, arithmetic reasoning, code generation, and instruction following. The separate figures distinguish reduced computation from realized elapsed-time gains. The results support contextual sparsity as a way to add practical acceleration to parameter-efficient fine-tuning, beyond reducing how many parameters are updated.
summary.tldr: SparseLoRA dynamically limits fine-tuning computation to selected weights, achieving measured speedups of up to 1.6 times while maintaining accuracy.

title: SparseLoRA: Accelerating LLM Fine-Tuning with Contextual Sparsity

abstract: Low rank adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as a prominent technique for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) thanks to its superb efficiency gains over previous methods. While extensive studies have examined the performance and structural properties of LoRA, its behavior upon training-time attacks remain underexplored, posing significant security risks. In this paper, we theoretically investigate the security implications of LoRA’s low-rank structure during fine-tuning, in the context of its robustness against data poisoning and backdoor attacks. We propose an analytical framework that models LoRA’s training dynamics, employs the neural tangent kernel to simplify the analysis of the training process, and applies information theory to establish connections between LoRA’s low rank structure and its vulnerability against training-time attacks. Our analysis indicates that LoRA exhibits better robustness to backdoor attacks than full fine-tuning, while becomes more vulnerable to untargeted data poisoning due to its over-simplified information geometry. Extensive experimental evaluations have corroborated our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation makes language-model fine-tuning efficient, but its restricted update structure can also affect security. This paper investigates how that structure changes vulnerability to training-time attacks. It distinguishes backdoor attacks from untargeted data poisoning, allowing the analysis to reveal different robustness behavior across the two attack types.

The authors build a framework for LoRA’s training dynamics, use the neural tangent kernel to simplify the training analysis, and apply information theory to connect low-rank structure with vulnerability. Extensive experimental evaluations corroborate these theoretical findings. The answer to the title’s question therefore depends on the attack being considered: the reported robustness difference changes direction between backdoors and untargeted poisoning. The paper’s contribution is explaining that distinction through the structure of the adaptation process, rather than assigning LoRA a single overall security advantage or disadvantage.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments indicate that LoRA resists backdoors better than full fine-tuning but is more vulnerable to untargeted poisoning.

title: Does Low Rank Adaptation Lead to Lower Robustness against Training-Time Attacks?

abstract: Recently, the expansion of Variance Reduction (VR) to Riemannian stochastic non-convex optimization has attracted increasing interest. Inspired by recursive momentum, we first introduce Stochastic Recursive Variance Reduced Gradient (SRVRG) algorithm and further present Stochastic Recursive Gradient Estimator (SRGE) in Euclidean spaces, which unifies the prevailing variance reduction estimators. We then extend SRGE to Riemannian spaces, resulting in a unified Stochastic rEcursive vaRiance reducEd gradieNt frAmework (SERENA) for Riemannian non-convex optimization. This framework includes the proposed R-SRVRG, R-SVRRM, and R-Hybrid-SGD methods, as well as other existing Riemannian VR methods. Furthermore, we establish a unified theoretical analysis for Riemannian non-convex optimization under retraction and vector transport. The IFO complexity of our proposed R-SRVRG and R-SVRRM to converge to $\varepsilon$-accurate solution is $\mathcal{O}\left(\min \{n^{1/2}{\varepsilon^{-2}}, \varepsilon^{-3}\}\right)$ in the finite-sum setting and ${\mathcal{O}\left( \varepsilon^{-3}\right)}$ for the online case, both of which align with the lower IFO complexity bound. Experimental results indicate that the proposed algorithms surpass other existing Riemannian optimization methods.

paragraphs: Variance reduction improves stochastic optimization by making gradient estimates less noisy, but transferring these methods to curved parameter spaces requires careful geometric handling. This paper develops a common recursive framework for nonconvex optimization on Riemannian manifolds. It aims to connect several existing estimators and derive new ones within the same analysis.

The authors first introduce a recursive gradient estimator in Euclidean space, then extend it to manifolds as SERENA. The framework includes R-SRVRG, R-SVRRM, R-Hybrid-SGD, and earlier Riemannian variance-reduction methods. Experiments outperform compared Riemannian optimizers. The contribution combines an organizing framework with efficient algorithms, under the nonconvex and geometric assumptions of the analysis.
summary.tldr: SERENA unifies recursive variance reduction on manifolds and provides methods with optimal stated oracle-complexity guarantees.

title: SERENA: A Unified Stochastic Recursive Variance Reduced Gradient Framework for Riemannian Non-Convex Optimization

abstract: Many existing interpretation methods are based on Partial Dependence (PD) functions that, for a pre-trained machine learning model, capture how a subset of the features affects the predictions by averaging over the remaining features. Notable methods include Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) which computes feature contributions based on a game theoretical interpretation and PD plots (i.e., 1-dim PD functions) that capture average marginal main effects. Recent work has connected these approaches using a functional decomposition and argues that SHAP values can be misleading since they merge main and interaction effects into a single local effect. However, a major advantage of SHAP compared to other PD-based interpretations has been the availability of fast estimation techniques, such as TreeSHAP. In this paper, we propose a new tree-based estimator, FastPD, which efficiently estimates arbitrary PD functions. We show that FastPD consistently estimates the desired population quantity – in contrast to path-dependent TreeSHAP which is inconsistent when features are correlated. For moderately deep trees, FastPD improves the complexity of existing methods from quadratic to linear in the number of observations. By estimating PD functions for arbitrary feature subsets, FastPD can be used to extract PD-based interpretations such as SHAP, PD plots and higher-order interaction effects.

paragraphs: Partial dependence describes how selected input features affect a trained model's predictions after averaging over the other features. It underlies several interpretation methods, including partial-dependence plots and SHAP. The paper highlights a tension: efficient SHAP estimation is available, but a single contribution can combine a feature's main effect with its interactions.

This broader target allows the same estimation machinery to support individual feature effects and higher-order interactions. The authors prove consistency for the desired population quantity, contrasting it with path-dependent TreeSHAP, which is inconsistent when features are correlated.

That qualification matters because the computational claim is tied to tree depth. The method can produce SHAP values, partial-dependence plots, and interaction effects. Its contribution is thus both computational and interpretive: it makes a wider range of dependence-based explanations available through efficient, statistically consistent estimation.
summary.tldr: FastPD efficiently and consistently estimates partial dependence for tree models, supporting feature effects and higher-order interactions.

title: Fast Estimation of Partial Dependence Functions using Trees

abstract: Although transformers have demonstrated impressive capabilities for in-context learning (ICL) in practice, theoretical understanding of the underlying mechanism that allows transformers to perform ICL is still in its infancy. This work aims to theoretically study the training dynamics of transformers for in-context classification tasks. We demonstrate that, for in-context classification of Gaussian mixtures under certain assumptions, a single-layer transformer trained via gradient descent converges to a globally optimal model at a linear rate. We further quantify the impact of the training and testing prompt lengths on the ICL inference error of the trained transformer. We show that when the lengths of training and testing prompts are sufficiently large, the prediction of the trained transformer approaches the ground truth distribution of the labels. Experimental results corroborate the theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Transformers can use examples in a prompt to perform a task, but explaining how training produces this ability remains difficult. This paper studies that question in a specific mathematical setting: in-context classification of Gaussian mixtures. It examines both optimization during training and prediction error when the trained model receives a prompt.

Under the paper's assumptions, a single-layer transformer trained with gradient descent converges to a globally optimal model at a linear rate. This gives a concrete convergence result for the specified architecture and task family. It connects the training procedure to successful model optimization within that setting.

The authors also quantify how training-prompt and testing-prompt lengths affect inference error. When both are sufficiently large, the trained transformer's predictions approach the true distribution of labels. Experiments corroborate the theory. Together, the results explain how optimization and the amount of prompt information interact in this setting, with the guarantees explicitly tied to the Gaussian-mixture classification problem and its assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under specified assumptions, a single-layer transformer learns Gaussian-mixture in-context classification with linear convergence and improving predictions as prompts become sufficiently long.

title: On the Training Convergence of Transformers for In-Context Classification of Gaussian Mixtures

abstract: While score-based generative models are the model of choice across diverse domains, there are limited tools available for controlling inference-time behavior in a principled manner, e.g. for composing multiple pretrained models. Existing classifier-free guidance methods use a simple heuristic to mix conditional and unconditional scores to approximately sample from conditional distributions. However, such methods do not approximate the intermediate distributions, necessitating additional ‘corrector’ steps. In this work, we provide an efficient and principled method for sampling from a sequence of annealed, geometric-averaged, or product distributions derived from pretrained score-based models. We derive a weighted simulation scheme which we call Feynman-Kac Correctors (FKCs) based on the celebrated Feynman-Kac formula by carefully accounting for terms in the appropriate partial differential equations (PDEs). To simulate these PDEs, we propose Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) resampling algorithms that leverage inference-time scaling to improve sampling quality. We empirically demonstrate the utility of our methods by proposing amortized sampling via inference-time temperature annealing, improving multi-objective molecule generation using pretrained models, and improving classifier-free guidance for text-to-image generation.

summary.tldr: Feynman-Kac Correctors use weighted simulation and resampling to improve principled inference-time control and composition of pretrained diffusion models.

title: Feynman-Kac Correctors in Diffusion: Annealing, Guidance, and Product of Experts

abstract: We study an infinite-armed bandit problem where actions’ mean rewards are initially sampled from a reservoir distribution. Most prior works in this setting focused on stationary rewards (Berry et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2008; Bonald and Proutiere, 2013; Carpentier and Valko, 2015) with the more challenging adversarial/non-stationary variant only recently studied in the context of rotting/decreasing rewards (Kim et al., 2022; 2024). Furthermore, optimal regret upper bounds were only achieved using parameter knowledge of non-stationarity and only known for certain regimes of regularity of the reservoir. This work shows the first parameter-free optimal regret bounds while also relaxing these distributional assumptions. We also study a natural notion of significant shift for this problem inspired by recent developments in finite-armed MAB (Suk & Kpotufe, 2022). We show that tighter regret bounds in terms of significant shifts can be adaptively attained. Our enhanced rates only depend on the rotting non-stationarity and thus exhibit an interesting phenomenon for this problem where rising non-stationarity does not factor into the difficulty of non-stationarity.

paragraphs: An infinite-armed bandit models decision-making with an unlimited supply of possible actions, whose initial mean rewards come from a reservoir distribution. When rewards change over time, selecting good actions becomes harder. Previous optimal regret guarantees required knowledge of non-stationarity parameters and applied only under particular regularity conditions on that reservoir.

This paper establishes parameter-free optimal regret bounds while relaxing those distributional assumptions. It also develops a notion of significant shifts, aiming to characterize the changes that meaningfully affect the decision problem. The authors show that algorithms can adaptively attain tighter regret bounds expressed through these significant shifts.

A notable feature of the enhanced rates is that they depend only on rotting, or decreasing, rewards. Rising rewards do not contribute to the non-stationarity difficulty measured by these bounds. This distinguishes the direction of reward changes within the analysis rather than treating every fluctuation as equally costly. The result provides a sharper account of adaptation while removing the need for advance parameter knowledge.
summary.tldr: Parameter-free bandit guarantees adapt to significant reward shifts, with enhanced rates depending on decreases rather than increases.

title: Tracking Most Significant Shifts in Infinite-Armed Bandits

abstract: Equipping large language models (LLMs) with latent-space memory has attracted increasing attention as they can extend the context window of existing language models. However, retaining information from the distant past remains a challenge. For example, MemoryLLM (Wang et al., 2024a), as a representative work with latent-space memory, compresses past information into hidden states across all layers, forming a memory pool of 1B parameters. While effective for sequence lengths up to 16k tokens, it struggles to retain knowledge beyond 20k tokens. In this work, we address this limitation by introducing M+, a memory-augmented model based on MemoryLLM that significantly enhances long-term information retention. M+ integrates a long-term memory mechanism with a co-trained retriever, dynamically retrieving relevant information during text generation. We evaluate M+ on diverse benchmarks, including long-context understanding and knowledge retention tasks. Experimental results show that M+ significantly outperforms MemoryLLM and recent strong baselines, extending knowledge retention from under 20k to over 160k tokens with similar GPU memory overhead.

paragraphs: Latent-space memory stores past information in a language model’s hidden representations, offering a way to extend access beyond its ordinary context window. Retaining distant information remains difficult, however. The paper describes MemoryLLM as effective for sequences up to 16,000 tokens but struggling to retain knowledge beyond 20,000, despite its billion-parameter memory pool.

M+ extends MemoryLLM with a long-term memory mechanism and a retriever trained alongside it. During text generation, the retriever dynamically brings back relevant stored information. This couples memory storage with a learned process for deciding which past information should be available when producing the current response.

The evaluation covers long-context understanding and knowledge-retention tasks. M+ significantly outperforms MemoryLLM and recent strong baselines in the reported experiments, extending retention from below 20,000 to above 160,000 tokens with similar GPU memory overhead. The result shows that the added storage-and-retrieval mechanism can substantially lengthen usable memory in the tested setting without a comparable increase in GPU memory requirements.
summary.tldr: M+ adds long-term memory and a co-trained retriever to MemoryLLM, extending reported knowledge retention beyond 160,000 tokens.

title: M+: Extending MemoryLLM with Scalable Long-Term Memory

abstract: Recent advances in generative models have made it increasingly difficult to distinguish real data from model-generated synthetic data. Using synthetic data for successive training of future model generations creates “self-consuming loops,” which may lead to model collapse or training instability. Furthermore, synthetic data is often subject to human feedback and curated by users based on their preferences. Ferbach et al. (2024) recently showed that when data is curated according to user preferences, the self-consuming retraining loop drives the model to converge toward a distribution that optimizes those preferences. However, in practice, data curation is often noisy or adversarially manipulated. For example, competing platforms may recruit malicious users to adversarially curate data and disrupt rival models. In this paper, we study how generative models evolve under self-consuming retraining loops with noisy and adversarially curated data. We theoretically analyze the impact of such noisy data curation on generative models and identify conditions for the robustness and stability of the retraining process. Building on this analysis, we design attack algorithms for competitive adversarial scenarios, where a platform with a limited budget employs malicious users to misalign a rival’s model from actual user preferences. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.

However, in practice, data curation is often noisy or adversarially manipulated. For example, competing platforms may recruit malicious users to adversarially curate data and disrupt rival models. In this paper, we study how generative models evolve under self-consuming retraining loops with noisy and adversarially curated data. We theoretically analyze the impact of such noisy data curation on generative models and identify conditions for the robustness and stability of the retraining process. Building on this analysis, we design attack algorithms for competitive adversarial scenarios, where a platform with a limited budget employs malicious users to misalign a rival’s model from actual user preferences. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: Generative models can enter self-consuming loops when their synthetic outputs become training data for later generations. User preferences also influence which outputs are retained. This paper examines what happens when that curation is noisy or deliberately manipulated, changing the feedback that shapes future models.

The authors theoretically analyze how noisy curation affects the evolution of models across repeated retraining. They identify conditions under which the process remains robust and stable. This extends the preference-driven view of self-consuming training by considering whether the apparent preferences reflected in curated data faithfully represent the users a model is meant to serve.

Building on the analysis, the paper develops attack algorithms for competitive settings in which a platform has a limited budget for malicious users who curate a rival's data. The aim is to move the rival model away from actual user preferences. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the algorithms' effectiveness. The work makes curation quality a central part of understanding retraining dynamics, alongside the already recognized risks of repeatedly learning from synthetic content.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes stability under noisy synthetic-data curation and develops budget-limited attacks that steer rivals away from user preferences.

title: Self-Consuming Generative Models with Adversarially Curated Data

abstract: We propose HyperIV, a novel approach for real-time implied volatility smoothing that eliminates the need for traditional calibration procedures. Our method employs a hypernetwork to generate parameters for a compact neural network that constructs complete volatility surfaces within 2 milliseconds, using only 9 market observations. Moreover, the generated surfaces are guaranteed to be free of static arbitrage. Extensive experiments across 8 index options demonstrate that HyperIV achieves superior accuracy compared to existing methods while maintaining computational efficiency. The model also exhibits strong cross-asset generalization capabilities, indicating broader applicability across different market instruments. These key features – rapid adaptation to market conditions, guaranteed absence of arbitrage, and minimal data requirements – make HyperIV particularly valuable for real-time trading applications. We make code available at https://github.com/qmfin/hyperiv.

The paper replaces traditional calibration with a learned mechanism that produces the parameters needed to construct the surface, targeting the demands of real-time use.

The mechanism is a hypernetwork: a neural network that generates parameters for another network. Here, it supplies a compact neural network that builds the volatility surface. They also guarantee that the resulting surfaces are free of static arbitrage, adding a financial consistency property to the speed and data-efficiency claims.

These findings make the combination significant: sparse observations, rapid surface construction, and a stated arbitrage guarantee address different requirements of real-time trading applications.
summary.tldr: HyperIV generates statically arbitrage-free volatility surfaces within two milliseconds from nine market observations using a hypernetwork.

title: HyperIV: Real-time Implied Volatility Smoothing

abstract: The distribution shifts and the scarcity of labels prevent graph learning methods, especially graph neural networks (GNNs), from generalizing across domains. Compared to Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) with embedding alignment, Unsupervised Graph Domain Adaptation (UGDA) becomes more challenging in light of the attribute and topology entanglement in the representation. Beyond embedding alignment, UGDA turns to topology alignment but is limited by the ability of the employed topology model and the estimation of pseudo labels. To alleviate this issue, this paper proposed a Disentangled Graph Spectral Domain adaptation (DGSDA) by disentangling attribute and topology alignments and directly aligning flexible graph spectral filters beyond topology. Specifically, Bernstein polynomial approximation, which mimics the behavior of the function to be approximated to a remarkable degree, is employed to capture complicated topology characteristics and avoid the expensive eigenvalue decomposition. Theoretical analysis reveals the tight GDA bound of DGSDA and the rationality of polynomial coefficient regularization. Quantitative and qualitative experiments justify the superiority of the proposed DGSDA.

paragraphs: Graph models face a difficult transfer problem when the data distribution changes and labels are scarce. Their representations combine node attributes with graph connectivity, so aligning representations across domains can mix together two different sources of mismatch. Existing approaches that align topology also depend on the expressiveness of their topology model and the quality of estimated labels.

DGSDA separates attribute alignment from topology alignment and works directly with flexible graph spectral filters. These filters offer a way to describe how graph structure influences the representation. The method approximates them with Bernstein polynomials, allowing it to capture complicated topological characteristics without performing an expensive eigenvalue decomposition. This changes both the object being aligned and the computational machinery used to represent it.

The paper provides a tight graph domain adaptation bound and theoretical support for regularizing the polynomial coefficients. Quantitative and qualitative experiments report advantages over the compared methods. Together, these findings support separating the sources of domain shift and aligning structural behavior through spectral filters, rather than relying only on a combined embedding.
summary.tldr: DGSDA separates attribute and topology alignment and uses polynomial graph spectral filters to improve adaptation across graph domains.

title: Disentangled Graph Spectral Domain Adaptation

abstract: Traditional autonomous driving systems often struggle to connect high-level reasoning with low-level control, leading to suboptimal and sometimes unsafe behaviors. Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), which process both visual and textual data, offer an opportunity to unify perception and reasoning. However, effectively embedding precise safety knowledge into MLLMs for autonomous driving remains a significant challenge. To address this, we propose SafeAuto, a framework that enhances MLLM-based autonomous driving by incorporating both unstructured and structured knowledge. First, we introduce a Position-Dependent Cross-Entropy (PDCE) loss to improve low-level control signal predictions when values are represented as text. Second, to explicitly integrate safety knowledge, we develop a reasoning component that translates traffic rules into first-order logic (e.g., "red light =$>$ stop") and embeds them into a probabilistic graphical model (e.g., Markov Logic Network) to verify predicted actions using recognized environmental attributes. Additionally, our Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) model leverages video, control signals, and environmental attributes to learn from past driving experiences. Integrating PDCE, MLN, and Multimodal RAG, SafeAuto outperforms existing baselines across multiple datasets, enabling more accurate, reliable, and safer autonomous driving. The code is available at https://github.com/AI-secure/SafeAuto.

paragraphs: Autonomous driving requires connecting an understanding of the scene with precise control actions. SafeAuto addresses this through a framework that brings together control prediction, structured traffic rules, and information retrieved from previous driving experiences.

A separate reasoning component translates traffic rules into first-order logic and places them in a probabilistic graphical model, such as a Markov Logic Network. Recognized environmental attributes then help this component verify predicted actions against the encoded rules.

A multimodal retrieval-augmented generation component uses video, control signals, and environmental attributes to draw on past experience. The framework combines this experiential knowledge with explicit rule checking and improved numerical prediction. Across multiple datasets, the authors report better accuracy, reliability, and safety than existing baselines. These are empirical improvements from the integrated system, rather than a guarantee of safe behavior in every driving situation.
summary.tldr: SafeAuto combines better control prediction, probabilistic traffic-rule checking, and multimodal retrieval to improve evaluated autonomous driving performance and safety.

title: SafeAuto: Knowledge-Enhanced Safe Autonomous Driving with Multimodal Foundation Models

abstract: Budget-feasible procurement auctions play a pivotal role in various AI-driven marketplaces, such as data acquisition and crowdsourcing, where a buyer with a limited budget seeks to procure services from strategic sellers with private costs. While numerous budget-feasible mechanisms have been proposed for the classic objective of maximizing the buyer’s valuation, the more challenging and economically significant objective of social welfare maximization has only recently been studied, and existing approaches still sacrifice budget feasibility, thereby limiting their practical applicability. In this paper, we bridge this gap by proposing BFM-SWM, the first budget-feasible mechanism with provable approximation guarantees for submodular welfare maximization in procurement auctions. Our mechanism satisfies standard economic properties, including truthfulness, individual rationality, and non-negative auctioneer surplus. As a by-product, we develop BFM-VM, a variant tailored for valuation maximization, which achieves a deterministic approximation ratio of $1/(12+4\sqrt{3})$ for general submodular functions, substantially improving upon the best-known deterministic ratio of $1/64$ established by [Balkanski et al., SODA 2022], while reducing the running time from $\mathcal{O}(n^2\log n)$ to $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our mechanisms.

In applications such as data acquisition and crowdsourcing, the buyer must also respect a limited budget. This paper addresses social welfare maximization with submodular objectives, where existing approaches described in the abstract give up strict budget feasibility.

The proposed BFM-SWM mechanism combines budget feasibility with provable approximation guarantees for this welfare objective. It also satisfies truthfulness, individual rationality, and non-negative auctioneer surplus. These properties matter together: a useful selection rule must account for strategic cost reports and participation incentives while staying within the available funds.

The authors additionally develop BFM-VM for maximizing the buyer's valuation. For general submodular functions, it improves the stated deterministic approximation ratio from 1/64 to 1/(12 + 4√3), while reducing running time from O(n² log n) to O(n log n). Those numerical guarantees apply to the valuation variant. Experiments support the efficiency and effectiveness of both mechanisms, complementing the welfare mechanism's theoretical budget and incentive guarantees.
summary.tldr: BFM-SWM provides budget-feasible procurement with welfare approximation guarantees, while a valuation variant improves approximation and running time.

title: Budget-Feasible Mechanisms for Submodular Welfare Maximization in Procurement Auctions

abstract: The pursuit of spatial intelligence fundamentally relies on access to large-scale, fine-grained 3D data. However, existing approaches predominantly construct spatial understanding benchmarks by generating question–answer (QA) pairs from a limited number of manually annotated datasets, rather than systematically annotating new large-scale 3D scenes from raw web data. As a result, their scalability is severely constrained, and model performance is further hindered by domain gaps inherent in these narrowly curated datasets. In this work, we propose Holi-Spatial, the first fully automated, large-scale, spatially-aware multimodal dataset, constructed from raw video inputs without human intervention, using the proposed data curation pipeline. Holi-Spatial supports multi-level spatial supervision, ranging from geometrically accurate 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstructions with rendered depth maps to object-level and relational semantic annotations, together with corresponding spatial Question–Answer (QA) pairs. Following a principled and systematic pipeline, we further construct Holi-Spatial-4M, the first large-scale, high-quality 3D semantic dataset, containing 12K optimized 3DGS scenes, 1.3M 2D masks, 320K 3D bounding boxes, 320K instance captions, 1.2M 3D grounding instances, and 1.2M spatial QA pairs spanning diverse geometric, relational, and semantic reasoning tasks. Holi-Spatial demonstrates exceptional performance in data curation quality, significantly outperforming existing feed-forward and per-scene optimized methods on datasets such as ScanNet, ScanNet++, and DL3DV. Furthermore, fine-tuning Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on spatial reasoning tasks using this dataset has also led to substantial improvements in model performance.

Holi-Spatial instead introduces a fully automated pipeline that constructs spatially annotated data directly from raw videos without human intervention.

summary.tldr: Holi-Spatial automatically turns raw videos into reconstructed and annotated 3D scenes that improve vision-language models’ spatial reasoning.

title: Holi-Spatial: Evolving Video Streams into Holistic 3D Spatial Intelligence

abstract: Existing time series tokenization methods predominantly encode a constant number of samples into individual tokens. This inflexible approach can generate excessive tokens for even simple patterns like extended constant values, resulting in substantial computational overhead. Inspired by the success of byte pair encoding, we propose the first pattern-centric tokenization scheme for time series analysis. Based on a discrete vocabulary of frequent motifs, our method merges samples with underlying patterns into tokens, compressing time series adaptively. Exploiting our finite set of motifs and the continuous properties of time series, we further introduce conditional decoding as a lightweight yet powerful post-hoc optimization method, which requires no gradient computation and adds no computational overhead. On recent time series foundation models, our motif-based tokenization improves forecasting performance by 40% and boosts efficiency by 2314% on average. Conditional decoding further reduces MSE by up to 48%. In an extensive analysis, we demonstrate the adaptiveness of our tokenization to diverse temporal patterns, its generalization to unseen data, and its meaningful token representations capturing distinct time series properties, including statistical moments and trends.

paragraphs: Many time-series models turn fixed numbers of measurements into tokens. This can waste computation when a long stretch contains a simple, repeated pattern, because the representation remains lengthy despite the underlying simplicity. This paper proposes tokenizing around recurring patterns instead, drawing inspiration from byte pair encoding.

The method learns a discrete vocabulary of frequent motifs and merges samples into tokens according to those patterns. Compression therefore adapts to the series rather than following a fixed sample count. The authors also introduce conditional decoding, which uses the finite motif vocabulary and the continuous properties of time series to refine decoding afterward. It requires no gradient computation and is reported to add no computational overhead.

On recent time-series foundation models, the authors report an average 40% improvement in forecasting performance and a 2314% efficiency increase. Conditional decoding further reduces mean squared error by up to 48%. Their analysis also finds adaptation to diverse temporal patterns, generalization to unseen data, and tokens that capture properties such as statistical moments and trends. Together, these results suggest that pattern-aware compression can improve both representation quality and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: A motif-based tokenizer adaptively compresses time series, improving reported forecasting quality and efficiency while supporting lightweight conditional decoding.

title: Byte Pair Encoding for Efficient Time Series Forecasting

abstract: The Edge of Stability (EoS) is a phenomenon where the sharpness (largest eigenvalue) of the Hessian approaches and then hovers near the stability threshold $2/\eta$ during gradient descent (GD) with step size $\eta$. Despite (apparently) violating classical smoothness assumptions, EoS has been widely observed in deep learning, but its theoretical foundations remain incomplete. We provide an interpretation of EoS through the lens of Directional Smoothness [Mishkin et al., 2024]. This interpretation naturally extends to non-Euclidean norms, which we use to define generalized sharpness under an arbitrary norm. Our generalized sharpness measure includes previously studied vanilla GD and preconditioned GD as special cases, as well as methods for which EoS has not been studied, such as $\ell_{\infty}$-descent, Block CD, Spectral GD, and their normalized versions. Through experiments on neural networks, we show that non-Euclidean GD with our generalized sharpness also exhibits progressive sharpening followed by oscillations around or above the threshold $2/\eta$. Practically, our framework provides a geometry-aware spectral diagnostic that can be applied across a broad class of non-Euclidean gradient methods.

paragraphs: During ordinary gradient descent, the largest Hessian eigenvalue can rise toward the stability threshold 2 divided by the step size and then hover nearby. This edge-of-stability behavior is widely observed in deep learning, although its theoretical explanation remains incomplete. The paper asks how to describe comparable behavior for optimization methods using different geometries.

The authors interpret the phenomenon through directional smoothness and define generalized sharpness for an arbitrary norm. Their definition includes ordinary and preconditioned gradient descent while extending to methods such as infinity-norm descent, block coordinate descent, spectral gradient descent, and normalized variants. It supplies a shared framework without measuring every optimizer solely through Euclidean geometry.

Neural-network experiments show progressive sharpening followed by oscillations around or above the corresponding threshold under this generalized measure. The contribution is a geometry-aware diagnostic that makes stability behavior comparable across a broader family of methods. The empirical observations extend the phenomenon’s reach, while the framework offers an interpretation rather than claiming to settle every aspect of its theoretical foundations.
summary.tldr: A geometry-aware sharpness measure extends edge-of-stability analysis to non-Euclidean gradient methods, with supporting neural-network experiments.

title: Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent Operates at the Edge of Stability

abstract: Neural speech codecs based on Vector-Quantized VAEs (VQ-VAEs) are core audio tokenizers for speech LLMs, yet their reconstruction fidelity is bottlenecked by quantization error. Modifying the quantizer or increasing model capacity are common fixes, but they complicate downstream language modeling. Our core idea is to align the decoder’s internal feature manifolds when processing both the quantized tokens and their original continuous embeddings, using a lightweight feature-mapping loss. This requires minimal training overhead and no inference-time changes. Applied to XCodec2, self-guidance improves all reconstruction metrics, achieving state-of-the-art low-bitrate performance. Notably, it enables a 4$\times$ codebook reduction without fidelity loss, which downstream TTS experiments show significantly improves LLM-based synthesis by simplifying the token modeling space. Multiple statistical observations and visualizations corroborate the enhanced internal manifold alignment in the decoder. Extensive experiments confirm its generality across various inductive biases. Self-guidance thus establishes an efficient, broadly applicable method for high-fidelity neural audio coding.

paragraphs: Neural speech codecs turn audio into discrete tokens that speech language models can use. Quantization introduces errors that limit reconstructed audio quality. Increasing model size or changing the quantizer can address those errors, but the resulting token representation can become harder for a downstream language model to handle.

Self-guidance trains the decoder to align its internal features when processing quantized tokens and the corresponding original continuous embeddings. A lightweight feature-mapping loss encourages those internal representations to agree. The method adds minimal training overhead and requires no changes at inference time, making the decoder's training behavior the main point of intervention.

Applied to XCodec2, self-guidance improves all reported reconstruction metrics and achieves state-of-the-art low-bitrate performance. It also supports a fourfold reduction in codebook size without fidelity loss. Downstream text-to-speech experiments show significantly better language-model-based synthesis with the simpler token space. Statistical analyses and visualizations support improved internal alignment, while experiments across different inductive biases support the method's broader applicability. The results connect better codec reconstruction with easier downstream token modeling.
summary.tldr: Aligning decoder features for continuous and quantized audio improves reconstruction and enables a fourfold smaller codebook without fidelity loss.

title: Self-Guidance: Enhancing Neural Codecs via Decoder Manifold Alignment

abstract: Latent actions serve as an intermediate representation that enables consistent modeling of vision-language-action (VLA) models across heterogeneous datasets. However, approaches to supervising VLAs with latent actions are fragmented and lack a systematic comparison. This work structures the study of latent action supervision from two perspectives: (i) regularizing the trajectory via image-based latent actions, and (ii) unifying the target space with action-based latent actions. Under a unified VLA baseline, we instantiate and compare four representative integration strategies. Our results reveal a formulation-task correspondence: image-based latent actions benefit long-horizon reasoning, whereas action-based latent actions excel at complex motor coordination. Furthermore, we find that directly supervising the VLM with discrete latent action tokens yields the most effective performance. Finally, our experiments offer initial insights into the benefits of latent action supervision in mixed-data, suggesting a promising direction for VLA training.

paragraphs: Latent actions provide an intermediate representation for training vision-language-action models across heterogeneous datasets. However, different ways of incorporating them have developed without a systematic comparison. This paper organizes those choices and evaluates four representative integration strategies using a unified model baseline, making their relative strengths easier to interpret.

The study distinguishes two roles for latent actions. Image-based representations regularize the trajectory, while action-based representations unify the target space that the model learns to predict. The experiments reveal a correspondence between formulation and task: image-based supervision benefits long-horizon reasoning, whereas action-based supervision performs particularly well on complex motor coordination.

Among the tested strategies, directly supervising the vision-language model with discrete latent action tokens gives the most effective performance. Experiments involving mixed data also provide initial evidence of benefits from latent action supervision. These findings offer guidance for choosing a representation according to the intended behavior, while the mixed-data results remain an early indication rather than an established general conclusion.
summary.tldr: A controlled comparison finds that latent-action supervision choices suit different robotic demands, with direct discrete-token supervision performing best among tested strategies.

title: From Pixels to Tokens: A Systematic Study of Latent Action Supervision for Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: Affective and cognitive disorders manifest as distributed, time-varying brain network dynamics across regions, channels, and time, challenging robust representation learning from EEG/sEEG for clinical diagnosis. We propose RECTOR (Masked Region–Channel–Temporal Modeling), an end-to-end self-supervised framework that unifies joint region-channel-temporal representation learning beyond fixed anatomical priors. At its core, RECTOR-SA is a hierarchical, block-sparse self-attention induced by Adaptive Functional Partitioning that evolves region structures from static anatomical definitions to adaptive functional regions. The self-supervision is driven by Masked Topology and Representation Learning, which jointly optimizes three complementary objectives: Masked Predictive Modeling, Topological Structure Modeling, and Cross-View Consistency. Across diverse benchmarks, RECTOR sets a new state-of-the-art in EEG emotion recognition and sEEG task-engagement classification. Crucially, its strong robustness to missing channels and cross-montage generalization underscores its potential for large-scale pre-training on heterogeneous EEG/sEEG, providing interpretable insights at both region and channel levels.

Across diverse benchmarks, RECTOR sets a new state-of-the-art in EEG emotion recognition and sEEG task-engagement classification. Crucially, its strong robustness to missing channels and cross-montage generalization underscores its potential for large-scale pre-training on heterogeneous EEG/sEEG, providing interpretable insights at both region and channel levels.

paragraphs: EEG and sEEG measurements reflect brain activity distributed across recording channels, brain regions, and time. RECTOR learns representations across all three dimensions through self-supervision. Its motivation is that fixed anatomical groupings may not capture the changing functional relationships needed to understand affective and cognitive activity.

The framework uses Adaptive Functional Partitioning to evolve region structures from anatomical definitions toward functional regions. Those partitions shape a hierarchical, block-sparse attention mechanism called RECTOR-SA. Training combines prediction of masked information, modeling of topological structure, and consistency across views. These complementary objectives encourage the representation to capture both the recorded activity and relationships among its components.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance in EEG emotion recognition and sEEG task-engagement classification. RECTOR also shows robustness when channels are missing and generalization across recording montages. These results support its potential for pretraining across heterogeneous recordings, while region-level and channel-level interpretations offer insight into the learned structure. The stated evaluation concerns these representation and classification tasks, rather than demonstrating clinical diagnosis.
summary.tldr: RECTOR learns adaptive brain-region, channel, and temporal structure to improve EEG and sEEG classification across varied recording conditions.

title: RECTOR: Masked Region-Channel-Temporal Modeling for Affective and Cognitive Representation Learning

abstract: The smoothness of the transformer architecture has been extensively studied in the context of generalization, training stability, and adversarial robustness. However, its role in transfer learning remains poorly understood. In this paper, we analyze the ability of vision transformer components to adapt their outputs to changes in inputs, or, in other words, their plasticity. Defined as an average rate of change, it captures the sensitivity to input perturbation; in particular, a high plasticity implies a low smoothness. Our theoretical analysis and extensive experiments – over $1,000$ finetuning runs on large-scale vision transformers – showcase that this perspective provides principled guidance in choosing the components to prioritize during adaptation. A key takeaway for practitioners is that the high plasticity of the attention modules and feedforward layers consistently leads to better finetuning performance. Our findings depart from the prevailing assumption that smoothness is desirable, offering a novel perspective on transformers’ functional properties. The code is available at https://github.com/ambroiseodt/vit-plasticity.

It offers practitioners a principled criterion for choosing adaptation targets based on their capacity to change outputs, supported by both analysis and extensive experiments.
summary.tldr: Vision-transformer fine-tuning benefits from prioritizing highly plastic attention and feedforward components, whose outputs respond more strongly to input changes.

title: Vision Transformer Finetuning Benefits from Non-Smooth Components

abstract: Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to Autoregressive Language Models (ARLMs), leveraging a denoising objective that, in principle, should enable more uniform context utilisation. In this work, we examine the context comprehension abilities of MDLMs and uncover two key limitations. First, despite their more global training objective and bidirectional attention mechanism, similarly to ARLMS, MDLMs exhibit a strong locality bias: performance is highly sensitive to the position of relevant information within the input, favouring local over distant context. Second, appending a large number of mask tokens—required for generation—can significantly degrade context comprehension in models trained from scratch. Through systematic ablations, we find that these masks act as distractors, reducing the model’s ability to process relevant information. To address and further study this undesirable behaviour, we introduce the mask-agnostic loss function that encourages predictions to remain invariant to the number of appended masks. Fine-tuning with this objective substantially mitigates the distracting effect of masks, improving robustness of MDLMs. Overall, our findings reveal critical limitations of the current MDLM training paradigm, with implications for training, evaluation and deployment.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion language models generate through denoising and use bidirectional attention, which might be expected to support broad use of context. This paper tests that expectation and finds a strong locality bias. Performance depends heavily on where relevant information appears, with nearby context favored over information located farther away.

The study identifies a second problem: appending many mask tokens, as required for generation, can substantially damage context comprehension in models trained from scratch. Systematic ablations indicate that these tokens act as distractors. The placeholders needed to generate an answer can therefore interfere with the model's ability to process the information needed for that answer.

To address this behavior, the authors introduce a mask-agnostic training loss that encourages predictions to stay consistent as the number of appended masks changes. Fine-tuning with the objective substantially reduces the distracting effect and improves robustness. The findings show why bidirectional attention alone does not ensure uniform context use and identify mask-count sensitivity as a concrete training and evaluation concern.
summary.tldr: Generation masks can distract diffusion language models from context, and a mask-agnostic fine-tuning loss substantially reduces this effect.

title: Masks Can Be Distracting: On Context Comprehension in Diffusion Language Models

abstract: This paper deals with stochastic optimization problems involving Markovian noise with a zero-order oracle. We present and analyze a novel derivative-free method for solving such problems in strongly convex smooth and non-smooth settings with both one-point and two-point feedback oracles. Using a randomized batching scheme, we show that when mixing time $\tau$ of the underlying noise sequence is less than the dimension of the problem $d$, the convergence estimates of our method do not depend on $\tau$. This observation provides an efficient way to interact with Markovian stochasticity: instead of invoking the expensive first-order oracle, one should use the zero-order oracle. Finally, we complement our upper bounds with the corresponding lower bounds. This confirms the optimality of our results.
